why_important: A spectral gap is the compact-group analogue of an expander: random words in a few rotations fill SU(2) at the optimal exponential rate. It governs how efficiently a finite universal set of single-qubit gates approximates every gate, and the cases proved so far needed the sum–product machinery of additive combinatorics.
where_it_stands: Proved for elements with algebraic entries (Bourgain–Gamburd, Invent. Math. 171 (2008)), extended to SU(d) (Bourgain–Gamburd, arXiv:1108.6264) and to compact simple Lie groups (Benoist–de Saxcé 2016) [verify], always under an algebraicity or Diophantine condition. Fisher (2006) proved a zero–one law for n ≥ 3, so that either almost every n-tuple has a gap or almost none does [verify]; Pikhurko and Sakamoto (arXiv:2603.17869, 2026) proved the zero–one law for n = 2. The almost-every statement is open.

title: Critical exponents and scaling limit of the three-dimensional self-avoiding walk
domain_name: Lattice statistical mechanics (Ising, Potts, O(n), gauge fields, polymers, spin glasses)
statement: For the uniformly distributed n-step self-avoiding walk ω on Z³ started at the origin, there are exponents ν and γ such that E|ω(n)|² = n^{2ν + o(1)} and c_n = μ^n n^{γ − 1 + o(1)}, where c_n is the number of such walks and μ the connective constant; moreover there is a normalisation a_n = n^{ν + o(1)} such that the linearly interpolated path t ↦ ω(nt)/a_n converges in distribution, uniformly on compact time intervals, to a nondegenerate continuum random curve.
statement_caveat: Numerically ν = 0.58759700(40) (Clisby–Dünweg 2016) and γ = 1.15695300(95) (Clisby 2017) [verify], close to but not equal to Flory's ν = 3/5. The continuum limit has no candidate description: unlike two dimensions (SLE(8/3), T003) there is no conformal-invariance prediction to aim at. T015 asks for the inequality E|ω(n)|² ≥ c n, a different statement that does not follow from the existence of ν.
source: N. Madras and G. Slade, The Self-Avoiding Walk, Birkhäuser (1993) [verify]; R. Bauerschmidt, H. Duminil-Copin, J. Goodman and G. Slade, Lectures on self-avoiding walks, arXiv:1206.2092 (2012)
locator: Bauerschmidt–Duminil-Copin–Goodman–Slade, arXiv:1206.2092, Section 1.6.3
why_important: The self-avoiding walk is the standard model of a linear polymer in a good solvent, and three dimensions is the physical case. Proving that its critical exponents exist below dimension four is one of the central open problems of the subject.
where_it_stands: For d ≥ 5 the walk is diffusive with a Brownian scaling limit (Hara–Slade 1992). In three dimensions it is known that the walk is subballistic, E|ω(n)|² = o(n²) (Duminil-Copin–Hammond 2013), and the counting bound c_n ≤ μ^n exp(O(n^{2/5} log n)) goes back to Kesten (1964; Madras–Slade, Theorem 3.3.1) [verify]; the e^{o(√n)} improvement of the Hammersley–Welsh bound by Hutchcroft (arXiv:1708.09460) matters in two dimensions. The existence of ν and γ, and any scaling limit, are open.

title: Logarithmic corrections at the critical point of the four-dimensional Ising model
domain_name: Lattice statistical mechanics (Ising, Potts, O(n), gauge fields, polymers, spin glasses)
statement: For the nearest-neighbour Ising model on Z⁴, as β ↑ β_c the susceptibility, the correlation length (the inverse exponential decay rate of the two-point function) and the specific heat satisfy χ(β) ~ A t^{−1} |log t|^{1/3}, ξ(β) ~ B t^{−1/2} |log t|^{1/6} and C(β) ~ D |log t|^{1/3}, where t = β_c − β; at β_c the two-point function decays like c|x|^{−2}, without a logarithmic factor.
statement_caveat: These are the one-component cases of the renormalisation-group predictions for the four-dimensional n-component |φ|⁴ model, whose logarithm exponents are (n + 2)/(n + 8), (n + 2)/(2(n + 8)) and (4 − n)/(n + 8). The self-avoiding walk is the case n = 0 (T043).
source: F. J. Wegner and E. K. Riedel, Logarithmic corrections to the molecular-field behavior of critical and tricritical systems, Phys. Rev. B 7 (1973) 248–256 [verify]; M. Aizenman and H. Duminil-Copin, Marginal triviality of the scaling limits of critical 4D Ising and φ⁴₄ models, Ann. of Math. 194 (2021), arXiv:1912.07973
why_important: Dimension four is the upper critical dimension of the Ising model, where mean-field behaviour holds up to logarithms; the logarithms are the visible trace of the marginal triviality of φ⁴₄, and deriving them for the lattice Ising model itself, rather than for a weakly coupled model, would be a renormalisation-group computation at strong coupling.
where_it_stands: The critical scaling limit in four dimensions is Gaussian (Aizenman–Duminil-Copin 2021), and mean-field bounds hold up to logarithmic factors; neither gives the logarithms. The predicted logarithms are proved for the weakly coupled n-component |φ|⁴ model (Hara–Tasaki 1987; Bauerschmidt–Brydges–Slade 2014) [verify] and for the weakly self-avoiding walk, by rigorous renormalisation group; for the nearest-neighbour Ising model they are open. Simulations disagree about the specific heat: Lundow and Markström (arXiv:2209.05292) conclude that it stays bounded at criticality and that the Ising and φ⁴ models are in different classes, while Li, Xiao, Zhou and Fang (arXiv:2408.15230) report finite-size evidence for the predicted logarithmic corrections.

title: Absence of a spin-glass phase in the two-dimensional Edwards–Anderson model
domain_name: Lattice statistical mechanics (Ising, Potts, O(n), gauge fields, polymers, spin glasses)
statement: For the Edwards–Anderson model on Z² with Hamiltonian H(σ) = −Σ_{x∼y} J_xy σ_x σ_y, iid standard Gaussian couplings J_xy and no external field, at every inverse temperature β < ∞ there is, for almost every realisation of the couplings, a unique infinite-volume Gibbs measure, and its correlations decay exponentially.
statement_caveat: This is the expected picture of a transition only at zero temperature, with a correlation length that diverges as the temperature tends to 0. Uniqueness is the strong form; the weaker statement that the Edwards–Anderson order parameter vanishes at every positive temperature is also open [verify]. Ground states (β = ∞) are a different question (T052, retired: a claimed proof for the periodic-boundary metastate).
source: C. M. Newman and D. L. Stein, Spin Glasses and Complexity, Princeton University Press (2013) [verify]; A. Bovier, Statistical Mechanics of Disordered Systems, Cambridge University Press (2006) [verify]
why_important: Two dimensions is the one finite dimension in which the physics of short-range spin glasses is settled numerically, with no transition at positive temperature; a proof would separate the two-dimensional model rigorously from the three-dimensional one, where a positive-temperature transition is expected (T025).
where_it_stands: Uniqueness is known at high temperature and in one dimension. In two dimensions the results concern ground states: uniqueness of the ground-state pair on the half-plane (Arguin–Damron–Newman–Stein 2010) [verify], and Newman and Stein (arXiv:2510.27507v2, revised 2026) claim that in two dimensions the metastate generated by, for example, periodic boundary conditions is unique and supported on a single pair of spin-reversed ground states (T052). No uniqueness or decay result is known at low positive temperature. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment).

title: The value of the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant
domain_name: Stochastic and geometric probability
statement: If X_1, X_2, … are independent uniform points in the unit square and L_n is the length of the shortest closed tour through X_1, …, X_n, then L_n/√n → β almost surely (Beardwood, Halton and Hammersley 1959). Determine β; numerically β ≈ 0.7124.
statement_caveat: No closed form for β is known or conjectured, so the row asks for the value, or for any description of β beyond simulation. In dimension d the analogous constants are predicted to satisfy β_d ~ √(d/(2πe)) as d → ∞ (Percus–Martin) [verify].
source: J. Beardwood, J. H. Halton and J. M. Hammersley, The shortest path through many points, Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 55 (1959) 299–327; J. M. Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, SIAM (1997) [verify]
why_important: It is the founding theorem of the probabilistic analysis of combinatorial optimisation (Karp's partitioning algorithm for the travelling salesman problem rests on it), and its constant has resisted every method; the value would require understanding the local structure of optimal tours, which statistical physicists treat with the cavity method.
where_it_stands: Beardwood, Halton and Hammersley proved 0.625 ≤ β ≤ 0.9212 [verify]; later work (Steinerberger 2015; Gaudio–Jaillet 2020) [verify] brought this to 0.6277 ≤ β ≤ 0.90367, and Dong and Cao (arXiv:2610.02809, October 2026) prove 0.6421 ≤ β ≤ 0.8810, with 0.6536 ≤ β ≤ 0.8749 holding with probability at least 1 − 2·10⁻⁴ over their importance-sampling procedure (a randomized bound, not a deterministic one). Simulations give β ≈ 0.7124 (Johnson–McGeoch–Rothberg 1996; Percus–Martin 1996) [verify]. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a famous constant rather than a conjecture.

title: The strange attractor of the Hénon map at the classical parameters
domain_name: Ergodic theory and stationary processes
statement: The Hénon map H(x, y) = (1 − a x² + y, b x) with a = 1.4, b = 0.3 has a strange attractor carrying a unique SRB (physical) measure μ: for Lebesgue-almost every initial point z in its basin the empirical measures (1/n) Σ_{k<n} δ_{H^k(z)} converge to μ, and μ has a positive Lyapunov exponent.
statement_caveat: The competing possibility usually discussed is that the observed attractor is a stable periodic orbit of very long period, which simulations cannot rule out; for the same reason the question is not settled by computation.
source: M. Hénon, A two-dimensional mapping with a strange attractor, Comm. Math. Phys. 50 (1976) 69–77; M. Benedicks and L. Carleson, The dynamics of the Hénon map, Ann. of Math. 133 (1991) 73–169
why_important: The Hénon map is the standard example of a strange attractor in a dissipative system, and its description by an SRB measure is the model case of the programme, going back to Sinai, Ruelle and Bowen, that describes chaotic dynamics by invariant probability measures and their limit theorems.
where_it_stands: Benedicks and Carleson proved that for small b and a positive-measure set of a near 2 the map has a strange attractor, and Benedicks and Young (1993) constructed SRB measures for those parameters; Wang and Young extended the theory to wider classes of rank-one attractors [verify]. By Newhouse's theory of homoclinic tangencies, parameters at which the map has periodic sinks accumulate on such parameters (under that theory's hypotheses) [verify], so the classical values cannot be reached by perturbation. Computer-assisted work at the classical parameters locates a trapping region and many periodic orbits (Galias–Tucker 2015) [verify] without deciding the question. Open.
note: Fame as a probability problem borderline (my judgment): a problem of smooth ergodic theory.

title: Amenability of Thompson's group F (Kesten's criterion)
domain_name: Random walks, Markov chains and mixing
statement: Let F = ⟨x_0, x_1 | [x_0 x_1^{−1}, x_0^{−1} x_1 x_0], [x_0 x_1^{−1}, x_0^{−2} x_1 x_0²]⟩ be Richard Thompson's group, and p_{2n} the probability that simple random walk on F with steps x_0^{±1}, x_1^{±1} is at the identity at time 2n. Decide whether p_{2n}^{1/(2n)} → 1, that is, whether the spectral radius of the walk is 1; by Kesten's theorem this holds if and only if F is amenable.
statement_caveat: The question is usually posed in group-theoretic language (Geoghegan 1979) [verify]; it is on this list because Kesten's criterion makes it a question about return probabilities of a random walk, and numerical attacks on it are random-walk computations. Neither answer is proved.
source: R. Geoghegan, question of 1979 recorded in problem lists on infinite groups [verify]; H. Kesten, Symmetric random walks on groups, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 92 (1959) 336–354; V. Guba, Amenability problem for Thompson's group F: state of the art, arXiv:2305.07113
why_important: F has no free subgroups, so if it is not amenable it is a natural finitely presented counterexample to the von Neumann–Day problem, far simpler than the known ones; if it is amenable it is amenable without being elementary amenable. As a random-walk problem it asks for the exponential decay rate of return probabilities on one explicit Cayley graph.
where_it_stands: F has no free subgroup (Brin–Squier 1985) and is not elementary amenable (Chou 1980) [verify]. Estimates of the cogrowth and of the norm of the Markov operator, partly computer-assisted (Elder–Rechnitzer–Janse van Rensburg; Haagerup–Haagerup–Ramirez-Solano) [verify], and density estimates for finite subgraphs of the Cayley graph of F (Guba, arXiv:2305.07113, Theorem 2.7, finite subgraphs of average degree above 3.5 out of the 4 that amenability requires in the limit) [verify] have not decided the question. Open.
note: Fame as a probability problem borderline (my judgment): a group-theory problem with a random-walk formulation.

title: Local universality of the two-dimensional Coulomb gas at every temperature
domain_name: Random matrices and random operators
statement: Let x_1, …, x_N ∈ R² have joint density proportional to exp(−β H_N(x)), where H_N(x) = Σ_{i<j} −log|x_i − x_j| + N Σ_i V(x_i), β > 0 is fixed and V is smooth and grows fast enough at infinity. Let z be an interior point of the support of the equilibrium measure at which its density m(z) is positive. Then the rescaled configuration {√(N m(z)) (x_i − z)} converges in law as N → ∞, and the limit point process depends on β alone, not on V or on z.
statement_caveat: At β = 2 the gas is the eigenvalue law of the random normal matrix model, a determinantal process, and local universality is proved there (Ameur–Hedenmalm–Makarov, Duke Math. J. 159 (2011); Hedenmalm–Wennman, Acta Math. 227 (2021); both as cited by Serfaty): the bulk limit is the infinite Ginibre point process scaled to unit intensity. For V(x) = |x|²/2 the gas at β = 2 is the Ginibre ensemble itself, the eigenvalues of an N × N matrix with independent complex Gaussian entries of variance 1/N. For β ≠ 2 no limit has been identified, and convergence along the full sequence, rather than along subsequences, is part of the question. The analogous statement for one-dimensional β-ensembles is a theorem (Bourgade–Erdős–Yau, Duke Math. J. 163 (2014) 1127–1190). Crystallisation of the gas at low temperature is a separate question (compare T044).
source: S. Serfaty, Lectures on Coulomb and Riesz gases, arXiv:2407.21194 (2024)
locator: Serfaty, arXiv:2407.21194, Section 1.3 'Questions', paragraph 'Universality, phase portrait, phase transitions', printed p. 17: that the local arrangement of the particles does not depend on V 'has been proven only in the one-dimensional logarithmic case of β-ensembles …, and in the two-dimensional Coulomb case only for β = 2'
why_important: The two-dimensional one-component plasma is the basic classical model of a charged gas, and at β = 2 it is the eigenvalue process of non-Hermitian random matrices. Local universality would say that its microscopic structure at a given temperature is the same at every bulk point and for every confining potential, the planar counterpart of bulk universality for one-dimensional β-ensembles.
where_it_stands: Proved at β = 2 only. For every β > 0 there are a large deviation principle for the empirical field (Leblé–Serfaty, Invent. Math. 210 (2017) 645–757), local laws down to the microscopic scale with the existence of limit point processes along subsequences, generalising the Ginibre process (Armstrong–Serfaty, arXiv:1906.09848), and Gaussian fluctuations of smooth linear statistics, the electrostatic potential converging to a Gaussian free field (Leblé–Serfaty, arXiv:1609.08088; Bauerschmidt–Bourgade–Nikula–Yau, arXiv:1609.08582). Recent exact results are again at β = 2 (Nagao, arXiv:2603.26280, correlation functions on an annulus; Ma–Meng, arXiv:2608.27880, edge statistics for radial potentials). Uniqueness of the limit and its independence of V and z are open for every β ≠ 2. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): posed prominently in Serfaty's lecture notes (Courant, ENS and the 2024 Saint-Flour school) and well known among workers on Coulomb gases and non-Hermitian random matrices, less so beyond.

title: Existence of Kesten's incipient infinite cluster in three dimensions
domain_name: Percolation and spatial random graphs
statement: For critical Bernoulli bond percolation on Z³, with B_n = [−n, n]³, the conditional laws P_{p_c}( · | 0 ↔ ∂B_n) converge as n → ∞, on events that depend on finitely many edges, to a limiting law: the incipient infinite cluster.
statement_caveat: Kesten defined the incipient infinite cluster in the plane both by this limit and as the limit of P_p( · | 0 ↔ ∞) as p ↓ p_c, and proved that the two limits exist and agree. If θ(p_c) > 0 on Z³ the limit above exists trivially and equals P_{p_c}( · | 0 ↔ ∞); the content of the question is the case θ(p_c) = 0, which is itself open (T001). The three-dimensional critical exponents are T087, and random walk on the planar incipient cluster is T102.
source: H. Kesten, The incipient infinite cluster in two-dimensional percolation, Probab. Theory Related Fields 73 (1986) 369–394; D. Basu and A. Sapozhnikov, Kesten's incipient infinite cluster and quasi-multiplicativity of crossing probabilities, arXiv:1603.06884
locator: Basu–Sapozhnikov, arXiv:1603.06884v2, p. 2: 'the existence of Kesten's IIC on Z^d for d ≥ 3 is still an open problem'; Theorem 1.1 (existence under (A1), at most one infinite cluster at every p, and (A2), quasi-multiplicativity of crossing probabilities near p_c) and Comment 5 on p. 3 ((A2) is believed to hold on Z^d for d < 6 and to fail for d > 6)
why_important: The incipient infinite cluster is critical percolation seen from a typical point of a large cluster. Random walk on it is the model of anomalous diffusion at criticality (the Alexander–Orbach question), and its existence is a first step towards any description of the large critical clusters in three dimensions, where neither conformal invariance nor the lace expansion is available.
where_it_stands: Known in two dimensions (Kesten 1986; further constructions by Járai, Ann. Probab. 31 (2003); a short quantitative construction by Hillairet, arXiv:2509.18852) and in high dimensions through the lace expansion (van der Hofstad–Járai, J. Stat. Phys. 114 (2004); Heydenreich–van der Hofstad–Hulshof, J. Stat. Phys. 155 (2014), arXiv:1108.4325; Chatterjee–Chinmay–Hanson–Sosoe, arXiv:2502.10882; a bi-infinite version by Cabezas–Fribergh–Heydenreich–Járai, arXiv:2506.06559). Basu–Sapozhnikov (arXiv:1603.06884) prove existence on slabs Z² × {0, …, k}^{d−2}, and on any bounded-degree graph with at most one infinite cluster, which holds on Z³, on which crossing probabilities are quasi-multiplicative; they expect quasi-multiplicativity on Z^d for d < 6, but it is not proved for Z³. Analogues are known for the FK–Ising model on Z^d, d ≥ 3 (Panis, arXiv:2406.15243) and for the metric-graph Gaussian free field (Cai–Ding, arXiv:2412.05709). Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a standard open problem of three-dimensional critical percolation, ranked high by the w673 audit; it sits next to T001 and T087.

title: The scaling limit of the three-dimensional uniform spanning tree
domain_name: Branching processes, trees and genealogies
statement: Let U be the uniform spanning tree of Z³ and β ≈ 1.624 the growth exponent of three-dimensional loop-erased random walk. Show that the rescaled trees (U, δ^β d_U, δ³ μ_U, δ φ_U, ρ_U), with d_U the intrinsic metric, μ_U the counting measure, φ_U the embedding into R³ and ρ_U the root at the origin, converge in law as δ → 0 to a single limit, in the Gromov–Hausdorff-type topology on measured, rooted, spatial trees used by Angel, Croydon, Hernandez-Torres and Shiraishi.
statement_caveat: Tightness, and convergence along one particular sequence of scales, are known; what is missing is convergence along all scales, that is, uniqueness of the subsequential limits. The growth exponent β itself is the subject of T103. Convergence statements for three-dimensional loop-erased random walk do not transfer to the whole tree without a joint argument for the branches built by Wilson's algorithm.
source: O. Angel, D. A. Croydon, S. Hernandez-Torres and D. Shiraishi, Scaling limits of the three-dimensional uniform spanning tree and associated random walk, Ann. Probab. 49 (2021) 3032–3105, arXiv:2003.09055
locator: Angel–Croydon–Hernandez-Torres–Shiraishi, arXiv:2003.09055, Section 1.2 ('uniqueness of the scaling limit is as yet unproved') and the definition (1) in Section 1.1 (read by the w673 audit)
why_important: In two dimensions the uniform spanning tree converges to an object described by SLE(8) and SLE(2) (Lawler–Schramm–Werner). In three dimensions there is no conformal invariance, and the tree is one of the few three-dimensional critical models where a full scaling limit is within reach, through Kozma's scaling limit of loop-erased random walk and Wilson's algorithm; it would give the first scaling limit of a critical spatial tree in three dimensions.
where_it_stands: Tightness and convergence along a particular sequence of scales, with Hausdorff dimension 3/β for the intrinsic metric of any limit, and the walk dimension, spectral dimension and heat-kernel estimates for the limiting diffusion (Angel–Croydon–Hernandez-Torres–Shiraishi, arXiv:2003.09055). Li, Liu and Shiraishi (arXiv:2605.19419, May 2026) obtain sharp tail exponents for the past of the origin and apply them to three-dimensional sandpile avalanches; they do not address uniqueness of the limit. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a precise question from a major paper, well known to people working on three-dimensional loop-erased walk and spanning trees, less so beyond; a neighbour of T103.
retired_reason: REPORTED SOLVED: S. Hernández-Torres, X. Li and D. Shiraishi, Sharp one-point estimates and Minkowski content for the scaling limit of three-dimensional loop-erased random walk, arXiv:2403.07256v2 (21 Dec 2025), Remark 1.10(1), p. 9: with their Theorems 1.3, 1.7 and 1.8, 'the convergence of the scaling limit of the UST on Z3 now holds for arbitrary scaling', in the Gromov–Hausdorff–Prohorov topology with the locally uniform topology for the embedding used by Angel–Croydon–Hernández-Torres–Shiraishi. The restriction to dyadic scales in that paper came from its loop-erased random walk inputs (Remark 1.2 there). The value of the growth exponent stays open (T103).

title: The upper tail problem for subgraph counts (the 'infamous upper tail')
domain_name: Random graphs and random constraint satisfaction
statement: For a fixed graph H with e_H ≥ 1 edges let X_H be the number of copies of H in the binomial random graph G(n, p), and let m_H be the maximum of e_F/v_F over the subgraphs F of H. Determine, for every H, every fixed ε > 0 and every p = p(n) with n^{−1/m_H} ≪ p and (1 + ε) p^{e_H} ≤ 1, the order of magnitude of −log P(X_H ≥ (1 + ε) E X_H), and where possible its asymptotics.
statement_caveat: The first condition puts p above the threshold for the appearance of H; the second excludes p so close to 1 that (1 + ε) E X_H exceeds the number of copies of H in K_n, where the probability is 0. Janson, Oleszkiewicz and Ruciński determined −log P up to a factor of order log(1/p) for every H, which settles constant p. DeMarco and Kahn (2011) conjectured a formula for the order of magnitude for every H, and Šileikis and Warnke disproved it near the appearance threshold with an infinite family of balanced graphs (arXiv:1809.09595). For p → 0 one also asks when log P is asymptotic to the solution of a mean-field variational problem, and which structures (planted cliques or hubs) a graph conditioned on the upper tail contains.
source: S. Janson and A. Ruciński, The infamous upper tail, Random Structures Algorithms 20 (2002) 317–342; S. Janson, K. Oleszkiewicz and A. Ruciński, Upper tails for subgraph counts in random graphs, Israel J. Math. 142 (2004) 61–92
locator: Šileikis–Warnke, arXiv:1809.09595, Problem 1 on p. 1 (the order of magnitude for fixed ε and arbitrary p; abstract: 'this so-called infamous upper tail problem remains a challenging testbed for concentration inequalities') and Conjecture 1 on p. 2 (the DeMarco–Kahn formula for n^{−1/m_H} < p ≤ (1 + ε)^{−1/e_H}, refuted by their Theorem 1)
why_important: It is the standard test of concentration inequalities for sums of dependent indicators. The lower tail is governed by Janson's inequality, but the upper tail of even the triangle count resisted martingale and polynomial-concentration methods for years, and its resolution for cliques came from the nonlinear large deviation theory and the entropic-stability method developed largely for this problem.
where_it_stands: Solved for cliques, and for arithmetic progressions of fixed length in random subsets of the integers, by the entropic-stability method, with a short solution for triangles when n^{−1} log n ≪ p ≪ 1 (Harel–Mousset–Samotij, arXiv:1904.08212), after work of Chatterjee and of DeMarco–Kahn on triangles (Random Structures Algorithms 40 (2012)) and the nonlinear large deviation theory of Chatterjee–Dembo (Adv. Math. 299 (2016)) and Eldan (Geom. Funct. Anal. 28 (2018)), refined by Cook–Dembo and Augeri [verify]. Progress for regular H (Bhattacharya–Ganguly–Lubetzky–Zhao, Adv. Math. 319 (2017); Harel–Mousset–Samotij); stars in the sparse range (Akhmejanova–Šileikis, arXiv:2501.03404); irregular H for n^{−1/Δ} ≪ p ≪ 1 and the Poisson range for strictly balanced H, with the intermediate range settled for stars (Basak–Karmakar, arXiv:2503.05311, v4 September 2026). Hypergraph versions are also studied (Cook–Nguyen, arXiv:2509.26569). The order of magnitude for general H over all p has been open since the DeMarco–Kahn formula failed. Open.
note: Fame: the name 'infamous upper tail' is standard in probabilistic combinatorics; the problem is well known there.

title: Gaussian free field fluctuations of lozenge tilings of general domains (Kenyon–Okounkov)
domain_name: SLE, Gaussian fields, Liouville quantum gravity and random planar maps
statement: Let D be a bounded simply connected planar domain with boundary height data h: ∂D → R that admit a limit shape. Let D_N be tileable domains of the triangular lattice such that N^{−1} D_N approximates D, let H_N be the integer-valued height function of a uniformly random lozenge tiling of D_N, whose rescaled boundary values N^{−1} H_N(N ·) converge to h, and let L be the liquid region of the limit shape. Then the centred height H_N(N u) − E H_N(N u), u ∈ L, converges to π^{−1/2} times the Gaussian free field on L with Dirichlet boundary conditions in the Kenyon–Okounkov complex structure, that is, the pull-back by a uniformising map φ: L → C₊ of the field on the upper half-plane with covariance (2π)^{−1} log|(z − w̄)/(z − w)|.
statement_caveat: Convergence may be asked in the sense of moments at distinct points, as in the polygonal case, or as random distributions. If L has several components, the Dirichlet field on L is a family of independent fields on the components (Huang, Remark 2.7, expects exactly this). Points at which the boundary data force the height are frozen, and the tiling then splits into separate domains. On non-simply-connected domains the prediction fails as stated: a discrete Gaussian component appears (Borot–Gorin–Guionnet, arXiv:2601.16377). Laslier (arXiv:2102.05544) shows that for every limit shape without frozen regions some sequence of domains has that limit shape and fluctuations converging to a variant of the Gaussian free field; the question is for a given domain. The six-vertex analogue is T063.
source: R. Kenyon and A. Okounkov, Limit shapes and the complex Burgers equation, Acta Math. 199 (2007) 263–302, arXiv:math-ph/0507007; R. Kenyon, Height fluctuations in the honeycomb dimer model, Comm. Math. Phys. 281 (2008) 675–709
locator: Huang, arXiv:2609.04789, Conjecture 2.3 on p. 12 (the prediction, attributed to Kenyon–Okounkov 2007 and Kenyon 2008), with the normalisation of (2.13)–(2.15) and Theorem 2.8 on pp. 13–14 (the polygonal case, under Assumption 2.6)
why_important: Uniform lozenge tilings, equivalently dimers on the hexagonal lattice or stepped surfaces, are the basic exactly solvable model of random surfaces. The prediction is that their fluctuations are universal, a Gaussian free field whose conformal structure is set by the limit shape, and it is the model case of the expected Gaussian free field behaviour of random height functions.
where_it_stands: Proved for a class of domains without frozen regions (Kenyon, Comm. Math. Phys. 281 (2008)), for families of polygons by Petrov (Ann. Probab. 43 (2015) 1–43), Bufetov–Gorin (Adv. Math. 338 (2018)) and Huang (arXiv:2011.01751, polygons with one horizontal upper boundary edge), and, in the sense of moments at distinct points, for the domains N P with P any simply connected polygon whose 3d sides cycle through the three lattice directions, provided the liquid region is non-empty and connected and the boundary data force the height at no point (Huang, arXiv:2609.04789, 4 Sep 2026, Theorem 2.8 under Assumption 2.6). Domains that are not polygons, general approximating sequences, and polygons with a disconnected liquid region or a non-empty forced set are not covered. Open.
note: Fame borderline-to-strong (my judgment): a central prediction of integrable probability. Its polygonal case was proved in September 2026; the row keeps the general domain, which is how the prediction was made.

title: Ibragimov's conjecture: the central limit theorem for φ-mixing sequences
domain_name: Ergodic theory and stationary processes
statement: Let (X_k, k ∈ Z) be a strictly stationary sequence that is φ-mixing (uniformly mixing), with E X_0² < ∞ and Var(X_1 + … + X_n) → ∞. Then (S_n − E S_n)/√Var(S_n) converges in law to the standard normal distribution, where S_n = X_1 + … + X_n.
statement_caveat: Here φ(n) is the supremum of |P(B | A) − P(B)| over events A with P(A) > 0 measurable with respect to the past up to time 0 and events B measurable with respect to the future from time n, and φ-mixing means φ(n) → 0, with no rate. Iosifescu conjectured that under the same hypotheses the weak invariance principle holds. Under the weaker strong (α-) mixing condition the central limit theorem can fail: Herrndorf constructed strictly stationary strongly mixing sequences that do not satisfy it (Ann. Probab. 11 (1983) 809–813) [verify the exact hypotheses].
source: I. A. Ibragimov and Yu. V. Linnik, Independent and Stationary Sequences of Random Variables, Wolters-Noordhoff, Groningen (1971), p. 393, problem (3) [verify]; R. C. Bradley, Basic properties of strong mixing conditions. A survey and some open questions, Probab. Surveys 2 (2005) 107–144, arXiv:math/0511078
locator: Bradley, arXiv:math/0511078, Section 2.3, p. 114 of the journal pagination (read 14 Oct): 'These conjectures remain unsolved.'
why_important: φ-mixing is one of the classical mixing conditions under which limit theorems for dependent sequences are proved. The conjecture asks whether uniform mixing alone, with no rate of mixing and no growth condition beyond Var S_n → ∞, already gives the central limit theorem, as finite variance does for independent sequences. It is tied to an open question in the hierarchy of mixing conditions: if φ-mixing implied ρ*-mixing (Bradley's Question 2), the conjecture would follow from known central limit theorems under ρ*-mixing.
where_it_stands: Peligrad (Ann. Probab. 13 (1985) 1304–1313, Corollary 2.2) proved the central limit theorem and the invariance principle under the stronger hypothesis lim inf Var(S_n)/n > 0. Bradley's survey records both conjectures as unsolved and connects them with his Question 2; Bradley (1999, 'Can a theorem of Csáki and Fischer provide a key to Ibragimov's conjecture?', Bolyai Soc. Math. Stud. 9, 11–42) examines one approach. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a classical conjecture of the limit theory of dependent sequences, well known to specialists in mixing conditions, less so elsewhere.
retired_reason: REPORTED DISPROVED: a strictly stationary, centred, φ-mixing sequence with finite second moments and Var(S_n) → ∞ whose normalised sums S_n/√Var(S_n) converge to 0 in probability along a subsequence, with a Lean 4 proof of the negation of the Formal Conjectures statement (T. Adamczewski, proof written by the AI system GPT-6 Astra, https://github.com/tadamcz/phi-mixing-clt, September 2026, unrefereed). The submitted statement and definitions are identical to the challenge file, which states the conjecture as here (the φ coefficient over all past and future σ-fields of the sequence, centring, E X_0² < ∞, Var(S_n) → ∞, weak convergence to N(0, 1)) for a sequence indexed by N; nothing is lost, since a strictly stationary sequence indexed by N extends to one indexed by Z with the same finite-dimensional laws and the same φ coefficients; the recorded comparator run reports that Lean's default kernel accepts the disproof with only the standard axioms. If the proof stands it also refutes Iosifescu's invariance principle. Not yet independently rebuilt; restore the row if it fails.

title: Positive recurrence of semimartingale reflecting Brownian motion in four and more dimensions
domain_name: Queueing and stochastic networks
statement: Let Z be a semimartingale reflecting Brownian motion (SRBM) in the orthant R^d_+ with drift θ, nonsingular covariance matrix Σ and reflection matrix R (completely-S, so that Z exists and is unique in law). Find necessary and sufficient conditions on (θ, Σ, R) for Z to be positive recurrent, that is, for the expected time to hit any open neighbourhood of the origin to be finite from every starting state, in every dimension d ≥ 4.
statement_caveat: Sufficient conditions exist in every dimension, for example the fluid criterion of Dupuis and Williams (every path of the associated fluid model is attracted to the origin). In d = 3 this criterion is also necessary, but Bramson's examples in d = 6 show that it is not necessary in high dimensions, so a different kind of condition is needed.
source: M. Bramson, J. G. Dai and J. M. Harrison, Positive recurrence of reflecting Brownian motion in three dimensions, Ann. Appl. Probab. 20 (2010) 753–783, arXiv:1009.5746
locator: Bramson–Dai–Harrison, arXiv:1009.5746, abstract: 'The problem of recurrence classification for SRBMs in four and higher dimensions remains open.'
why_important: SRBMs are the heavy-traffic diffusion limits of open multiclass queueing networks, and their positive recurrence is the diffusion counterpart of network stability. The instability examples for multiclass networks (Rybko–Stolyar, Bramson's FIFO networks) show that the usual traffic condition is not enough, and the SRBM question asks for the right condition in the limit.
where_it_stands: Settled for d = 2, and for d = 3 by Bramson, Dai and Harrison, who, building on El Kharroubi, Ben Tahar and Yaacoubi (Stochastics Stochastics Rep. 68 (2000); Math. Methods Oper. Res. 56 (2002)), give necessary and sufficient conditions that are simple to check; in d = 3 positive recurrence holds if and only if every fluid path is attracted to the origin. In d = 6 Bramson (arXiv:1010.1751) gives positive recurrent examples with a divergent linear fluid path. Recent work concerns stationary distributions in low dimension (Flin, arXiv:2604.27951, the half-plane with two-sided reflection), not the classification. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a well-known question in applied probability and queueing theory, less known outside it.

title: The capacity region of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
domain_name: Statistics, optimal transport and information inequalities
statement: For the two-user Gaussian interference channel Y_1 = X_1 + √a X_2 + Z_1, Y_2 = √b X_1 + X_2 + Z_2, with independent standard Gaussian noise and average power constraints P_1, P_2, determine the capacity region, in particular for weak interference (a, b < 1) and mixed interference (a < 1 ≤ b).
statement_caveat: The question is for a computable, single-letter description; the multi-letter Han–Kobayashi region is known to be the capacity region (Liu, arXiv:2209.00163, p. 2). A long-standing expectation is that the Han–Kobayashi scheme, in which each receiver decodes part of the interfering message and treats the rest as noise, achieves capacity with suitable Gaussian inputs. Unrefereed preprints claim the capacity region of the one-sided channel (Vaezi–Poor, arXiv:1509.02953, 2015), a solution for weak interference (Khandani, arXiv:2011.12981 and arXiv:2501.14941, v13 of 24 Sep 2026) and a finite characterisation of general multiuser capacity regions with the interference channel as the main example (Cioffi, arXiv:2609.17212, 15 Sep 2026); later work, for example Liu (arXiv:2209.00163), still treats even the one-sided (Z) channel as open.
source: T. S. Han and K. Kobayashi, A new achievable rate region for the interference channel, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 27 (1981) 49–60; R. Etkin, D. Tse and H. Wang, Gaussian interference channel capacity to within one bit, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 54 (2008) 5534–5562
locator: Liu, arXiv:2209.00163, Section I, pp. 1–2: the interference channel's 'single-letter rate region has remained open after decades of efforts', and it is unknown whether Gaussian inputs are optimal for the Han–Kobayashi bound on the Gaussian Z-interference channel, which would resolve 'the longstanding open problem about the rate region'
why_important: It is the simplest network in which two independent transmissions interfere, the basic model for wireless systems with uncoordinated users, and one of the oldest open problems of network information theory; the probabilistic content is an optimisation of mutual information over input distributions that is not known to be attained by Gaussian inputs.
where_it_stands: Known: strong and very strong interference (Carleial; Sato; Han–Kobayashi) [verify]; the sum capacity in a noisy-interference part of the weak regime, where treating interference as noise is optimal (Shang–Kramer–Chen, Motahari–Khandani, Annapureddy–Veeravalli, 2009) [verify]; the whole region to within one bit (Etkin–Tse–Wang 2008). Temporally correlated Gaussian inputs do not enlarge the Han–Kobayashi region with Gaussian inputs (Nair–Ng, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 65 (2019) 1372–1374). For the Gaussian Z-interference channel, Costa, Nair, Ng and Wang conjectured that a Gaussian stationary point is the global optimiser of an inequality whose truth would make the Han–Kobayashi region with Gaussian inputs optimal there; Liu (arXiv:2209.00163) gave counterexamples in some regimes, which make Gaussian inputs suboptimal for the Han–Kobayashi region under constant power control, showed that with variable power control the Gaussian optimisers lie in the regime where the stationary point is stable, and proposed an amended conjecture. Local optimality of Gaussian inputs for the Han–Kobayashi bound on the Z-channel is studied by Nair and Zhao (ISIT 2026). Open.
note: Fame: a famous open problem of information theory, included for its probabilistic content (the optimisation of mutual information over input laws); information theory is kept to at most three rows.

title: Relaxation time of the flip walk on triangulations of a convex polygon
domain_name: Random walks, Markov chains and mixing
statement: Let T_n be the set of triangulations of a convex (n+2)-gon, and consider the flip walk on T_n: at each step choose one of the n − 1 diagonals uniformly at random and replace it by the other diagonal of the quadrilateral it bisects (a lazy version keeps the state with probability 1/2). Aldous conjectured that the relaxation time (inverse spectral gap) of this chain is Θ(n^{3/2}).
statement_caveat: The state space is in bijection with binary trees with n internal nodes (the flip is a rotation), so |T_n| is the n-th Catalan number. A lower bound Ω(n^{3/2}) on the mixing time is due to Molloy, Reed and Steiger. The analogous question for triangulations of the sphere or of planar maps, where the walk moves on combinatorial maps rather than on polygon dissections, is different and is not covered here (Budzinski, arXiv:1611.07324, lower bound n^{5/4} for the sphere; Caraceni–Stauffer, arXiv:2001.04166, a polynomial upper bound for edge rotations on planar maps).
source: V. L. Alev, D. Frishberg, M. Sarantis and P. Tetali, Faster mixing for triangulations via transport flows, arXiv:2605.02067 (2026); the conjecture is attributed to D. Aldous [verify the original source]
locator: Alev–Frishberg–Sarantis–Tetali, arXiv:2605.02067v2, abstract: 'The previous state of the art for the mixing time of this chain, due to Eppstein and Frishberg, was Õ(n^3), while the best known lower bound on the mixing time, due to Molloy, Reed, and Steiger, is Ω(n^{3/2}). Our relaxation time bound makes significant progress towards Aldous' conjectured bound of Θ(n^{3/2}) for the relaxation time.'
why_important: The flip walk is the basic local Markov chain on a Catalan family and a standard test case for comparison and multicommodity-flow methods. For two decades the upper bound stayed polynomially far from the conjectured order, so the gap between n^{3/2} and the available bounds measures how well current techniques handle chains whose state space has no product structure.
where_it_stands: McShine and Tetali (1997) proved the first polynomial bound, O(n^5 log n) on the mixing time. Eppstein and Frishberg (arXiv:2207.09972) improved this to O(n^3 log^3 n), the first progress since 1997, using a decomposition into products of smaller associahedra. Alev, Frishberg, Sarantis and Tetali (arXiv:2605.02067) prove Õ(n^2) for the relaxation time and the log-Sobolev time, hence Õ(n^2) mixing. The conjectured order n^{3/2} is not proved. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a well-known conjecture in Markov chain mixing, cited in every paper on the triangulation and associahedron walks.

title: Mixing time of the lozenge-tiling Glauber dynamics on domains with frozen regions
domain_name: Random walks, Markov chains and mixing
statement: Let D be a simply connected planar domain and D_δ its approximation by the triangular lattice of mesh δ, chosen so that D_δ admits lozenge tilings. Consider the continuous-time single-flip Glauber dynamics on lozenge tilings of D_δ, which rotates each hexagon of three lozenges at rate 1 when possible; its stationary law is the uniform measure on tilings. The conjecture is that its mixing time is δ^{−2+o(1)} as δ → 0 for general domains, including those whose limit shape has frozen regions (facets).
statement_caveat: The prediction comes from the heuristic that the height function moves by mean-curvature flow (the Lifshitz law), which gives a time scale δ^{−2} in every dimension. For the hexagon of side N (so δ ~ 1/N), the limit shape has six frozen corners and a disordered region bounded by the inscribed circle; that case is now proved (below). For general domains with facets, and for the related dynamics on domino tilings, the δ^{−2+o(1)} order is not established. Compare T046 (the Lifshitz law for low-temperature Ising Glauber dynamics) and T163 (Gaussian free field fluctuations of lozenge tilings).
source: B. Laslier and F. L. Toninelli, The mixing time of the lozenge tiling Glauber dynamics, Ann. Henri Lebesgue 6 (2023) 907–940, arXiv:2207.01444
locator: Laslier–Toninelli, arXiv:2207.01444, abstract: 'the conjecture T_mix=δ^{-2+o(1)} has been proven, so far, only in the situation where φ is an affine function. In this work, we prove the conjecture under the sole assumption that the limit shape φ contains no frozen regions (facets).' Aggarwal–Toninelli, arXiv:2605.26664, abstract: 'This was predicted to hold on fairly general domains of diameter N (on the basis of the "Lifshitz law" heuristic) but had previously only been established in domains such that the associated limit shape has no frozen facets.'
why_important: Lozenge tilings are the cleanest discrete model of a (2+1)-dimensional random interface, and the mixing time question asks whether the Glauber dynamics relaxes on the diffusive time scale that mean-curvature motion predicts. Frozen regions are the generic situation for polygonal domains, and they are exactly where the existing comparison arguments break down.
where_it_stands: Wilson (Ann. Appl. Probab. 14 (2004)) proved δ^{−2}|log δ| bounds for a non-local lozenge dynamics in which one update can flip of order δ^{−1} tiles. Caputo, Martinelli and Toninelli proved T_mix = δ^{−2+o(1)} for the single-flip dynamics when the limit shape is affine (as cited by Laslier–Toninelli). Laslier and Toninelli (arXiv:2207.01444) proved δ^{−2+o(1)} whenever the limit shape has no frozen regions. Aggarwal and Toninelli (arXiv:2605.26664) proved N^{2+o(1)} for the size-N hexagon by a multi-scale comparison with the limit shape of a volume-tilted tiling. General domains with facets remain unproved. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a recognised conjecture in the dynamics of random interfaces, known to specialists in dimers and Glauber dynamics.

title: Coexistence in the Neuhauser–Pacala spatial Lotka–Volterra model
domain_name: Interacting particle systems, growth and KPZ
statement: In the Neuhauser–Pacala model each site of Z^d carries a plant of type 0 or 1. With f_i(x, ξ) the fraction of neighbours of x (under a fixed symmetric finite-range kernel p) of type i, a type-i plant at x dies at rate f_i + α_i f_{1−i}, where α_0, α_1 ≥ 0 are competition parameters, and is replaced by the type of a neighbour chosen according to p. Conjecture 1 of Neuhauser and Pacala: when α_0 = α_1 < 1, the two types coexist, that is, there is a stationary distribution under which both types have positive density.
statement_caveat: With α_0 = α_1 = 1 the model is the voter model, which clusters in d ≤ 2 and has a one-parameter family of extremal invariant laws in d ≥ 3. The dimensions covered by the conjecture are those in Neuhauser–Pacala's paper [verify; d ≥ 2 is the natural range]. Their Conjecture 2 asks that one type takes over on the other side of the coexistence region near (1, 1). The model is monotone when α_0 ∧ α_1 ≥ 1/2 (Cox–Durrett–Perkins, eq. (1.30), citing Proposition 8.1 of Cox–Perkins).
source: C. Neuhauser and S. W. Pacala, An explicitly spatial version of the Lotka–Volterra model with interspecific competition, Ann. Appl. Probab. 9 (1999) 1226–1259, Conjecture 1
locator: J. T. Cox, R. Durrett and E. A. Perkins, Voter model perturbations and reaction diffusion equations, arXiv:1103.1676, p. 12: 'Neuhauser and Pacala [37] conjectured that coexistence holds for all α0 = α1 < 1 (see Conjecture 1 of that paper) and proved it for αi sufficiently small.'
why_important: The model is a standard example of an interacting particle system that is not attractive in general and whose behaviour is governed by competition rather than by a single threshold, so coexistence cannot be read off from a monotone comparison. It is also the main test case for the theory of voter model perturbations, which connects the particle system to reaction–diffusion equations and to super-Brownian motion with drift.
where_it_stands: Neuhauser and Pacala proved coexistence for α_i small. Cox and Perkins proved coexistence near the voter point (1, 1) (Probab. Theory Related Fields 139 (2007) 89–142 for d ≥ 3; Ann. Appl. Probab. 18 (2008) 747–812, arXiv:0804.0158, for d = 2), and Cox, Durrett and Perkins (arXiv:1103.1676, Theorems 1.8 and 1.9) showed for d ≥ 3 that the coexistence boundary near (1, 1) is asymptotically sharp and proved takeover on the other side, Conjecture 2 near the voter point. Cox and Perkins proved complete convergence theorems for voter model perturbations including Lotka–Volterra models near the voter model in d ≥ 3 (Ann. Appl. Probab. 24 (2014) 150–197, arXiv:1210.0830) and in d = 2 (arXiv:2310.00812). Coexistence for every α_0 = α_1 < 1, away from both corners, is not proved. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a well-known conjecture among researchers on interacting particle systems and spatial ecology models.

title: The Eden model limit shape is not a Euclidean ball in low dimensions
domain_name: Percolation and spatial random graphs
statement: Consider first-passage percolation on Z^d with independent exponential passage times of mean 1 on the edges (equivalently the Eden growth model, or the Richardson model). By the shape theorem the set of sites reached by time t, scaled by 1/t, converges almost surely to a deterministic compact convex set B. Show that for every d ≥ 2, B is not a Euclidean ball.
statement_caveat: The Eden conjecture was the opposite statement, that B is a Euclidean ball; simulations in d = 2 show a shape that looks circular to the eye. B has the symmetries of Z^d and is convex with nonempty interior, but no other qualitative property of B is known for any d ≥ 2 and any non-degenerate distribution (compare T050 on strict convexity and curvature of the limit shape in general FPP, and T095).
source: A. Auffinger, M. Damron and J. Hanson, 50 years of first-passage percolation, University Lecture Series 68, AMS (2017), arXiv:1511.03262, Question 33
locator: Auffinger–Damron–Hanson, arXiv:1511.03262, Section 6.1, p. 130: 'Eden and Richardson observed by simulation that the limit shape looks circular in dimension two. However, one of the most fascinating long-standing questions remains: Question 33. Show that for d ≥ 2, the limit shape of the Eden model is not an Euclidean ball.'
why_important: Identifying the limit shape is the central unsolved problem of first-passage percolation, and the exponential case is the most tractable one because the growing cluster is a Markov process. Ruling out the ball in the plane would be the first rigorous qualitative statement about the shape for a natural model in low dimension.
where_it_stands: Kesten proved that B is not a ball for d > 650,000, using Dhar's asymptotics of the time constant (Dhar 1988; μ(d) d / log d → 1/2). Couronné, Enriquez and Gerin (arXiv:1008.5069) lowered the dimension to d ≥ 35 by constructing short paths. Bertrand and Pertinand (arXiv:1705.08143), pushing Dhar's computation further, report that the Eden conjecture fails for d > 22. No result is known in dimensions 2 to 22. Open.
note: Fame: listed as Question 33 of the Auffinger–Damron–Hanson survey and called there one of the most fascinating long-standing questions of the subject.

title: The planar minimal spanning tree scaling limit is not conformally invariant
domain_name: Percolation and spatial random graphs
statement: Assign independent uniform [0, 1] weights to the edges of a planar lattice (for definiteness the triangular-lattice version used by Garban, Pete and Schramm) with mesh η, and let MST_η be the minimal spanning tree of the whole plane. Garban, Pete and Schramm proved that MST_η has a scaling limit MST_∞ as η → 0, invariant under translations, rotations and scalings. Show that MST_∞ is not conformally invariant, and in particular that it differs from the scaling limit of the uniform spanning tree. Show also that the scaling limit of the invasion percolation tree is not conformally invariant.
statement_caveat: The construction of MST_∞ goes through near-critical percolation, whose scaling limit is conformally covariant rather than invariant; this is the reason non-invariance is expected. The uniform spanning tree limit is conformally invariant and is described by SLE(2) and SLE(8). Physicists had proposed that the minimal spanning tree is in the universality class of dense polymers, which would make its limit conformally invariant (Jacobsen–Read–Saleur, cond-mat/0403277); the simulations cited by Garban–Pete–Schramm point the other way.
source: C. Garban, G. Pete and O. Schramm, The scaling limits of the minimal spanning tree and invasion percolation in the plane, Ann. Probab. 46 (2018) 3501–3557 [verify], arXiv:1309.0269, Conjecture 8.1
locator: Garban–Pete–Schramm, arXiv:1309.0269, Section 8, p. 50, Conjecture 8.1: '(i) Show that MST∞ is not conformally invariant. In particular, show that it is different from the scaling limit of the Uniform Spanning Tree... (ii) Show that InvPerc∞ is not conformally invariant.' The abstract adds: 'However, they are not expected to be conformally invariant.'
why_important: Most planar scaling limits that probabilists can describe are conformally invariant and come with an SLE description; the minimal spanning tree is a natural model whose limit exists and is expected to break that pattern. A proof would need a quantitative handle on how near-critical percolation transforms under conformal maps, which is not available.
where_it_stands: Existence and uniqueness of the limit, its rotation and scaling invariance, and several topological properties (no pinching points, all degrees at most 4, at most countably many points of degree 4, and a trunk of Hausdorff dimension strictly below 7/4) are proved in arXiv:1309.0269, building on the near-critical percolation limit (Garban–Pete–Schramm, arXiv:1008.1378). The conjecture is supported by simulations [Wilson 2004] cited there. No proof of non-invariance has appeared. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a well-known conjecture of Garban, Pete and Schramm, central to the study of near-critical planar percolation.

title: Optimal queue-size scaling Θ(n/(1−ρ)) in an n × n input-queued switch
domain_name: Queueing and stochastic networks
statement: An n × n input-queued switch has n² queues (i, j); in each time slot a matching between inputs and outputs is served, one packet per matched pair, and packets arrive to queue (i, j) by independent processes with rates λ_ij, with load ρ = max over rows and columns of the row and column sums of (λ_ij). The conjecture is that there is a scheduling policy under which the expected total queue size in steady state is O(n/(1−ρ)), uniformly in n and in ρ < 1, which matches the Ω(n/(1−ρ)) lower bound for every policy.
statement_caveat: The usual statement takes uniform arrival rates λ_ij = ρ/n, where the lower bound n/(1−ρ) comes from the n outputs each behaving at least like a single-server queue at load ρ. Maximum-weight scheduling is throughput optimal, and its heavy-traffic queue length is known for fixed n as ρ → 1 (Maguluri–Srikant and later work), but that limit is not uniform in n.
source: D. Shah, J. N. Tsitsiklis and Y. Zhong, Optimal scaling of average queue sizes in an input-queued switch: an open problem, Queueing Syst. 68 (2011) 375–384
locator: Shah–Tsitsiklis–Zhong, On queue-size scaling for input-queued switches, Stoch. Syst. 6 (2016) 1–25, arXiv:1405.4764, abstract: 'We study the optimal scaling of the expected total queue size in an n×n input-queued switch, as a function of the number of ports n and the load factor ρ, which has been conjectured to be Θ(n/(1-ρ)). In a recent work, the validity of this conjecture has been established for the regime where 1-ρ = O(1/n^2).'
why_important: The input-queued switch is the basic model of a switched network and of scheduling under matching constraints, and the question asks whether such constraints cost more than a constant factor in delay over the trivial lower bound. It was posed as an explicit open problem in Queueing Systems and has driven a line of work on scheduling policies and on heavy-traffic analysis of switched networks.
where_it_stands: Shah, Walton and Zhong (arXiv:1110.4697) proved the conjecture when 1 − ρ = O(1/n²). Shah, Tsitsiklis and Zhong (arXiv:1405.4764) obtained O(n^{1.5}(1−ρ)^{−1} log(1/(1−ρ))) when 1 − ρ = O(1/n). Xu and Zhong (arXiv:1903.00398) obtained O(n(1−ρ)^{−4/3} log max{1/(1−ρ), n}) over all n and ρ for uniform arrivals. Heavy-traffic results for fixed n (arXiv:2004.12271, 2006.06150, 2206.06504) do not address uniformity in n. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a well-known open problem in stochastic networks, posed as such in Queueing Systems; less known outside applied probability.

title: Stability region of slotted ALOHA with four or more users
domain_name: Queueing and stochastic networks
statement: N users share a channel in discrete time. User i has an infinite buffer fed by i.i.d. Bernoulli(λ_i) arrivals, and in each slot each user with a nonempty buffer transmits its head-of-line packet with fixed probability p_i, independently; a transmission succeeds if and only if no other user transmits in that slot. Determine, for N ≥ 4, the set of arrival-rate vectors (λ_1, …, λ_N) for which the joint queue process is stable (positive recurrent).
statement_caveat: The difficulty is the coupling between queues: the success probability of user i depends on which other buffers are empty, so the region is defined through stationary probabilities of the joint process that are not known in closed form. Stochastic dominance arguments give inner and outer bounds. Versions with non-Bernoulli arrivals, multiple receivers, or adaptive retransmission probabilities are separate problems.
source: B. S. Tsybakov and V. A. Mikhailov, Ergodicity of a slotted ALOHA system, Problemy Peredachi Informatsii 15 (1979) 73–87; status as in C. Bordenave, D. McDonald and A. Proutière, Asymptotic stability region of slotted Aloha, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 58 (2012) 5841–5855
locator: Bordenave–McDonald–Proutière, arXiv:0809.5023, abstract: 'The stability of such systems has been open since their very first analysis in 1979 by Tsybakov and Mikhailov.' p. 2: 'For N = 3 and Bernoulli arrivals, the stability region can be characterized [26]' and 'When the number of users N exceeds 3, it becomes impossible to derive explicit stability conditions ... These probabilities are unknown in general, and so is the stability region.'
why_important: Slotted ALOHA is the founding model of random multiple access, and its stability region is the most basic performance question for it. The problem is a standard example of interacting queues whose stability depends on the joint stationary law, a feature shared by many wireless and network models.
where_it_stands: For N = 2 the region is known exactly (Tsybakov–Mikhailov; Saadawi–Ephremides; Nain, as cited by Bordenave–McDonald–Proutière). For N = 3 with Bernoulli arrivals it was characterised by Szpankowski. Anantharam (IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 37 (1991) 535–540) gave an explicit condition under an extra assumption. Bordenave, McDonald and Proutière (arXiv:0809.5023) determine the region asymptotically as N → ∞ via a mean-field limit. For fixed N ≥ 4 no exact characterisation is known. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a classical open problem in queueing and information theory, well known in the random-access literature.

title: The critical value p_max of 1-independent bond percolation on Z^2
domain_name: Percolation and spatial random graphs
statement: A 1-independent bond percolation model on a graph G is a random spanning subgraph in which the states of edges in any two vertex-disjoint edge sets are independent. Let p_max(G) be the supremum of those p for which some 1-independent model on G, with every edge present with probability at least p, does not percolate (has no infinite component almost surely). Determine p_max(Z^2), and determine lim_{n→∞} p_max(Z^n).
statement_caveat: For independent bond percolation on Z^2 the threshold is 1/2 (Harris–Kesten); 1-independence allows positive correlations along paths, so p_max(Z^2) is strictly larger. Balister and Bollobás proved p_max(G) ≥ 1/2 for every locally finite connected infinite graph and determined p_max(T) for trees in terms of the branching number. p_max(Z^n) is non-increasing in n. 1-independent models are the output of renormalisation arguments throughout percolation theory, so bounds on p_max translate into thresholds elsewhere.
source: P. Balister and B. Bollobás, Critical probabilities of 1-independent percolation models, Combin. Probab. Comput. 21 (2012) 11–22, Questions 1.1 and 1.2 as numbered by Balister–Johnston–Savery–Scott
locator: Balister–Johnston–Savery–Scott, Improved bounds for 1-independent percolation on Z^n, Electron. J. Probab. 30 (2025), arXiv:2206.12335v2, abstract: 'A fundamental and challenging problem in this area is to determine the value of p_max(G) when G is the lattice graph Z^2.' Section 1: 'Question 1.1 ([2]). What is the value of pmax(Z2)? ... Question 1.2 ([2]). What is the value of limn→∞pmax(Zn)?'
why_important: Renormalisation arguments routinely reduce a dependent model to a 1-independent one and then need a threshold above which it surely percolates; p_max is exactly that threshold, so its value bounds what such arguments can give. The question is also a natural extremal problem over dependent measures, and the gap between the known bounds on Z^2 is still large.
where_it_stands: Day, Falgas-Ravry and Hancock gave p_max(Z^n) ≥ 4 − 2√3 ≈ 0.5359 for all n ≥ 2, and Falgas-Ravry and Pfenninger (Random Structures Algorithms 62 (2023) 887–910, arXiv:2106.08674) conjectured equality for some n ≥ 3. Balister, Bollobás and Walters proved p_max(Z^2) ≤ 0.8639. Balister, Johnston, Savery and Scott (arXiv:2206.12335) proved 0.5551 ≤ p_max(Z^2) ≤ 0.8457 (the lower bound is (35 − 3√33)/32) and lim p_max(Z^n) ≤ 0.5847, and give a high-confidence computer-assisted bound p_max(Z^2) ≥ 0.5921. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): called fundamental by the specialists; known mainly in the combinatorial percolation community.

title: Alon's conjecture on Ramsey Cayley graphs
domain_name: Boolean functions, concentration and probabilistic inequalities
statement: There is an absolute constant C such that every finite group G of order N has a Cayley graph Cay(G, S) (with S = S^{−1}, 1 ∉ S) whose clique number and independence number are both at most C log N.
statement_caveat: By Erdős's random graph bound almost every graph on N vertices has clique and independence number at most 2 log₂ N, and by Erdős–Szekeres no graph has both below (1/2) log₂ N, so the conjecture asks for Ramsey graphs with the additional symmetry of a Cayley graph. A uniformly random Cayley graph does not always work: on F_2^n its clique number is Ω(log N log log N) with high probability. The problem of Alon and Orlitsky on self-complementary Ramsey Cayley graphs, motivated by zero-error information theory, is solved for vector spaces of characteristic 1 mod 4 (below).
source: N. Alon, Research problems, Discrete Math. 138 (1995) 405–411; see also N. Alon, Graph powers, in Contemporary Combinatorics, Bolyai Soc. Math. Stud. 10 (2002) 11–28
locator: D. Conlon, J. Fox, H. T. Pham and L. Yepremyan, On the clique number of random Cayley graphs and related topics, arXiv:2412.21194, Section 1.2: 'Conjecture 1.9 (Alon). There is a constant C such that every finite group has a C-Ramsey Cayley graph.' Concluding remarks: 'Alon's conjecture remains wide open for F_2^n and F_3^n.'
why_important: Explicit or structured Ramsey graphs are a central theme of combinatorics, and Cayley graphs are the natural structured candidates (the Paley graphs are the classical example). The conjecture asks whether group structure is ever an obstruction to Ramsey behaviour, and it connects to additive combinatorics through counting sets with small sumset.
where_it_stands: Green (Combinatorica 25 (2005) 307–326) proved the conjecture for cyclic groups by showing that a random Cayley graph on Z_N has clique number O(log N); Green and Morris (Combinatorica 36 (2016)) sharpened the counting. Conlon, Fox, Pham and Yepremyan (arXiv:2412.21194) proved that a random Cayley graph on any group of order N has clique number O(log N log log N), proved the conjecture for every abelian group whose order has {2,3}-part at most (log N)^{1/1000}, hence for all abelian groups of order N for almost all N, and gave Cayley graphs on vector spaces of characteristic at least 5 with clique and independence numbers at most (2 + o(1)) log₂ N. F_2^n, F_3^n and non-abelian groups in general remain open. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a well-known conjecture of Alon in probabilistic and additive combinatorics.

title: The mixing time of the Thorp shuffle
domain_name: Random walks, Markov chains and mixing
statement: The Thorp shuffle on a deck of n cards (n even) cuts the deck into two halves of n/2 cards and, for each k = 1, …, n/2, drops the k-th cards of the two halves in an order decided by an independent fair coin. Determine the order of magnitude of its total-variation mixing time as n → ∞.
statement_caveat: Each step uses n/2 coin flips, so at most 2^{n/2} permutations are reachable per step and a counting argument gives a lower bound of order log n. The best upper bounds are polylogarithmic with exponent 3 or 4, so the true exponent of log n is unknown; the analysis is harder than for the Gilbert–Shannon–Reeds riffle shuffle because the Thorp shuffle is far from uniform on a single step and has no simple inverse description. The shuffle is used in format-preserving encryption, where explicit mixing bounds matter.
source: B. Morris, Improved mixing time bounds for the Thorp shuffle, Combin. Probab. Comput. 22 (2013) 118–132, arXiv:0912.2759; the problem is attributed there to P. Diaconis
locator: Morris, arXiv:0912.2759, Section 1: 'The Thorp shuffle, despite its simple description, has been hard to analyze. Determining its mixing time has been called the "longest-standing open card shuffling problem" [3].' ([3] is a personal communication from P. Diaconis.)
why_important: Card shuffling is the classical testing ground for Markov chain mixing, and the Thorp shuffle is the standard example where coupling and representation-theoretic methods both fail to give the right order. The problem also has a practical side through the use of the shuffle as a block cipher on small domains.
where_it_stands: Morris (STOC 2005, math/0507307) proved the first polylogarithmic bound, O(log^44 n) for n a power of 2; Montenegro and Tetali improved it to O(log^29 n); Morris (Ann. Probab. 37 (2009) 453–477) proved O(log^4 n) for all even n, and O(log^3 n) for n a power of 2 (arXiv:0912.2759). Czumaj and Vöcking (ICALP 2014, LNCS, pp. 344–355) studied the shuffle through non-Markovian couplings [verify the bound obtained]. The order is not determined. Open.
note: Fame: called the 'longest-standing open card shuffling problem' by Diaconis, as quoted by Morris.

title: The critical regime of the Derrida–Retaux recursive model
domain_name: Branching processes, trees and genealogies
statement: Fix an integer m ≥ 2 and a Z_+-valued random variable X_0, and define X_{n+1} = (X_n^{(1)} + … + X_n^{(m)} − 1)^+, where X_n^{(1)}, …, X_n^{(m)} are independent copies of X_n. Assume the critical condition (m − 1)E(X_0 m^{X_0}) = E(m^{X_0}) < ∞. Chen, Derrida, Hu, Lifshits and Shi conjecture that P(X_n ≠ 0) ~ (4/(m − 1)²) n^{−2} as n → ∞, and that conditionally on X_n ≠ 0 the law of X_n converges to the geometric law P(Y = k) = (m − 1)/m^k, k ≥ 1; consequently E(X_n) ~ (4m/(m − 1)³) n^{−2}.
statement_caveat: The recursion describes a hierarchical renormalisation model for the depinning transition with strong disorder, and it appears earlier as a spin-glass toy model of Collet, Eckmann, Glaser and Martin, who identified the critical condition. A separate conjecture of Derrida and Retaux concerns the near-critical free energy: for X_0 with law (1 − p)δ_0 + pP_{Y_0} and p_c > 0, F_∞(p) = exp(−(K + o(1))(p − p_c)^{−1/2}) as p ↓ p_c, an infinite-order phase transition. The present row is the critical-point conjecture, not the free-energy one.
source: X. Chen, B. Derrida, Y. Hu, M. Lifshits and Z. Shi, A max-type recursive model: some properties and open questions, in Sojourns in Probability Theory and Statistical Physics III, Springer Proc. Math. Stat. 300 (2019) 166–186; B. Derrida and M. Retaux, J. Stat. Phys. 156 (2014) 268–290
locator: Chen–Derrida–Hu–Lifshits–Shi, arXiv:1705.04787v2, Section 1, Theorem 2: 'Assume (4). Then lim_{n→∞} E(m^{X_n}) = 1.' Conjecture 1: 'Assume (4). Then we have P(X_n ≠ 0) ∼ 4/(m−1)² · 1/n², n → ∞.' and 'When m = 2, Conjecture 1 was already given by Collet et al. [3] (see their equation (AIII.10)) and by Derrida and Retaux [5].'
why_important: The Derrida–Retaux recursion is the simplest model believed to sit in the universality class of hierarchical pinning with relevant disorder, and the critical asymptotics are the quantitative signature of that class. The n^{−2} law and the geometric conditional limit are predicted by physicists and have been the target of a sequence of probabilistic papers since 2017.
where_it_stands: Chen, Hu and Shi (arXiv:2108.05610) proved P(X_n > 0) = n^{−2+o(1)} at criticality, described by the authors as a weaker confirmation of the predictions. Chen, Dagard, Derrida, Hu, Lifshits and Shi (Ann. Probab. 49 (2021) 637–670, arXiv:1907.01601) confirmed the free-energy conjecture under an integrability condition, as reported in arXiv:2405.09741 [verify the precise form proved]. Exactly solvable relatives are treated by Hu, Mallein and Pain (arXiv:1811.08749, continuous time on a Yule tree) and by Alsmeyer, Hu and Mallein (arXiv:2502.02991, geometric Galton–Watson tree); the dual subcritical regime is in arXiv:2306.12717; Duquesne and Shi (arXiv:2609.11435) study the continuous Derrida–Retaux branching process, conjectured to be the scaling limit of the discrete model. The sharp asymptotics of Conjectures 1 and 2 remain unproved. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): central in the probabilistic study of hierarchical renormalisation models and well known to specialists in branching and recursive distributional equations; less known outside that community.

title: Recurrence and transience of rotor walk on Z^d with i.i.d. uniform initial rotors
domain_name: Random walks, Markov chains and mixing
statement: On Z^d each vertex x carries a rotor ρ(x) ∈ {±e_1, …, ±e_d}, and the rotors advance through the 2d directions in a fixed cyclic order. A particle at x first advances the rotor at x to the next direction and then steps to x + ρ(x). Choose the initial rotors independently and uniformly at random. Is the resulting rotor walk started at the origin recurrent (returns to the origin infinitely often) almost surely in dimension d = 2, and transient almost surely in dimensions d ≥ 3?
statement_caveat: By Angel and Holroyd, two initial configurations differing in finitely many rotors are both recurrent or both transient, so recurrence of the i.i.d. configuration is a tail event and has probability 0 or 1. Schramm showed that rotor walk is at least as recurrent as simple random walk for every initial configuration, so the question is the transience half in d ≥ 3 and the recurrence half in d = 2 for this particular random environment. The deterministic aligned configuration in d ≥ 3 is transient (Florescu–Ganguly–Levine–Peres). Compare T101 (the Lorentz mirror model), whose connection to rotor walks with random initial rotors is used in the Manhattan-lattice result below.
source: L. Florescu, S. Ganguly, L. Levine and Y. Peres, Escape rates for rotor walk in Z^d, SIAM J. Discrete Math. 28 (2014) 323–334 [verify journal reference]; the recurrence question for rotor walk goes back to J. Propp's 2003 lecture
locator: Florescu–Ganguly–Levine–Peres, arXiv:1301.3521v2, 'Some open questions': 'Let us choose initial rotors ρ(x) for x ∈ Z^d independently and uniformly at random from {±e1, . . . , ±ed}. Is the resulting rotor walk recurrent in dimension 2 and transient in dimensions d ≥ 3?' followed by 'Hence the set of recurrent ρ is a tail event and consequently has probability 0 or 1.'
why_important: Rotor walk is the standard deterministic analogue of random walk, and the i.i.d. uniform configuration is the most natural random environment for it, sitting between random walk in random environment and self-organised models such as the abelian sandpile. Whether the Pólya dichotomy survives derandomisation in this setting has been asked since Propp's lecture and is unresolved in every dimension.
where_it_stands: On regular trees Angel and Holroyd showed that the i.i.d. uniform configuration has escape rate 1/b on the b-ary tree for b ≥ 3 and is recurrent for b = 2. Florescu, Levine and Peres (arXiv:1408.5533) proved that the range of any rotor walk on a periodic Eulerian graph in R^d is at least of order t^{d/(d+1)}, and used the mirror model and critical percolation to prove recurrence with i.i.d. uniform rotors on the Manhattan lattice and the F-lattice. Kaiser and Sava-Huss (arXiv:2210.00810) proved recurrence on the Sierpinski gasket graph; Huss and Sava-Huss (arXiv:1805.05746, 1805.11983) studied range and speed on trees. No result is known for Z^d with d ≥ 2 [verify]. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a well-known question in the rotor-router literature, posed by Propp and repeated by Peres and coauthors; known mainly within discrete probability.

title: Uniqueness in law for the stochastic heat equation with non-degenerate Hölder noise coefficient below exponent 2/3
domain_name: Brownian motion, stochastic analysis and SPDE
statement: On the one-dimensional torus T consider ∂_t u = Δu + g(u)Ẇ with Ẇ space-time white noise, where g is uniformly elliptic (|g| bounded away from 0) and globally β-Hölder continuous. Weak uniqueness (uniqueness in law) is known for β > 2/3. Does it hold for every β ∈ (0, 2/3], or at least for β > 1/2?
statement_caveat: Without ellipticity uniqueness can fail: Mueller, Mytnik and Perkins constructed non-unique solutions for g(x) = |x|^γ with γ < 3/4, as described by Han, so the role of the condition |g| ≥ c > 0 is the whole question. Pathwise uniqueness for β > 3/4, without ellipticity, is due to Mytnik and Perkins. The finite-dimensional analogue (uniqueness in law for SDEs with uniformly elliptic continuous diffusion coefficient, Stroock–Varadhan) suggests that ellipticity alone might give uniqueness for every β > 0, and Han records that no counterexample is known for any β > 0.
source: Y. Han, Stochastic heat equation with nondegenerate Hölder diffusion coefficient: uniqueness below the three-fourth threshold, arXiv:2608.01279 (2026)
locator: Han, arXiv:2608.01279, Section 1.3.1: 'We conjecture that 2/3 is not the sharp threshold for weak uniqueness, as no counterexamples are known for non-degenerate g for any β > 0. The two natural thresholds beyond 2/3 are thus β > 1/2 and β > 0.'
why_important: Uniqueness for stochastic PDEs with non-Lipschitz noise coefficients is one of the basic open themes in SPDE theory, motivated by super-Brownian motion and the Fleming–Viot process, where the coefficient is √u. The elliptic case isolates whether the infinite-dimensional problem behaves like the finite-dimensional theory of Stroock and Varadhan, where continuity and ellipticity suffice.
where_it_stands: Mytnik and Perkins (Probab. Theory Related Fields 149 (2011) 1–96) proved pathwise uniqueness for β > 3/4. Mueller, Mytnik and Perkins (Ann. Probab. 42 (2014) 2032–2112) gave non-uniqueness for non-elliptic coefficients with exponent below 3/4 [verify whether pathwise or in law]. Bass and Perkins proved uniqueness for elliptic coefficients 1/2 + ε-Hölder in an enhanced norm that does not cover pointwise coefficients. Han's generalized coupling method gave weak uniqueness for elliptic g with β > 3/4, and Han (arXiv:2608.01279) lowered this to β > 2/3. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): the general question of uniqueness for SPDEs with Hölder coefficients is well known in stochastic analysis; this elliptic threshold form is recent.

title: The optimal competitive ratio for the prophet secretary problem
domain_name: Statistics, optimal transport and information inequalities
statement: Independent nonnegative random variables X_1, …, X_n with known distributions are revealed in a uniformly random order, and a gambler must accept or reject each value irrevocably on seeing it, receiving the accepted value. Determine the largest constant c such that for every n and every choice of distributions some online stopping rule achieves expected reward at least c · E[max_i X_i].
statement_caveat: With adversarial order the optimal constant is 1/2 (Krengel–Sucheston, Garling); with i.i.d. values it is about 0.745 (Hill–Kertz, Correa–Foncea–Hoeksma–Oosterwijk–Vredeveld). The random-order constant lies between these. The related order-selection problem, where the gambler chooses the order, has its own optimal constant, also unknown; Bubna and Chiplunkar separated the two settings.
source: H. Esfandiari, M. Hajiaghayi, V. Liaghat and M. Monemizadeh, Prophet secretary, SIAM J. Discrete Math. 31 (2017) 1685–1701 [verify]; status as in Z. Chen, Z. Huang, D. Li and Z. G. Tang, arXiv:2411.01191
locator: Chen–Huang–Li–Tang, arXiv:2411.01191, Section 1: 'The study of prophet secretary was initiated by Esfandiari et al. [16], who designed a 1−1/e ≈ 0.632 competitive algorithm and provided an upper bound of 0.75.' and 'The state-of-the-art lower and upper bounds are 0.672 by Harb [25] and 0.723 by Giambartolomei et al. [23] respectively.' Bubna–Chiplunkar, arXiv:2211.04145, abstract: 'the optimum ratio still remains unknown in the order selection setting, as well as in prophet secretary, where the items arrive in a random order.'
why_important: Prophet inequalities are the basic comparison between online and offline optimal stopping, with applications to posted-price mechanisms. The random-order version is the natural intermediate between the classical adversarial bound 1/2 and the i.i.d. bound, and pinning down its constant has resisted a decade of work on both the algorithmic and the hardness side.
where_it_stands: Esfandiari et al. obtained 1 − 1/e. Azar, Chiplunkar and Kaplan, and Correa, Saona and Ziliotto improved this, the latter showing that blind strategies cannot exceed 0.675. Harb (arXiv:2307.00971) obtained 0.672, and Chen, Huang, Li and Tang (arXiv:2411.01191) obtained 0.688 with a non-blind algorithm. On the hardness side Bubna and Chiplunkar (arXiv:2211.04145) showed 0.7254, and Giambartolomei et al. obtained 0.723 as cited by Chen et al. [verify whether a later bound improves 0.723]. Open.
note: Fame borderline (my judgment): a well-known open problem in optimal stopping and algorithmic game theory; prominent in theoretical computer science, less so in classical probability.

title: Exact decay rate of the Favard length (Buffon needle probability) of the four-corner Cantor set
domain_name: Stochastic and geometric probability
statement: Let K_n be the n-th generation of the four-corner Cantor set: the union of the 4^n squares of side 4^{−n} obtained from the unit square by keeping the four corner squares of side 1/4 and iterating. Fav(K_n), the average over directions of the length of the orthogonal projection of K_n, is proportional to the probability that a randomly thrown long needle meets K_n. Determine the exact rate at which Fav(K_n) tends to 0.
statement_caveat: Fav(K_n) → 0 by Besicovitch's projection theorem, since K is purely unrectifiable. A lower bound c/n follows from Mattila's capacity bound, and Nazarov, Peres and Volberg note that a random analogue has Fav comparable to 1/n while it is not clear whether the deterministic set decays at that rate. The natural conjecture is Fav(K_n) ≈ n^{−1} up to logarithmic factors [verify that this is stated as a conjecture in the literature].
