why_important: It is the canonical exactly solvable model of a statistical-computational gap in learning a neural network.
where_it_stands: Open (non-rigorous large-K analysis).
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2018; standard reference in the physics of learning.

title: Bayes-optimal learning of extensive-width networks with quadratically many samples
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Learn a two-layer teacher network with width m proportional to the input dimension d from n = alpha·d² samples. Maillard, Troiani, Martin, Krzakala and Zdeborová obtain the Bayes-optimal error for quadratic activation by mapping to extensive-rank matrix denoising, and conjecture a formula for general activations. Prove the Bayes-optimal error for a general activation (e.g. ReLU or tanh) in this regime, and decide whether gradient descent achieves it.
statement_caveat: For quadratic activation the formula rests on a matrix-denoising reduction (rigorous status to verify); the general case is conjectural.
source: A. Maillard, E. Troiani, S. Martin, F. Krzakala and L. Zdeborová, Bayes-optimal learning of an extensive-width neural network from quadratically many samples, arXiv:2408.03733 (2024)
locator: to verify: main result and the discussion of general activations.
why_important: Extensive width is the regime of real networks; this is the first solvable step toward Bayes-optimal learning there.
where_it_stands: Open beyond quadratic activation as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: a 2024 NeurIPS result; active frontier of the physics of learning.

title: Bayes-optimal extensive-rank matrix factorization
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Observe Y = (1/sqrt(N)) U Vᵀ + W with U ∈ R^{N×M}, V ∈ R^{P×M} with iid priors (not rotationally invariant, e.g. Rademacher or sparse) and Gaussian noise W, with M, N, P → ∞ proportionally. Compute the limiting mutual information per entry and minimum mean-square error for estimating U Vᵀ (and U, measured by a loss invariant under the column sign and permutation symmetries: for symmetric priors the raw MMSE of U equals the prior variance), and prove it.
statement_caveat: For rotationally invariant priors the denoising problem is solved by spectral methods (rotationally invariant estimators); low-rank (M fixed) is solved by the replica formula. Earlier extensive-rank replica predictions (Kabashima et al. 2016) are believed incorrect.
source: A. Maillard, F. Krzakala, M. Mézard and L. Zdeborová, Perturbative construction of mean-field equations in extensive-rank matrix factorization and denoising, arXiv:2110.08775 (2021)
locator: to verify: introduction (status of the extensive-rank problem as open).
why_important: Extensive-rank factorization underlies dictionary learning and the Bayes-optimal analysis of networks with width proportional to dimension (T286).
where_it_stands: Open (a well-known hard problem in the statistical physics of inference).
note: Fame: regarded as one of the main open problems of the field (Zdeborová, Krzakala surveys).

audit.status_ref: Maillard-Krzakala-Mezard-Zdeborova2110.08775 PDF pp1-3 and p29 Conclusion and openings, opened in full, describe a perturbative construction and the need for all-order corrections; no deciding theorem for the broad limiting mutual information/product-MMSE formula was opened. Current general non-Gaussian extensive-rank status is not cleared.
audit.statement_ok: NO: product-MMSE and raw-factor-MMSE must be separated. For the explicitly proposed Rademacher or sign-symmetric sparse priors, the joint posterior is invariant under paired column signs, so E[U|Y]=0 and raw factor-MMSE equals prior variance at every SNR. An aligned or anchored factor loss is needed for the intended factor-recovery question. Also specify variances, aspect ratios and noise level.
audit.replace_with: Ask for the limiting mutual information and product-MMSE under fixed aspect ratios and a specified symmetric finite-variance prior/noise model. If factors are included, define loss modulo their gauge or add anchoring side information.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: raw-factor sign-gauge calculation completed in T287_factor_gauge.md; a rigorous small-SNR expansion with controlled remainder is a possible narrower route. Full extensive-rank formula remains a programme.
audit.locator: 2110.08775 PDF p3, Model FX and discussion of higher-order correlations; PDF p29 Conclusion and openings explicitly proposes resummation. The paper normalizes by sqrt(rank), whereas the row uses sqrt(ambient dimension); proportional ranks permit an explicit SNR rescaling.

title: Rigorous replica formula for deep multilayer generalized linear models
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Data are generated by a depth-L network with iid Gaussian weight matrices of sizes proportional to the input dimension (a multilayer GLM), and one observes n = alpha·d input-output pairs or noisy outputs of a random input. Prove the replica-symmetric formula for the mutual information and the Bayes-optimal error for every fixed L ≥ 3 and general Lipschitz activations, and the optimality of multilayer approximate message passing in the easy phase.
statement_caveat: The single-layer case is proved (Barbier, Krzakala, Macris, Miolane and Zdeborová); Gabrié et al. prove the formula for two layers under assumptions on the weights. Depth L ≥ 3 with iid Gaussian weights is the open part (to verify).
source: M. Gabrié et al., Entropy and mutual information in models of deep neural networks, arXiv:1805.09785 (2018); J. Barbier, F. Krzakala, N. Macris, L. Miolane and L. Zdeborová, Optimal Errors and Phase Transitions in High-Dimensional Generalized Linear Models, arXiv:1708.03395 (2017)
locator: to verify: Gabrié et al., the rigorous part (two layers) and the conjectured multi-layer formula.
why_important: Multilayer GLMs are the exactly solvable model of information flow through deep random networks.
where_it_stands: Open for L ≥ 3 as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: the Barbier et al. PNAS paper is the reference theorem of the area.

title: The algorithmic threshold of the symmetric binary perceptron
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: The symmetric binary perceptron asks for x ∈ {−1,1}^n with |<g_a, x>| ≤ kappa·sqrt(n) for M = alpha·n iid Gaussian vectors g_a. Its satisfiability threshold alpha_c(kappa) is known (Perkins–Xu; Abbe–Li–Sly), and typical solutions are isolated (frozen). Determine the largest alpha_alg(kappa) up to which a polynomial-time algorithm finds a solution with high probability, and prove matching hardness for stable algorithms (or all algorithms under an assumption).
statement_caveat: Known algorithms (Bansal–Spencer-type discrepancy minimization, Kim–Roche) work at small densities; multi-OGP hardness for stable algorithms holds above a density that does not yet match (Gamarnik, Kizildag, Perkins and Xu).
source: E. Abbe, S. Li and A. Sly, Proof of the Contiguity Conjecture and Lognormal Limit for the Symmetric Perceptron, arXiv:2102.13069 (2021); D. Gamarnik, E. C. Kizildag, W. Perkins and C. Xu, Algorithms and Barriers in the Symmetric Binary Perceptron Model, arXiv:2203.15667 (2022)
locator: to verify: Gamarnik et al., introduction (the gap between algorithmic and OGP thresholds).
why_important: It is the cleanest model of learning a binary-weight network and of the 'frozen solutions yet efficient algorithms' paradox in neural-network landscapes (Baldassi–Zecchina dense clusters).
where_it_stands: Open (gap between algorithms and barriers; to verify 2024-26 progress).
note: Fame: the perceptron and its dense-cluster paradox are well known in statistical physics and probability.

title: The capacity of the negative spherical perceptron
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Let g_1, ..., g_M be iid N(0, I_n), M = alpha·n, and kappa < 0. Determine alpha_c(kappa) such that with high probability there exists x on the sphere of radius sqrt(n) with <g_a, x> ≥ kappa·sqrt(n) for all a when alpha < alpha_c(kappa), and none when alpha > alpha_c(kappa); prove the full-RSB formula predicted by physics. Also decide whether a polynomial-time algorithm finds a solution for every alpha < alpha_c(kappa).
statement_caveat: For kappa ≥ 0 the problem is convex and the Gardner formula is proved (Shcherbina–Tirozzi; Stojnic). For kappa < 0 Gardner's formula is only an upper bound; Montanari et al. study the algorithmic side and show tractability results from overparameterization.
source: A. Montanari, Y. Zhong and K. Zhou, Tractability from overparametrization: The example of the negative perceptron, arXiv:2110.15824 (2021)
locator: to verify: introduction (status of the capacity for negative kappa).
why_important: The negative perceptron is the simplest nonconvex model of fitting data with a network (it is a toy for the interpolation threshold of overparameterized models).
where_it_stands: Bounds known; exact capacity and algorithmic threshold open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: Gardner's capacity problem (1988) is classical; the negative case is a known hard open problem.

title: Computational limits of weak learnability for multi-index models
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: For y = g(W x) with x ~ N(0, I_d), W ∈ R^{p×d} unknown with fixed p, and n = alpha·d samples, Troiani et al. characterize, by the optimal first-order (AMP) algorithm, which directions are learnable at which alpha (trivial, easy, hard subspaces) and the thresholds where weak learning becomes efficient. Prove that no polynomial-time algorithm (or no low-degree algorithm) beats these thresholds, i.e. that AMP is optimal among efficient algorithms for multi-index models.
statement_caveat: AMP optimality among first-order methods is known in related models (Celentano, Montanari and Wu); optimality among all polynomial-time algorithms is the open part.
source: E. Troiani, Y. Dandi, L. Defilippis, L. Zdeborová, B. Loureiro and F. Krzakala, Fundamental computational limits of weak learnability in high-dimensional multi-index models, arXiv:2405.15480 (2024)
locator: to verify: the conjecture on optimality of AMP in the conclusion.
why_important: Multi-index models are the canonical model of feature learning; their computational limits bound what any network can learn from proportional data.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: recent but central to the 2024-26 program on multi-index learning.

title: Efficient learning of one-hidden-layer ReLU networks under Gaussian inputs
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Let f(x) = Σ_{i=1}^k a_i ReLU(<w_i, x>) with x ~ N(0, I_d). Determine the time complexity of learning f to squared error epsilon from samples: in particular, whether for positive output weights a_i > 0 there is an algorithm running in time poly(d, k, 1/epsilon), and for general signs whether the statistical-query lower bound d^{Ω(k)} (or d^{Ω(sqrt k)}) is matched by an algorithm.
statement_caveat: SQ lower bounds of order d^{poly(k)} hold for general signs (Diakonikolas, Kane, Kontonis and Zarifis; Goel et al.); upper bounds exist with exponential dependence on k or for narrow networks (Chen and Narayanan). The precise complexity is the question.
source: I. Diakonikolas, D. M. Kane, V. Kontonis and N. Zarifis, Algorithms and SQ Lower Bounds for PAC Learning One-Hidden-Layer ReLU Networks, arXiv:2006.12476 (2020); S. Goel, A. Gollakota, Z. Jin, S. Karmalkar and A. Klivans, arXiv:2006.12011 (2020); S. Chen and S. Narayanan, Learning Narrow One-Hidden-Layer ReLU Networks, arXiv:2304.10524 (2023)
locator: to verify: Chen–Narayanan, introduction (state of the art and open questions).
why_important: Learning a single hidden layer is the most basic computational question about neural networks.
where_it_stands: Open (gap between upper and lower bounds; to verify 2024-26 progress).
note: Fame: long-standing COLT-community open problem.

title: Hardness of learning random-weight neural networks
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Daniely and Vardi ask whether networks with random weights (e.g. iid Gaussian), the 'typical' networks, are hard to learn. Prove (under a standard average-case assumption) that learning a depth-2 ReLU network with random Gaussian first-layer weights and width polylog(d) or larger, under Gaussian inputs, is computationally hard, or give a polynomial-time algorithm.
statement_caveat: Hardness is known for depth 3 (or two hidden layers) under cryptographic assumptions, also with noise-free labels (Chen, Gollakota, Klivans and Meka); the depth-2 random-weights case is the question (to verify current state).
source: A. Daniely and G. Vardi, Hardness of Learning Neural Networks with Natural Weights, arXiv:2006.03177 (2020); S. Chen, A. Gollakota, A. R. Klivans and R. Meka, Hardness of Noise-Free Learning for Two-Hidden-Layer Neural Networks, arXiv:2202.05258 (2022)
locator: to verify: Daniely–Vardi, open questions in the conclusion.
why_important: Worst-case hardness says little about practice; hardness (or easiness) for random weights is the average-case version that matters.
where_it_stands: Open for depth 2 as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: well-known question in computational learning theory.

title: Learning hierarchical generative models: Mossel's problem and the random hierarchy model
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Mossel proposes tree-structured generative models (a broadcast process on a tree whose leaves are the data) as a setting where deep algorithms should provably succeed and shallow ones fail. Cagnetta et al. define the random hierarchy model (random context-free production rules of depth L, vocabulary v, multiplicity m) and find numerically that deep networks learn it with n ≈ m^L samples, polynomial in the input size. Prove that gradient descent on a deep (convolutional) network learns the random hierarchy model with n = poly(input size) samples, and that any algorithm of bounded depth or any kernel method needs exponentially many.
statement_caveat: Mossel proves that shallow algorithms in a certain sense fail and that belief propagation succeeds; a theorem for gradient-trained networks is open.
source: E. Mossel, Deep Learning and Hierarchal Generative Models, arXiv:1612.09057 (2016); F. Cagnetta, L. Petrini, U. M. Tomasini, A. Favero and M. Wyart, How Deep Neural Networks Learn Compositional Data: The Random Hierarchy Model, arXiv:2307.02129 (2023)
locator: to verify: Mossel, the stated open problems; Cagnetta et al., Section 5.
why_important: It is the cleanest candidate explanation of why depth matters for natural (compositional) data, tied to the reconstruction problem on trees.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: Mossel's question is well known; the random hierarchy model (PRX 2024) is influential.

title: Gradient descent from random initialization for phase retrieval with linearly many samples
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Observe y_i = <a_i, x*>² for i ≤ n with a_i ~ N(0, I_d). Chen, Chi, Fan and Ma prove that vanilla gradient descent on the square loss from a random initialization finds x* (up to sign) in O(log d + log(1/epsilon)) iterations when n ≳ d·poly log(d). Prove the same with n = C·d samples for an absolute constant C, with a stated step-size schedule and a polylog(d)·log(1/epsilon) iteration count (at n = C·d the Hessian of the quartic loss has norm of order log d near x*, so a fixed step independent of d is locally unstable), or determine the smallest alpha = n/d at which randomly initialized gradient descent succeeds.
statement_caveat: Spectral initialization works at n = O(d) and the information-theoretic threshold is n ≈ d; the question is about randomly initialized vanilla GD.
source: Y. Chen, Y. Chi, J. Fan and C. Ma, Gradient Descent with Random Initialization: Fast Global Convergence for Nonconvex Phase Retrieval, arXiv:1803.07726 (2018)
locator: to verify: the conclusion (sample complexity with logarithmic factors posed as open).
why_important: Phase retrieval is a single quadratic neuron; it is the simplest nonconvex learning problem where randomly initialized GD can be fully analysed.
where_it_stands: Open in the linear-sample regime as far as the writer knows (physics predictions of the GD threshold exist: Sarao Mannelli et al.).
note: Fame: the Chen–Chi–Fan–Ma paper is a standard reference (Math. Programming).

audit.status_ref: Chen-Chi-Fan-Ma1803.07726 Theorem1 PDF p5, opened in full: Gaussian design, normalized Gaussian random initialization and fixed sufficiently small dimension-independent step c/||x*||^2 yield logarithmic burn-in plus linear convergence when samples exceed dimension times polylog(sample count). This is not the requested linear-sample theorem. Own necessary local-step obstruction at linear samples is proved in T295_constant_step_obstruction.md; it does not establish failure from random initialization.
audit.statement_ok: NO: same iteration complexity needs a step-size convention and local-stability qualification. At m=C*d, fixed positive step independent of d is unstable at the exact solution with high probability because the empirical quartic-loss Hessian has largest eigenvalue at least c_C*log(d). A stable fixed step must be O(1/log(d)); this necessary condition alone does not rule out all finite-accuracy random-initialization behavior.
audit.replace_with: Specify m=ceil(alpha*d), the exact quartic loss, initialization, dimension-dependent step, target error and success quantifiers. Ask for an admissible step schedule and a rigorously defined threshold for random-init recovery; distinguish weak recovery from exact injectivity.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: the Gaussian extreme-row Hessian calculation is completed; next derive a matching upper bound on local curvature or test a normalized/truncated update. No general threshold solution claimed.
audit.locator: 1803.07726 PDF p3 equations2-3 objective/update; Theorem1 PDF p5. Exact conclusion sentence posing removal of logarithms was not located and remains unverified.

title: Optimality of approximate message passing among all polynomial-time estimators
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: For high-dimensional estimation problems with a Bayes-optimal AMP (e.g. generalized linear models y = g(Xw*) with Gaussian X and n = alpha·d, or spiked matrix models), Celentano, Montanari and Wu prove that AMP achieves the smallest error among all 'general first-order methods' run for a bounded number of iterations. Prove that AMP is optimal among all polynomial-time estimators (under a standard hardness assumption), for some natural model where a statistical-computational gap exists.
statement_caveat: Low-degree evidence and first-order lower bounds exist; a reduction from a standard assumption is the open part.
source: M. Celentano, A. Montanari and Y. Wu, The estimation error of general first order methods, arXiv:2002.12903 (2020); M. Celentano and A. Montanari, Fundamental Barriers to High-Dimensional Regression with Convex Penalties, arXiv:1903.10603 (2019)
locator: to verify: Celentano–Montanari–Wu, introduction (the conjecture that AMP is optimal among polynomial-time algorithms).
why_important: 'AMP is optimal among efficient algorithms' is the working hypothesis behind every computational threshold computed in the statistical physics of learning.
where_it_stands: Open.
note: Fame: a central working conjecture of the area (Montanari, Zdeborová–Krzakala surveys).

title: Exact asymptotics of feature learning beyond one gradient step
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Ba et al. and Cui et al. show that one large gradient step on the first layer of a two-layer network (with n, d, width proportional) adds a spike to the feature matrix and give exact test-error asymptotics for ridge regression on the updated features. Extend the exact asymptotics to a fixed number t ≥ 2 of gradient steps, and to step sizes that scale with d so the update has rank growing with t, and determine how many steps are needed to learn a given multi-index target.
statement_caveat: Results for multiple steps exist with sample splitting or in special scalings (to verify). The question is the full description without sample splitting.
source: J. Ba, M. A. Erdogdu, T. Suzuki, Z. Wang, D. Wu and G. Yang, High-dimensional Asymptotics of Feature Learning: How One Gradient Step Improves the Representation, arXiv:2205.01445 (2022); H. Cui, L. Pesce, Y. Dandi, F. Krzakala, Y. M. Lu, L. Zdeborová and B. Loureiro, Asymptotics of feature learning in two-layer networks after one gradient-step, arXiv:2402.04980 (2024)
locator: to verify: Cui et al., conclusion.
why_important: This is the most precise rigorous handle on feature learning in the proportional regime; going beyond one step is the next frontier.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: Ba et al. (NeurIPS 2022) started a widely followed line.

title: Effective dynamics of SGD for networks with growing width
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Ben Arous, Gheissari and Jagannath prove that for online SGD in high dimension, a finite family of summary statistics (overlaps) satisfies an autonomous ODE or SDE limit ('effective dynamics') at a critical step-size scaling, with applications to Gaussian mixtures and two-layer networks of fixed width. Extend this to two-layer networks whose width p grows with d (p → ∞ with p ≪ d, and p ∝ d), where the number of summary statistics grows: prove a limit theorem for the empirical measure of the overlaps and identify the plateaus and their escape times.
statement_caveat: Fixed width is done; width growing with d needs a mean-field description of order parameters.
source: G. Ben Arous, R. Gheissari and A. Jagannath, High-dimensional limit theorems for SGD: Effective dynamics and critical scaling, arXiv:2206.04030 (2022)
locator: to verify: conclusion (growing number of summary statistics as open).
why_important: It would unify the high-dimensional (T230) and mean-field (T223) pictures of SGD in one theorem.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2022 outstanding paper award line (to verify); central to the Ben Arous school.

title: The hard phase of the teacher-student binary perceptron
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: A binary-weight student perceptron learns a binary teacher w* ∈ {−1,1}^d from n = alpha·d Gaussian examples with labels sign(<w*, x>). The Bayes-optimal error drops to zero (perfect learning) at alpha_IT ≈ 1.249 (proved: Barbier et al.), while approximate message passing reaches perfect learning only at alpha_alg ≈ 1.493. Prove that no polynomial-time algorithm (or no low-degree / no stable algorithm) achieves perfect or near-perfect generalization for alpha in (alpha_IT, alpha_alg).
statement_caveat: The information-theoretic threshold is rigorous; the computational threshold is the physics prediction.
source: J. Barbier, F. Krzakala, N. Macris, L. Miolane and L. Zdeborová, Optimal Errors and Phase Transitions in High-Dimensional Generalized Linear Models, arXiv:1708.03395 (2017); L. Zdeborová and F. Krzakala, Statistical physics of inference: Thresholds and algorithms, arXiv:1511.02476 (2015)
locator: to verify: Barbier et al., the perceptron example (thresholds 1.249 and 1.493).
why_important: The perceptron is the oldest model of a learning machine; its hard phase is a textbook example of a statistical-computational gap, still without a hardness proof.
where_it_stands: Open (computational part).
note: Fame: the Gardner–Derrida teacher-student perceptron (1989) is classical.

title: Langevin and gradient-descent thresholds versus AMP in planted models
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: In the spiked matrix-tensor model, Sarao Mannelli et al. predict (by dynamical mean-field theory) that gradient descent and Langevin dynamics from random initialization recover the signal only at a signal-to-noise ratio strictly larger than the AMP threshold, because of spurious local minima. Prove that the threshold of gradient flow (or Langevin dynamics at fixed temperature) in this model is strictly larger than the AMP threshold, and compute it.
statement_caveat: The DMFT equations for such models are proved in some settings; the gap between local dynamics and message passing is the open claim.
source: S. Sarao Mannelli, F. Krzakala, P. Urbani and L. Zdeborová, Passed & Spurious: Descent Algorithms and Local Minima in Spiked Matrix-Tensor Models, arXiv:1902.00139 (2019)
locator: to verify: main results and their non-rigorous status.
why_important: It decides whether gradient-based learning is inherently weaker than the best efficient algorithm, which is the question behind every comparison of SGD with optimal algorithms.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: ICML 2019; part of the glassy-dynamics program of Urbani, Zdeborová and coauthors.

title: Depth separation between depth-3 and depth-4 networks
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: Depth-3 networks of polynomial size can express functions that depth-2 networks of polynomial size cannot even approximate (Eldan–Shamir; Telgarsky). Prove that there is a function on R^d (or on {0,1}^d) expressible by a depth-4 ReLU network with poly(d) width and poly(d)-bounded weights that no depth-3 ReLU network with poly(d) width and bounded weights approximates within a constant in L2 of a natural input distribution.
statement_caveat: Vardi, Reichman, Pitassi and Shamir show that such separations for networks with polynomially bounded weights would imply breakthroughs in circuit lower bounds (a natural-proofs-type barrier), so the problem is at least as hard as known open problems in complexity.
source: G. Vardi, D. Reichman, T. Pitassi and O. Shamir, Size and Depth Separation in Approximating Benign Functions with Neural Networks / Neural Networks with Small Weights and Depth-Separation Barriers, arXiv:2006.00625 (2020); R. Eldan and O. Shamir, The Power of Depth for Feedforward Neural Networks, arXiv:1512.03965 (2015); M. Telgarsky, Benefits of depth in neural networks, arXiv:1602.04485 (2016)
locator: to verify: Vardi et al. 2006.00625, the barrier theorem in the introduction.
why_important: Why depth helps is the central representational question; beyond depth 3 it is connected to threshold-circuit lower bounds.
where_it_stands: Open, with a proven complexity barrier.
note: Fame: depth separation (Eldan–Shamir; Telgarsky) is one of the best-known theory results on deep networks.

title: Learning beyond statistical queries with standard SGD
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Abbe and Sandon show that SGD on polynomial-size networks with carefully designed initialization is poly-time universal (it can emulate any efficient learning algorithm, e.g. Gaussian elimination for parities), whereas SGD with large batches or noise is limited to statistical-query algorithms. Decide whether noisy-free small-batch SGD on a standard architecture (fully connected, Gaussian initialization, polynomial width) can learn a sparse parity or a full parity of d bits with poly(d) samples and time, beyond the SQ lower bound.
statement_caveat: With standard initialization, known positive results for parities match SQ complexity (Barak et al.; Kou et al.); the question is whether standard SGD can ever go beyond SQ.
source: E. Abbe and C. Sandon, Poly-time universality and limitations of deep learning, arXiv:2001.02992 (2020); B. Barak, B. L. Edelman, S. Goel, S. Kakade, E. Malach and C. Zhang, Hidden Progress in Deep Learning: SGD Learns Parities Near the Computational Limit, arXiv:2207.08799 (2022)
locator: to verify: Abbe–Sandon, open questions on natural initializations.
why_important: It decides whether the SQ framework is the right model of what gradient-trained networks can learn.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: parity learning by SGD is a canonical test problem of learning theory.

title: The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: There is an absolute constant c > 0 such that every isotropic log-concave probability measure mu on R^n satisfies the Cheeger inequality mu(∂A) ≥ c·min(mu(A), 1 − mu(A)) for every Borel set A; equivalently its Poincaré constant is bounded by an absolute constant.
statement_caveat: Chen proved the bound n^{o(1)}; Klartag improved it to C·sqrt(log n). Bourgain's slicing problem, which KLS implies, was settled in December 2024 (Guan; Klartag and Lehec). KLS itself remains open.
source: R. Kannan, L. Lovász and M. Simonovits, Isoperimetric problems for convex bodies and a localization lemma, Discrete Comput. Geom. 13 (1995); Y. Chen, An Almost Constant Lower Bound of the Isoperimetric Coefficient in the KLS Conjecture, arXiv:2011.13661 (2020); B. Klartag, Logarithmic bounds for isoperimetry and slices of convex sets, arXiv:2303.14938 (2023); B. Klartag and J. Lehec, Affirmative Resolution of Bourgain's Slicing Problem using Guan's Bound, arXiv:2412.15044 (2024)
locator: to verify: Klartag 2303.14938, introduction (current bound and the conjecture).
why_important: KLS controls the mixing time of the ball walk and Langevin-type samplers on log-concave targets, and through stochastic localization it is the main bridge between convex geometry and sampling in high dimension.
where_it_stands: Open (bound C·sqrt(log n) known; slicing settled 2024).
note: Fame: one of the central conjectures of asymptotic convex geometry; Chen's 2021 breakthrough was widely reported.

title: The query complexity of sampling from strongly log-concave distributions
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: For targets pi ∝ exp(−f) on R^d with f m-strongly convex and L-smooth (condition number kappa = L/m), determine the minimal number of gradient (or value) queries needed to output a sample within total variation epsilon (or Wasserstein epsilon·sqrt(d/m)), as a function of d and kappa. In particular decide whether the d^{1/3} dimension dependence of the randomized midpoint method and the d^{1/2} of MALA from a warm start are optimal in their respective accuracy regimes.
statement_caveat: Chewi et al. give lower bounds in fixed dimension and some dimension-dependent bounds; in general dimension the upper and lower bounds do not meet.
source: S. Chewi, J. de Dios Pont, J. Li, C. Lu and S. Narayanan, Query lower bounds for log-concave sampling, arXiv:2304.02599 (2023); S. Chewi, P. Gerber, H. Lee and C. Lu, Fisher information lower bounds for sampling, arXiv:2210.02482 (2022); R. Shen and Y. T. Lee, The Randomized Midpoint Method for Log-Concave Sampling, arXiv:1909.05503 (2019); J. M. Altschuler and S. Chewi, Faster high-accuracy log-concave sampling via algorithmic warm starts, arXiv:2302.10249 (2023)
locator: to verify: Chewi et al. 2304.02599, introduction (open problems on dimension dependence).
why_important: It is the sampling analogue of the Nemirovski–Yudin lower bounds for convex optimization, and it bounds the cost of Bayesian inference and of the Langevin steps inside diffusion and energy-based models.
where_it_stands: Open (gap between upper and lower bounds in general dimension).
note: Fame: the central question of the log-concave sampling theory community (Chewi's book on log-concave sampling).

title: Does Metropolized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo mix in d^{1/4} steps?
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: For a strongly log-concave and smooth target on R^d with bounded condition number, prove that Metropolized HMC (leapfrog integrator with an accept-reject step) from a warm start reaches total variation epsilon in Õ(d^{1/4}) gradient evaluations for every such target, or exhibit targets that require more, under higher-order smoothness assumptions of the standard type.
statement_caveat: MALA's optimal dependence from a warm start is d^{1/2} (Chewi et al. 2012.12810). Chen and Gatmiry show MHMC improves on MALA under additional conditions; for product targets the d^{1/4} scaling is classical (Beskos et al.).
source: Y. Chen and K. Gatmiry, When does Metropolized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo provably outperform Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm?, arXiv:2304.04724 (2023); S. Chewi, C. Lu, K. Ahn, X. Cheng, T. Le Gouic and P. Rigollet, Optimal dimension dependence of the Metropolis-Adjusted Langevin Algorithm, arXiv:2012.12810 (2020)
locator: to verify: Chen–Gatmiry, conditions under which d^{1/4} is shown and what is left open.
why_important: HMC (via NUTS in Stan) is the default sampler of Bayesian statistics and of Bayesian neural networks; its dimension scaling is folklore known only for product measures.
where_it_stands: Open in general as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: the d^{1/4} folklore of HMC is widely cited (Neal 2011; Beskos, Pillai, Roberts, Sanz-Serna and Stuart 2013).

title: The optimal iteration complexity of diffusion-model samplers
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: For the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck forward process started at a law p on R^d with finite second moment and an L2(p_t)-accurate score estimate with error epsilon_score, samplers are compared with the smoothed law p_delta for a fixed small delta > 0 (p itself may be singular). Known: stochastic samplers reach KL(p_delta || output) <= epsilon^2 in O~(d/epsilon^2) steps (Benton et al., arXiv:2308.03686) and total variation epsilon in O~(d/epsilon) (Li and Yan, arXiv:2409.18959); Kou and Wang (arXiv:2610.09166) prove lower bounds of order d^(1/3) for near-isotropic mixtures and larger ones for anisotropic laws, and Xun and Price (arXiv:2604.10857) give further bounds. For a fixed score-oracle model and a class of laws with bounded second moment and bounded condition number, determine the optimal number of steps N(d, epsilon) to reach total variation epsilon from p_delta: is linear dependence on d necessary, and what does the pure probability-flow ODE without a corrector achieve?
statement_caveat: Under smoothness of the score, sqrt(d)-type rates are known for the probability-flow ODE with a corrector step (Chen et al. 2305.11798).
source: S. Chen, S. Chewi, J. Li, Y. Li, A. Salim and A. R. Zhang, Sampling is as easy as learning the score: theory for diffusion models with minimal data assumptions, arXiv:2209.11215 (2022); J. Benton, V. De Bortoli, A. Doucet and G. Deligiannidis, Nearly d-Linear Convergence Bounds for Diffusion Models via Stochastic Localization, arXiv:2308.03686 (2023); G. Li and Y. Yan, O(d/T) Convergence Theory for Diffusion Probabilistic Models under Minimal Assumptions, arXiv:2409.18959 (2024); S. Chen et al., The probability flow ODE is provably fast, arXiv:2305.11798 (2023)
locator: to verify: Li–Yan, discussion of lower bounds; Benton et al., conclusion.
why_important: Diffusion models are the dominant generative models; their sampling cost given a good score is a pure probability question about time-reversed diffusions.
where_it_stands: Open (no matching lower bound as far as the writer knows).
note: Fame: Chen et al. 2209.11215 (ICLR 2023 notable) started a large theory literature.

audit.status_ref: Li-Yan2409.18959 Theorem1 PDF p6, opened in full with Error metric p7, bounds TV(p_X1,p_Y1)<=c*d*log^3(T)/T+c*epsilon_score*sqrt(logT) for early-smoothed X1. Benton-et-al2308.03686 Theorem1/Corollary1 PDF p5, fully opened, bound KL(q_delta||p_tN), not raw-target KL. New Kou-Wang2610.09166 Theorems3.1/4.1 PDF pp7/13, fully opened with oracle/preliminaries pp4,6-7, give near-isotropic-mixture Omega-tilde(d^(1/3)) and anisotropic-box Omega(d) parallel-round lower bounds in their fixed approximate-score model. Further Xun-Price2604.10857 Theorem1.3 PDF p3, opened in full with Assumptions1-2 pp2-3, proves worst-case Omega-tilde(sqrt(d)) total score queries for TV error<.99 when the target is fixed-Gaussian-smoothed bounded support and scores are inverse-polynomial Lp-accurate at every noise level. Theorem1.6 p5 gives an Omega(d^(1/4)) lower bound under a subexponential error model.
audit.statement_ok: NO: raw target may be singular under finite-second-moment assumptions, while the cited guarantees compare to a positively smoothed law. Small smoothing time does not give raw-target TV/KL. The row also conflates TV with directed KL, pure deterministic ODE with stochastic correctors, and steps/queries with adaptive rounds. A complexity lower bound requires a fixed oracle model and score-error scaling.
audit.replace_with: Fix positive smoothing delta or a mixed Wasserstein-plus-TV/KL metric, a bounded moment scale, directed divergence and approximate-score oracle. Ask matching dimension/accuracy dependence under isotropy/conditioning assumptions; keep pure ODE and corrected samplers separate.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: singular-endpoint diagnostic completed in T306_singular_endpoint.md. Explicit Gaussian-family discretization lower bounds are a narrower route after checking recent oracle bounds; the unrestricted optimal complexity remains a programme.
audit.locator: 2409.18959 Theorem1 PDF p6, Error metric p7;2308.03686 Theorem1/Corollary1 p5 and Wasserstein smoothing discussion p6;2305.11798 Theorems2-3 pp6-7 (correctors);2610.09166 Eq1 p4, convention p7, Theorems3.1 p7/4.1 p13. Claimed author-posed exact lower-bound question remains unlocated. 2604.10857 Assumptions1-2/Theorem1.3 p3,Remark1.4/open gap p4,Theorem1.6 p5.

title: Statistical rates for scores learned by trained networks
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Oko, Akiyama and Suzuki prove that diffusion models whose score is the empirical risk minimizer over a suitable class of networks achieve minimax rates for density estimation in Besov classes (and adapt to low-dimensional supports). Prove a comparable rate for a score network trained by gradient descent (or SGD) on the denoising score matching loss, in some nontrivial class of densities, with polynomial width and time.
statement_caveat: Existing guarantees are for the exact ERM over a network class, or for kernel/random-feature scores, or for special data models (Gaussian mixtures, T309).
source: K. Oko, S. Akiyama and T. Suzuki, Diffusion Models are Minimax Optimal Distribution Estimators, arXiv:2303.01861 (2023); K. Zhang, H. Yin, F. Liang and J. Liu, Minimax Optimality of Score-based Diffusion Models: Beyond the Density Lower Bound Assumptions, arXiv:2402.15602 (2024)
locator: to verify: Oko et al., conclusion (training dynamics left open).
why_important: It asks whether what diffusion models learn in practice (by gradient training) is a statistically good estimator, not just whether a good estimator exists in the class.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: ICML 2023; part of the main thread of diffusion-model theory.

title: Why do trained diffusion models generalize instead of memorizing?
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: The exact minimizer of the empirical denoising score matching loss over all functions is the score of the empirical measure (Gaussian-smoothed training set), and the reverse process run with it reproduces training points. Biroli, Bonnaire, de Bortoli and Mézard identify, for data in dimension d with n = exp(alpha·d) samples, a 'collapse' time below which this happens. Prove, for a natural data model and a natural network class trained by gradient descent, that the learned score yields samples whose distribution is close to the population distribution and not to the empirical one, with n polynomial in d, and characterize the transition between memorization and generalization in n.
statement_caveat: Kadkhodaie et al. show empirically that networks trained on disjoint halves produce nearly identical samples once n is moderate and attribute it to geometry-adaptive harmonic bases.
source: Z. Kadkhodaie, F. Guth, E. P. Simoncelli and S. Mallat, Generalization in diffusion models arises from geometry-adaptive harmonic representations, arXiv:2310.02557 (2023); G. Biroli, T. Bonnaire, V. de Bortoli and M. Mézard, Dynamical Regimes of Diffusion Models, arXiv:2402.18491 (2024)
locator: to verify: Biroli et al., collapse time formula and the open question of finite-capacity scores.
why_important: It is the generative-model version of the generalization puzzle, with direct consequences for copyright and privacy of training data.
where_it_stands: Open.
note: Fame: Kadkhodaie et al. was an ICLR 2024 outstanding paper (to verify).

title: Computational complexity of learning Gaussian mixtures by score matching
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Shah, Chen and Klivans (arXiv:2307.01178) prove that gradient descent on the DDPM denoising objective with a suitable network learns mixtures of two, or of well-separated, spherical Gaussians; Chen, Kontonis and Shah (arXiv:2404.18893) learn well-conditioned mixtures with arbitrary covariances by score matching with d^poly(k tau/(lambda_min epsilon)) samples and time. For an explicit class (k components, minimum weight w_min, covariance condition number at most kappa, pairwise separation Delta), a specified score network and the empirical DDPM objective, decide whether gradient descent from a stated initialization learns the law to total variation epsilon in time poly(d, k, 1/epsilon, 1/w_min, kappa), or prove a statistical-query lower bound for that training procedure modelled as a bounded-precision SQ oracle.
statement_caveat: SQ lower bounds of d^{Ω(k)} exist for learning general Gaussian mixtures (Diakonikolas, Kane and Stewart), so the question is about natural sub-classes and about whether diffusion training avoids or meets these barriers.
source: K. Shah, S. Chen and A. Klivans, Learning Mixtures of Gaussians Using the DDPM Objective, arXiv:2307.01178 (2023); S. Chen, V. Kontonis and K. Shah, Learning general Gaussian mixtures with efficient score matching, arXiv:2404.18893 (2024)
locator: to verify: Chen–Kontonis–Shah, open questions in the conclusion.
why_important: Gaussian mixtures are the standard test case for whether diffusion training is a computationally efficient learning algorithm.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2023 / COLT-community thread on provable diffusion training.

audit.status_ref: Chen-Kontonis-Shah2404.18893 Theorem3.2 PDF p14, opened in full with Definition1.1/Theorem1.2 p4, learns well-conditioned arbitrary-covariance GMM distributions using d^poly(k*tau/(lambda_min*epsilon)) samples and sample-polynomial time. This is not poly(d)*exp(poly(k,1/epsilon)), nor a theorem about standard-network GD. Tyurin2606.19876 Theorem2.1 PDF p4 and Theorem3.2 p6, fully opened, concern reverse Fisher divergence, unit-covariance equal-weight components and specified initialization; Theorem3.3 p7 retains an explicit mixture-weight imbalance term in TV.
audit.statement_ok: NO: cited runtime exponent depends on k/accuracy/conditioning; arbitrary covariance and robust identifiability alone are not a specified learnable class. State covariance bounds, weights, separation, architecture, initialization, objective and whether estimating parameters or distribution. Reverse-Fisher results cannot be transferred to the forward DDPM denoising loss.
audit.replace_with: Pick a separated, bounded-condition-number GMM class with explicit minimum weights, an exact score-network parameterization and empirical DDPM objective. Ask a polynomial-time GD guarantee or a reduction under a stated bounded-precision SQ oracle. Correct the existing d-exponent first.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: write an SQ simulation for a particular finite-precision clipped-gradient training oracle, tracking query tolerance and variance. No transfer to unrestricted real-valued gradients or all identifiably separated GMMs is automatic.
audit.locator: 2404.18893 Introduction printed p1/PDF p3 (exact posed runtime question),Definition1.1 and Theorem1.2 PDF p4,formal Theorem3.2 PDF p14;2307.01178 Theorems1-2 PDF p3;2606.19876 equations1-3 pp2-4,Theorems2.1 p4,3.1-3.2 p6,3.3 p7.

title: A polynomial finite-particle rate for Stein variational gradient descent
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Stein variational gradient descent moves n particles by a kernelized Wasserstein gradient flow of KL(·|pi). Shi and Mackey prove the first finite-particle rate: the kernel Stein discrepancy of the n-particle empirical measure after suitable time decays like 1/sqrt(log log n). Prove a rate polynomial in 1/n (e.g. n^{−1/2} up to dimension-dependent factors) for a natural class of targets (e.g. strongly log-concave) and kernels.
statement_caveat: Mean-field (n = ∞) convergence is understood in several metrics; the particle approximation error is the open part.
source: J. Shi and L. Mackey, A Finite-Particle Convergence Rate for Stein Variational Gradient Descent, arXiv:2211.09721 (2022); Q. Liu and D. Wang, Stein Variational Gradient Descent: A General Purpose Bayesian Inference Algorithm, arXiv:1608.04471 (2016)
locator: to verify: Shi–Mackey, introduction and conclusion (the rate and its suboptimality).
why_important: SVGD is the main deterministic particle method for Bayesian inference in neural networks; without a polynomial particle rate it has no quantitative guarantee.
where_it_stands: Open (later improvements to verify, 2023-26).
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2023; the question was posed since Liu–Wang 2016.

title: Exponential convergence of mean-field SVGD and the Stein log-Sobolev inequality
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Mean-field SVGD for a Gaussian target pi = N(0, I_d) with a fixed Gaussian RBF kernel of bandwidth h. A Stein log-Sobolev inequality fails for bounded smooth translation-invariant kernels and such targets, so no uniform exponential rate holds (Duncan, Nuesken and Szpruch, arXiv:1912.00894, Lemma 39 and Corollary 42), while target-weighted kernels can restore one (Carrillo, Skrzeczkowski and Warnett, arXiv:2412.10295, Theorem 1.1). For initial laws in an explicit class (densities with bounded relative entropy, a bounded moment of stated order and a stated tail or smoothness condition), determine the decay of KL(mu_t | pi) along the mean-field SVGD flow: prove an upper bound of explicit form (for example polynomial in t) uniform over the class, and a lower bound on some member of the class showing that it is sharp; then the same question for a kernel whose bandwidth adapts to mu_t.
statement_caveat: The mean-field limit itself is established (Lu, Lu and Nolen). Counterexamples to the inequality are known for some kernel–target pairs (to verify).
source: A. Duncan, N. Nüsken and L. Szpruch, On the geometry of Stein variational gradient descent, arXiv:1912.00894 (2019); J. Lu, Y. Lu and J. Nolen, Scaling limit of the Stein variational gradient descent: the mean field regime, arXiv:1805.04035 (2018)
locator: to verify: Duncan–Nüsken–Szpruch, the Stein log-Sobolev section and open questions.
why_important: It decides whether the mean-field SVGD flow converges fast at all, the precondition for any useful finite-particle theory (T310).
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: JMLR 2023; standard reference for SVGD geometry.

audit.status_ref: Duncan, Nuesken and Szpruch,1912.00894: Remark38 eq(41), Lemma39 PDF p17 and Corollary42 p18. Lemma39 states inequalities(36),(39) only hold for lambda=0 under C^{1,1} kernel and integrability(42); Cor42 excludes local exponential convergence for decaying translation-invariant kernels under Lemma41 assumptions. These deciding statements were opened in full. Explicit Gaussian/RBF verification in T311_Gaussian_Stein_obstruction.md. Lu-Lu-Nolen1805.04035 Theorems2.4/2.7 give finite-time well-posedness/stability, not global exponential rate. Subsequent Carrillo-Skrzeczkowski-Warnett2412.10295 Theorem1.1 PDF p7, opened in full with equations1.5-1.10/H pp5-6, proves a positive Stein-LSI for target-weighted kernels K(x,y)=exp(V(x)-V0(x)/2) k(x-y) exp(V(y)-V0(y)/2), Fourier transform k comparable to (1+|xi|^2)^-1 and regularity H. This is not the fixed bounded translation-invariant Gaussian RBF kernel.
audit.statement_ok: NO: the proposed alternative to prove failure for smooth bounded translation-invariant kernels/Gaussian targets substantially repeats the cited paper's negative results. Failure of a uniform Stein-LSI does not by itself imply that every trajectory has a subexponential asymptotic rate. Need a fixed kernel/target/initial-law class and precise rate observable.
audit.replace_with: For a specified Gaussian target and a fixed admissible kernel, determine a quantitative KL decay bound on an explicitly norm/moment-controlled initial-density class, distinguishing local versus global and adaptive versus fixed kernels; first survey subsequent SVGD rate results. Remove the already-proved smooth-kernel obstruction alternative.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: verify the explicit Gaussian/RBF KL-to-Stein-information ratio; completed as a diagnostic in the accompanying note, not an open-problem solution. New rate progress needs a narrower corrected question.
audit.locator: 1912.00894 Section6, Remark38 eqs(40)-(41), Lemma39/Remark40 PDF p17; Section6.1 Lemma41 p17, Cor42 and Example1 pp18;1805.04035 Section2 Theorems2.4 and2.7 pp6-7. New:2412.10295 Theorem1.1 p7, target and weighted kernel equations1.5-1.6 p5; Fourier condition1.10 and density class H p6.

title: Convergence of gradient dynamics in generative adversarial networks
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Simultaneous or alternating gradient descent-ascent on a GAN objective min_G max_D V(G, D) can cycle or diverge. Mescheder, Geiger and Nowozin show local convergence near equilibria with gradient penalties and give the Dirac-GAN counterexample. Prove global convergence of gradient descent-ascent (with a natural regularization) to a point where the generator distribution equals the data distribution, for a nontrivial class of generators and discriminators (e.g. a one-hidden-layer generator and a discriminator class rich enough to separate distributions), or prove that no such result holds without strong structure.
statement_caveat: Results exist for linear/quadratic discriminators, for mean-field (infinite-width) limits, and for specific simple data; the general case is open.
source: L. Mescheder, A. Geiger and S. Nowozin, Which Training Methods for GANs do actually Converge?, arXiv:1801.04406 (2018)
locator: to verify: Mescheder et al., Section 2 (Dirac-GAN) and the discussion of global convergence.
why_important: Min-max training is the main source of instability in adversarial learning; its convergence is the GAN analogue of the trainability questions of T223-T242.
where_it_stands: Open in general.
note: Fame: ICML 2018, very widely cited.

title: Do GANs learn the distribution? Equilibria, finite discriminators and support size
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Arora, Ge, Liang, Ma and Zhang show that with a discriminator of finite capacity, a generator supported on a small number of points (polynomial in the discriminator size) can fool every discriminator in the class, so the GAN objective does not force learning the distribution, and approximate pure equilibria may fail to exist. Find a natural training objective and capacity condition under which every (approximate) equilibrium generator is close to the data distribution in a strong metric (Wasserstein or TV), with sample and network sizes polynomial in d, or prove a matching lower bound for a natural data class.
statement_caveat: Positive results exist when the discriminator class is designed for the generator class (e.g. Bai, Ma and Risteski, 'restricted approximability'); for standard architectures the question is open.
source: S. Arora, R. Ge, Y. Liang, T. Ma and Y. Zhang, Generalization and Equilibrium in Generative Adversarial Nets (GANs), arXiv:1703.00573 (2017); S. Arora and Y. Zhang, Do GANs actually learn the distribution? An empirical study, arXiv:1706.08224 (2017)
locator: to verify: Arora et al. 2017, the finite-support theorem and open questions.
why_important: It is the basic statistical question about adversarial generative modelling: whether winning the game means learning the distribution.
where_it_stands: Open for standard architectures.
note: Fame: ICML 2017; the 'birthday paradox' test for mode collapse is well known.

title: Sampling the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick Gibbs measure up to beta = 1 by stochastic localization
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke give a polynomial-time algorithm, based on algorithmic stochastic localization driven by approximate message passing (the diffusion-model sampling scheme with an AMP denoiser), that samples from the SK Gibbs measure within vanishing normalized Wasserstein distance for beta < 1/2, and prove that stable algorithms fail for beta > 1. Extend the algorithm (or another polynomial-time sampler) to every beta < 1.
statement_caveat: Compare T096 (rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics up to beta = 1), a different algorithm and metric. Improvements of 1/2 are reported (to verify 2023-26 progress, e.g. Celentano's work).
source: A. El Alaoui, A. Montanari and M. Sellke, Sampling from the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Gibbs measure via algorithmic stochastic localization, arXiv:2203.05093 (2022)
locator: to verify: El Alaoui–Montanari–Sellke, introduction (the beta < 1/2 range and the conjectured beta < 1).
why_important: It is the cleanest test of diffusion-model-style sampling (stochastic localization with a learned or computed denoiser) on a hard high-dimensional measure.
where_it_stands: Open for 1/2 ≤ beta < 1 as far as the writer knows (to verify).
note: Fame: FOCS 2022; started the algorithmic stochastic localization literature.

title: Learning restricted Boltzmann machines efficiently
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: A restricted Boltzmann machine is a bipartite Ising model with visible units x ∈ {±1}^n and hidden units h ∈ {±1}^m. Bresler, Koehler and Moitra learn ferromagnetic RBMs in polynomial time and show that learning general RBMs (even the distribution over visible units) is as hard as learning sparse parities with noise. Determine natural classes of non-ferromagnetic RBMs (e.g. bounded degree with bounded weights, or random weights) that can be learned in polynomial time from samples of the visible units, and whether contrastive-divergence-type training succeeds on them.
statement_caveat: Hardness for general RBMs is proved by reduction; the boundary of tractable classes is open.
source: G. Bresler, F. Koehler and A. Moitra, Learning Restricted Boltzmann Machines via Influence Maximization, arXiv:1805.10262 (2018)
locator: to verify: Bresler–Koehler–Moitra, open problems in the conclusion.
why_important: RBMs were the building block of the first deep generative models (Hinton's deep belief nets) and remain the simplest latent-variable energy-based model.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: STOC 2019.

title: Sampling multimodal distributions by tempering and annealing
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Ge, Lee and Risteski prove that simulated tempering combined with Langevin dynamics samples in polynomial time from a mixture of k Gaussians with the same covariance (or shifts of one log-concave distribution). Prove polynomial-time guarantees (polynomial in d, k and the inverse weights) for mixtures of Gaussians with different covariances, or for annealed Langevin / sequential Monte Carlo with a geometric or diffusion-based annealing path, or prove that natural tempering schemes mix torpidly for such mixtures.
statement_caveat: Torpid mixing of tempering is known for some mixtures with unequal variances (Woodard, Schmidler and Huber 2009).
source: R. Ge, H. Lee and A. Risteski, Beyond Log-concavity: Provable Guarantees for Sampling Multi-modal Distributions using Simulated Tempering Langevin Monte Carlo, arXiv:1710.02736 (2017)
locator: to verify: Ge–Lee–Risteski, the discussion of unequal covariances.
why_important: Multimodality is where Langevin samplers fail and where diffusion-based samplers are claimed to help; this is the basic rigorous test.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2018.

title: Convergence rates of iterative proportional fitting for Schrödinger bridges
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: The Schrödinger bridge between two distributions mu, nu on R^d with reference Brownian motion of variance epsilon is computed by iterative proportional fitting (continuous Sinkhorn), which underlies diffusion Schrödinger bridge generative models. Prove exponential (linear) convergence of IPF in relative entropy or Wasserstein distance with explicit dependence on epsilon and d, for unbounded supports (e.g. sub-Gaussian or log-concave marginals) and small epsilon, and determine the dependence on epsilon.
statement_caveat: Exponential convergence is known for bounded costs (Franklin–Lorenz type contraction) and for some log-concave settings with rates degrading badly in epsilon (to verify recent work of Conforti, Durmus and coauthors).
source: V. De Bortoli, J. Thornton, J. Heng and A. Doucet, Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge with Applications to Score-Based Generative Modeling, arXiv:2106.01357 (2021)
locator: to verify: De Bortoli et al., Section 3 (IPF convergence) and the open questions.
why_important: Schrödinger bridges connect optimal transport, diffusion models and stochastic control; IPF is the algorithm, and its rate in the regimes used is not known.
where_it_stands: Open in the stated generality as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2021; the continuous IPF question goes back to Fortet (1940) and Rüschendorf (1995).

title: The cold posterior effect in Bayesian deep learning
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Cold posteriors: Wenzel et al. (arXiv:2002.02405) observe that tempered posteriors p(theta | D)^(1/T) with T < 1 predict better than T = 1 for Bayesian neural networks. Averaged over the prior that generated the data, T = 1 is optimal for log-predictive risk, but at a fixed true parameter a colder posterior can win even in a scalar Gaussian model with the correct likelihood. Take a high-dimensional teacher (a random-features model, or a two-layer network with d, n and width growing proportionally), the correct likelihood, an inference prior, and true parameters drawn from a law that differs from that prior in a stated way (for example a different scale, or a planted low-dimensional structure). Compute the limiting excess log-predictive risk as a function of the temperature T, with the whole posterior or only the likelihood tempered (stated), and decide whether its minimizer stays below 1 by a margin that does not vanish as the dimension grows.
statement_caveat: Proposed explanations: data curation (Aitchison), data augmentation, misspecified priors; none has been proved to account for the effect in a model with networks.
source: F. Wenzel et al., How Good is the Bayes Posterior in Deep Neural Networks Really?, arXiv:2002.02405 (2020); L. Aitchison, A statistical theory of cold posteriors in deep neural networks, arXiv:2008.05912 (2020)
locator: to verify: Wenzel et al., Section 4 (hypotheses for the effect).
why_important: Bayesian deep learning rests on posteriors that, empirically, are not the best thing to sample; the effect is a direct challenge to its foundations.
where_it_stands: Open (the explanation is contested).
note: Fame: ICML 2020; widely discussed in Bayesian deep learning.

audit.status_ref: Current broad neural explanation not cleared. Wenzel et al.2002.02405 Section8 PDF p9 explicitly says the cause is not fully resolved; Aitchison2008.05912 Section2 eqs1-4 p2 separates cold/tempered posteriors and Section3 eqs6-10 pp2-3 supplies a curation mechanism. No numbered deciding theorem for the row's broad neural statement was found in these inspected passages. Own exact Gaussian calculation in T318_Gaussian_cold_posterior.md answers the weak fixed-truth/likelihood-only existential interpretation; not a literature novelty claim.
audit.statement_ok: NO: correct likelihood is weaker than the true joint prior/data law. Bayes log-predictive optimality is conditional/prior-averaged; it is not uniform in a fixed true parameter. A scalar Gaussian proxy already gives strictly optimal cold temperature T*=n/(n+a)<1 at truth0 with correct likelihood, whereas prior-averaged risk uniquely favors T=1. Loss and whole-posterior versus likelihood-only tempering must be explicit.
audit.replace_with: Specify a high-dimensional neural/random-feature teacher, correct likelihood and explicit relationship between true parameter law and inference prior; ask for a quantitative excess log-predictive-risk curve versus temperature and a nonvanishing benefit under a stated mismatch or fixed-truth criterion. Keep prior-averaged exact-model Bayes optimality separate.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: Gaussian proxy calculation completed in accompanying note, resolving the missing-quantifier diagnostic; check prior work before treating any proxy extension as new.
audit.locator: 2002.02405 Section8 Conclusion PDF p9 and prior discussion Section5.2;2008.05912 Section2 eqs1-4 PDF p2, Section3 eqs6-10 PDF pp2-3.

title: Compressed sensing with generative priors: efficient recovery near the information limit
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Recover x = G(z*) from y = A x with A ∈ R^{m×n} Gaussian, where G: R^k → R^n is a d-layer ReLU network with Gaussian weights. Hand and Voroninski show that the empirical risk has no spurious stationary points when m ≳ k·d·polylog and each layer expands by a logarithmic factor; Daskalakis, Rohatgi and Zampetakis reduce expansion to a constant. Prove that a polynomial-time algorithm recovers z* with m = O(k) measurements and constant expansion with no logarithmic factors, and decide whether gradient descent on ||A G(z) − y||² does so from a random initialization.
statement_caveat: Recovery with m = O(k log n)-type sample sizes is known for Lipschitz generators via ERM (Bora et al.); the computational question is open.
source: P. Hand and V. Voroninski, Global Guarantees for Enforcing Deep Generative Priors by Empirical Risk, arXiv:1705.07576 (2017); C. Daskalakis, D. Rohatgi and M. Zampetakis, Constant-Expansion Suffices for Compressed Sensing with Generative Priors, arXiv:2006.04237 (2020); A. Bora, A. Jalal, E. Price and A. G. Dimakis, Compressed Sensing using Generative Models, arXiv:1703.03208 (2017)
locator: to verify: Daskalakis et al., open problems on the measurement count.
why_important: Generative priors replaced sparsity in many inverse problems; random-weight generators are the solvable model of why gradient descent recovers signals.
where_it_stands: Partly solved (constant expansion); optimal measurement count open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: Bora et al. (ICML 2017) and Hand–Voroninski (COLT 2018) are standard references.

title: Depth needed by normalizing flows to approximate distributions
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Affine coupling flows are universal approximators of diffeomorphisms (Teshima et al.) and hence, in the limit, of distributions; Kong and Chaudhuri show that planar and Sylvester flows of bounded depth have limited expressive power. Give quantitative bounds: how many coupling layers (as a function of d and epsilon) are needed to push a standard Gaussian to within epsilon in Wasserstein or TV of a given smooth density on R^d (e.g. a mixture of two Gaussians), and prove matching lower bounds.
statement_caveat: Constructive upper bounds via triangular (Knothe) maps exist with depth depending on d; lower bounds for coupling architectures are scarce (to verify Koehler–Mehta–Risteski 2020).
source: Z. Kong and K. Chaudhuri, The Expressive Power of a Class of Normalizing Flow Models, arXiv:2006.00392 (2020); T. Teshima, I. Ishikawa, K. Tojo, K. Oono, M. Ikeda and M. Sugiyama, Coupling-based Invertible Neural Networks Are Universal Diffeomorphism Approximators, arXiv:2006.11469 (2020)
locator: to verify: Kong–Chaudhuri, open questions in the conclusion.
why_important: Flows (and flow matching, Lipman et al. 2210.02747) are exact-likelihood generative models; their approximation cost in depth is the analogue of depth separation for density models.
where_it_stands: Open (quantitative version).
note: Fame: moderate; flows are a standard generative-model family.

title: Polynomial-time mixing of Langevin dynamics for nonconvex learning objectives
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Fix a model: (i) real phase retrieval, y_i = (a_i . x)^2 with Gaussian a_i, m = alpha d samples, the square loss of the amplitudes squared; or (ii) a two-layer network of width m with a planted teacher, Gaussian inputs, and weight decay lambda. Let pi_beta be proportional to exp(-beta L), with beta = beta(d, epsilon) chosen so that pi_beta gives probability at least 1 - delta to {L <= min L + epsilon}. Prove that pi_beta satisfies a Poincare inequality with constant polynomial in d and 1/epsilon (say separately whether a log-Sobolev inequality, which is stronger, also holds), or show the constant is exponential in d. Then bound the time for discretized Langevin dynamics from a stated initialization to reach total variation or W2 accuracy, including the discretization error. Raginsky, Rakhlin and Telgarsky give bounds exponential in d through the spectral gap; the mean-field limit (T223-T225) is a different question.
statement_caveat: In the mean-field limit (T223-T225) the free energy is convex in the measure; for finite-dimensional parameters, polynomial-gap results are known only for special landscapes.
source: M. Raginsky, A. Rakhlin and M. Telgarsky, Non-convex learning via Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics: a nonasymptotic analysis, arXiv:1702.03849 (2017)
locator: to verify: Raginsky et al., discussion of the spectral gap dependence.
why_important: Langevin noise is the standard theoretical model of SGD noise and of Bayesian training; whether it is efficient on real learning landscapes is the question.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: COLT 2017 best paper (to verify).

audit.status_ref: Raginsky-Rakhlin-Telgarsky1702.03849 Theorem2.1 PDF p6, fully opened with A1-A5 pp5-6, gives SGLD excess-risk/time bounds in terms of uniform Gibbs Poincare gap lambda*. Discussion pp15-16 supplies an explicit Gaussian-convolved modified objective with inverse gap <=(beta gamma)^(-1) exp(4 beta gamma R^2), dimension-free at fixed beta gamma R^2, and explicitly asks for further small-inverse-gap settings. This is partial structured progress, not a general polynomial bound at the beta needed for raw finite-width-network near-minimization.
audit.statement_ok: NO: this is an existential research programme over unspecified natural losses. Fix a concrete architecture or planted model,data law,regularizer,temperature beta(d,epsilon), spectral-gap convention and success probability. A spectral gap and an LSI constant are distinct strengths; polynomial mixing also needs an initialization/discretization accuracy statement.
audit.replace_with: Specify one regularized finite-dimensional learning model and prove a Poincare/LSI bound uniformly on a stated data event at an explicit near-minimizer temperature. Distinguish raw parameters from quotienting prediction-equivalent states and warm-start-only sampling.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: T321_gap_diagnostic.md gives a globally smooth,dissipative double-well-plus-quadratic family with inverse gap exponential in beta, and near-minimizer concentration forces beta>=Omega(d/epsilon). A useful positive task must add geometry that removes this bottleneck.
audit.locator: 1702.03849 A1-A5 pp5-6;Theorem2.1 p6;Uniform spectral gap discussion Eq4.3 and modified objective p15,Gaussian-convolution bound and posing p16. Quote p16: "find other settings where 1/lambda* is indeed small".

title: Computationally efficient minimax estimation of optimal transport maps
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Hütter and Rigollet prove that the optimal transport map between two distributions on R^d whose Brenier map is alpha-smooth can be estimated from n samples of each at the minimax rate n^{−2α/(2α−2+d)} (up to logs), using an estimator that is not computable in polynomial time. Find a polynomial-time estimator achieving the minimax rate (e.g. entropic OT with a tuned epsilon, or a neural network trained by gradient descent), or prove a computational lower bound.
statement_caveat: Entropic and plug-in estimators achieve the rate in some smoothness ranges (Pooladian–Niles-Weed; Manole et al.); the full range is open (to verify).
source: J.-C. Hütter and P. Rigollet, Minimax estimation of smooth optimal transport maps, arXiv:1905.05828 (2019)
locator: to verify: Hütter–Rigollet, the computational question in the conclusion.
why_important: Transport maps are what flow matching and Schrödinger-bridge models learn; whether they can be learned efficiently at the optimal rate is the statistical core of those methods.
where_it_stands: Open in the full smoothness range as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: Annals of Statistics 2021; central in statistical optimal transport.

title: Clustering of tokens in self-attention dynamics
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: Model a deep transformer as an interacting particle system: n tokens x_i(t) on the unit sphere S^{d−1} evolve by dx_i/dt = P_{x_i}( (1/Z_i) Σ_j e^{beta <x_i, x_j>} x_j ), with P_x the projection to the tangent space and Z_i the softmax normalization. Geshkovski, Letrouit, Polyanskiy and Rigollet prove convergence to a single cluster for almost every initialization in several regimes (e.g. d ≥ 3, or beta small or large). Prove convergence to a single cluster for every d ≥ 2, every beta > 0 and almost every initial configuration, and extend clustering results to general query-key-value matrices (Q, K, V), where the limiting geometry (points, hyperplanes, low-rank sets) is conjectured to depend on the spectrum of V.
statement_caveat: The survey lists the d = 2 case for intermediate beta and the general (Q, K, V) case among its open problems.
source: B. Geshkovski, C. Letrouit, Y. Polyanskiy and P. Rigollet, The emergence of clusters in self-attention dynamics, arXiv:2305.05465 (2023); B. Geshkovski, C. Letrouit, Y. Polyanskiy and P. Rigollet, A mathematical perspective on Transformers, arXiv:2312.10794 (2023)
locator: to verify: 2312.10794, the numbered open problems (synchronization for all beta and d).
why_important: It is the mean-field particle-system description of what depth does to token representations in transformers, and a Kuramoto-type synchronization problem in its own right.
where_it_stands: Open in the stated generality.
note: Fame: the 'mathematical perspective on transformers' survey (Bull. AMS 2025, to verify) made this a standard open problem.

title: Metastable clustering times in mean-field transformer dynamics
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: In the self-attention particle system of T323 with large beta, tokens first form several clusters that persist for a time exponentially long in beta before merging. Bruno, Pasqualotto and Agazzi describe this metastable phase in the mean-field limit. Prove the number of metastable clusters and the exponential time scales of their merging (a Freidlin–Wentzell-type or slow-manifold description), for the deterministic dynamics and for the dynamics with small noise.
statement_caveat: Partial results describe the first stage (number of clusters ~ sqrt(beta) on the circle) in a linearized or mean-field regime.
source: G. Bruno, F. Pasqualotto and A. Agazzi, Emergence of meta-stable clustering in mean-field transformer models, arXiv:2410.23228 (2024); B. Geshkovski, C. Letrouit, Y. Polyanskiy and P. Rigollet, A mathematical perspective on Transformers, arXiv:2312.10794 (2023)
locator: to verify: Bruno et al., main theorem and open questions.
why_important: Real transformers have finite depth, so the metastable multi-cluster phase, not the final single cluster, is the regime they live in.
where_it_stands: Open (partial mean-field results).
note: Fame: recent, part of the T323 programme.

title: Do trained transformers learn in-context regression by gradient descent?
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: Pretrain a transformer on prompts (x_1, y_1, ..., x_N, y_N, x_query) with x_i ~ N(0, I_d), y_i = <w, x_i> and w ~ N(0, I_d). Zhang, Frei and Bartlett prove that gradient flow on a one-layer linear self-attention model from a suitable initialization converges to a predictor implementing one step of preconditioned gradient descent. Prove that gradient-based training of a multi-layer softmax transformer (or of a linear transformer with L ≥ 2 layers from a random initialization) converges to a predictor whose in-context risk approaches that of the Bayes-optimal ridge predictor as N → ∞, and identify the algorithm it implements.
statement_caveat: Constructions show transformers can implement gradient descent and ridge regression in context (von Oswald et al.; Akyürek et al.); stationary points of multi-layer linear models are characterized (Ahn et al.). Convergence of training beyond one layer is the open part.
source: R. Zhang, S. Frei and P. L. Bartlett, Trained Transformers Learn Linear Models In-Context, arXiv:2306.09927 (2023); J. von Oswald et al., Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent, arXiv:2212.07677 (2022); E. Akyürek et al., What learning algorithm is in-context learning? Investigations with linear models, arXiv:2211.15661 (2022); K. Ahn, X. Cheng, H. Daneshmand and S. Sra, Transformers learn to implement preconditioned gradient descent for in-context learning, arXiv:2306.00297 (2023); S. Garg, D. Tsipras, P. Liang and G. Valiant, What Can Transformers Learn In-Context? A Case Study of Simple Function Classes, arXiv:2208.01066 (2022)
locator: to verify: Zhang–Frei–Bartlett, conclusion (multi-layer and softmax as open).
why_important: In-context learning is the defining capability of large language models; linear regression in context is its solvable model.
where_it_stands: Open beyond one layer / linear attention as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: Garg et al. (NeurIPS 2022) and von Oswald et al. (ICML 2023) are among the most cited theory-of-LLM papers.

title: The task-diversity threshold for in-context learning
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: Pretrain on in-context regression prompts whose task vectors w are drawn from a finite set of M tasks (sampled once from N(0, I_d)). Raventós et al. observe a threshold in M: below it the trained transformer behaves like the Bayes predictor for the finite task prior (memorizing tasks), above it like ridge regression for the Gaussian prior (generalizing to new tasks). Prove the existence and location of this threshold (e.g. M ~ C·d or another scaling) for a solvable model (linear attention trained to optimality, or a random-features or kernel proxy), and relate it to the Bayesian picture of Xie et al.
statement_caveat: Wu et al. give the number of pretraining tasks needed for one-layer linear attention (sample complexity in tasks); the transition between the two Bayes predictors for trained softmax models is the open part.
source: A. Raventós, M. Paul, F. Chen and S. Ganguli, Pretraining task diversity and the emergence of non-Bayesian in-context learning for regression, arXiv:2306.15063 (2023); J. Wu et al., How Many Pretraining Tasks Are Needed for In-Context Learning of Linear Regression?, arXiv:2310.08391 (2023); S. M. Xie, A. Raghunathan, P. Liang and T. Ma, An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference, arXiv:2111.02080 (2021)
locator: to verify: Raventós et al., discussion of the transition.
why_important: It decides when a pretrained model generalizes to genuinely new tasks rather than recalling seen ones, a probabilistic question about posterior concentration under a learned prior.
where_it_stands: Open (partial results for linear attention).
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2023; Xie et al. (ICLR 2022) is the standard Bayesian account of in-context learning.

title: Gradient descent learns induction heads on Markov chains
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: Train a two-layer attention-only transformer by gradient descent on sequences from random Markov chains (transition matrix drawn from a Dirichlet prior for each sequence) to predict the next token. Edelman et al. observe staged learning (uniform, then unigram, then bigram statistics via an induction head). Prove that gradient descent from a small random initialization, with a softmax attention model of standard parameterization, converges to the in-context bigram (Bayes) predictor, and describe the plateaus between stages.
statement_caveat: Nichani, Damian and Lee prove convergence for a simplified two-stage training on a modified architecture; Bietti et al. analyse a memory-based simplification. The full joint training is open.
source: B. L. Edelman, E. Edelman, S. Goel, E. Malach and N. Tsilivis, The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains, arXiv:2402.11004 (2024); E. Nichani, A. Damian and J. D. Lee, How Transformers Learn Causal Structure with Gradient Descent, arXiv:2402.14735 (2024); A. Bietti, V. Cabannes, D. Bouchacourt, H. Jégou and L. Bottou, Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint, arXiv:2306.00802 (2023)
locator: to verify: Nichani et al., the simplifications and the stated open problems.
why_important: Induction heads are the best-understood mechanism of in-context learning; proving they emerge under gradient descent is the dynamics counterpart of T325.
where_it_stands: Open for joint training of standard architectures.
