Cai, Yang, Lee and Wang prove that neural TD and Q-learning with overparameterized two-layer networks converge to the global optimum of the projected Bellman equation in a lazy (NTK) regime. Prove convergence of TD(0) with a two-layer network in the mean-field (feature-learning) regime, or with a fixed-width network under a natural assumption on the Markov chain, to a fixed point with explicit approximation error, or construct a natural divergent example.
statement_caveat: Mean-field TD analyses exist under restrictive conditions (to verify Zhang et al. 2020); divergence examples exist for nonlinear approximators (Tsitsiklis and Van Roy 1997).
source: Q. Cai, Z. Yang, J. D. Lee and Z. Wang, Neural Temporal-Difference and Q-Learning Provably Converge to Global Optima, arXiv:1905.10027 (2019)
locator: to verify: Cai et al., the overparameterization assumption.
why_important: Deep reinforcement learning rests on TD with networks; it is a stochastic-approximation question with Markovian noise.
where_it_stands: Open beyond the lazy regime.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2019.

title: The deadly triad: when does off-policy TD with function approximation converge?
domain_name: Deep learning: training dynamics and optimization
statement: Off-policy linear TD(0) on a finite MDP with feature matrix Phi, behaviour policy mu, target policy pi and discount gamma. Its expected update is theta <- theta + alpha (b - A theta) with A = Phi^T D_mu (I - gamma P_pi) Phi, so for iid replay from d_mu the mean dynamics with small steps are stable exactly when every eigenvalue of A has positive real part (Baird's example violates it; emphatic TD, Sutton, Mahmood and White arXiv:1503.04269, makes the corresponding matrix positive definite). For samples along the mu-trajectory, give conditions on (mu, pi, Phi, gamma) and the step that are necessary and sufficient for (i) mean-square boundedness and convergence to a stationary law with constant steps, and (ii) almost-sure convergence with decreasing steps. Then, for a value function given by a two-layer network trained by TD with iid replay and a target network refreshed every tau steps, give a sufficient condition for stability in terms of tau, the step and the network Jacobian.
statement_caveat: Sufficient conditions are known (on-policy, emphatic weighting, small discount, target networks with regularization); a characterization is open (to verify).
source: R. S. Sutton, A. R. Mahmood and M. White, An Emphatic Approach to the Problem of Off-policy Temporal-Difference Learning, arXiv:1503.04269 (2015)
locator: to verify: Sutton–Mahmood–White, introduction on the off-policy problem; Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning (2nd ed.), Section 11.3 on the deadly triad.
why_important: Deep Q-learning works in practice despite having all three ingredients of the triad; why and when is unexplained.
where_it_stands: Open (characterization; neural case).
note: Fame: the deadly triad is a textbook open problem of reinforcement learning (Sutton–Barto).

audit.status_ref: Sutton-Mahmood-White1503.04269 Theorem1 Stability of Emphatic TD(lambda) PDF pp18-19, opened completely including conclusion, establishes positive definiteness of its emphasized A under stated finite-MDP,coverage,interest,feature and trace-expectation hypotheses. The following paragraph explicitly distinguishes stability from parameter convergence, referring the latter to a separate decreasing-step result. Own expected linear equation/single-state counterexample in T370_TD_convergence_modes.md.
audit.statement_ok: NO: define convergence mode and sampling law. For iid replay the expected linear ODE already has an exact spectral stability criterion; constant-step noisy TD generally has a stationary fluctuation law, not almost-sure point convergence. A nonlinear replay/target-network extension is a separate problem requiring replay distribution, target-update schedule, approximation class and success criterion.
audit.replace_with: For a finite MDP and specified iid replay or Markov trajectory, fix a step schedule and distinguish mean stability, mean-square boundedness, invariant-law convergence and almost-sure convergence. Then pose one explicit nonlinear target-network stability extension.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: exact expected-matrix spectral test and one-state constant-step counterexample completed in T370_TD_convergence_modes.md. Mean-square random-matrix stability for a specified small replay model is a finite-check route; unrestricted DQN is a programme.
audit.locator: 1503.04269 Section3 instability/coverage PDF p7;Theorem1 pp18-19 and immediately following stability-versus-convergence discussion p19. No source theorem poses the combined necessary-and-sufficient neural-DQN problem.

title: Global convergence and sample complexity of policy gradient with neural policies
domain_name: Deep learning: training dynamics and optimization
statement: Agarwal, Kakade, Lee and Mahajan prove global convergence of exact policy gradient for tabular softmax policies and give approximation-error bounds for log-linear and neural policies in terms of transfer errors. Prove that stochastic policy gradient (or natural policy gradient / PPO-style updates) with a two-layer neural policy, trained from samples in a Markov decision process with continuous states, converges to a near-optimal policy with sample complexity polynomial in the problem parameters, under assumptions that hold for a natural class of MDPs, without assuming the policy class is closed under policy improvement.
statement_caveat: Results with NTK-regime networks and strong concentrability assumptions exist.
source: A. Agarwal, S. M. Kakade, J. D. Lee and G. Mahajan, On the Theory of Policy Gradient Methods: Optimality, Approximation, and Distribution Shift, arXiv:1908.00261 (2019)
locator: to verify: Agarwal et al., discussion of neural policies.
why_important: Policy gradient is the method behind RL fine-tuning of language models (RLHF); its guarantees with networks are missing.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: JMLR 2021; the standard reference on policy-gradient theory.

title: The equilibrium of SGD with normalization and weight decay
domain_name: Deep learning: training dynamics and optimization
statement: For a network whose loss is scale-invariant in a weight vector w (because of batch or layer normalization), SGD with learning rate eta and weight decay lambda makes ||w|| converge to an equilibrium where the effective learning rate eta/||w||² is of order sqrt(eta·lambda) (Li and Arora; Wan et al., 'spherical motion dynamics'). Prove that SGD on such a loss converges to a stationary distribution on the sphere (in angle) with an explicit effective temperature, with convergence time of order 1/(eta·lambda), and characterize the stationary distribution near minima.
statement_caveat: Heuristic derivations and continuous-time models exist; a rigorous result for SGD with gradient noise is limited (to verify).
source: Z. Li and S. Arora, An Exponential Learning Rate Schedule for Deep Learning, arXiv:1910.07454 (2019); R. Wan, Z. Zhu, X. Zhang and J. Sun, Spherical Motion Dynamics: Learning Dynamics of Neural Network with Normalization, Weight Decay, and SGD, arXiv:2006.08419 (2020)
locator: to verify: Wan et al., assumptions of the equilibrium result.
why_important: Every modern network combines normalization and weight decay; this equilibrium sets its effective learning rate.
where_it_stands: Open (rigorous version).
note: Fame: ICLR 2020 for Li–Arora.

title: Size-independent sample complexity of deep networks
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Golowich, Rakhlin and Shamir prove Rademacher-complexity bounds for depth-L networks with Frobenius-norm-bounded weight matrices that are independent of width and depend on depth only through sqrt(L) (or independent of depth under extra Schatten-norm control). Bartlett, Foster and Telgarsky give spectrally-normalized margin bounds. Determine whether a generalization bound for deep ReLU networks that depends only on the product of spectral norms and a polylogarithmic factor in width and depth (no Frobenius or (2,1)-norm terms) is possible, and give matching lower bounds.
statement_caveat: Lower bounds show some norm-based dependence is necessary; whether spectral norms alone suffice is posed by Golowich et al.
source: N. Golowich, A. Rakhlin and O. Shamir, Size-Independent Sample Complexity of Neural Networks, arXiv:1712.06541 (2017); P. L. Bartlett, D. J. Foster and M. Telgarsky, Spectrally-normalized margin bounds for neural networks, arXiv:1706.08498 (2017)
locator: to verify: Golowich et al., the open questions in the conclusion.
why_important: Norm-based bounds are the main capacity-control explanation of generalization in overparameterized networks.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: COLT 2018; Bartlett–Foster–Telgarsky (NeurIPS 2017) is very widely cited.

title: Can uniform convergence explain generalization of SGD-trained networks?
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Nagarajan and Kolter construct settings (overparameterized linear classifiers and networks trained by gradient descent) in which every two-sided uniform-convergence bound over the set of hypotheses SGD can output, even with the best algorithm-dependent hypothesis class, is vacuous, while the test error is small. Determine whether some refined uniform-convergence framework (one-sided, or on the loss of interpolating predictors, as in Zhou, Sutherland and Srebro's 'uniform convergence of interpolators') yields tight bounds for gradient-trained networks, or prove a general impossibility for a natural network setting.
statement_caveat: For linear regression, uniform convergence of interpolators gives tight bounds (Koehler, Zhou, Sutherland and Srebro, 2021); networks are open.
source: V. Nagarajan and J. Z. Kolter, Uniform convergence may be unable to explain generalization in deep learning, arXiv:1902.04742 (2019)
locator: to verify: Nagarajan–Kolter, the discussion of possible fixes.
why_important: It is the methodological question of what kind of argument can explain deep-network generalization at all.
where_it_stands: Open for networks as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2019 outstanding new directions paper.

title: Generalization of minimum-norm infinite-width ReLU interpolants in high dimension
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Ongie, Willett, Soudry and Srebro characterize the representation cost (the minimal sum of squared weights) of a function as an infinite-width two-layer ReLU network via the Radon transform of its Laplacian power. Among all interpolants of n data points, consider the one of minimal representation cost. Determine its test error for data from a natural distribution in R^d (e.g. Gaussian inputs with labels from a single-index or smooth target plus noise), in particular whether it is consistent, tempered or catastrophic as n → ∞ with d fixed and with d growing.
statement_caveat: In one dimension min-norm interpolants are linear splines with tempered overfitting (Joshi, Vardi and Srebro, to verify); in higher dimension the behaviour is open.
source: G. Ongie, R. Willett, D. Soudry and N. Srebro, A Function Space View of Bounded Norm Infinite Width ReLU Nets: The Multivariate Case, arXiv:1910.01635 (2019)
locator: to verify: Ongie et al., conclusion.
why_important: Min-norm interpolation is the implicit bias of weight decay; its generalization is a geometric probability question about Radon-domain splines.
where_it_stands: Open in high dimension as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: ICLR 2020.

title: Do information-theoretic bounds explain generalization of SGD on networks?
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Xu and Raginsky bound the expected generalization gap of an algorithm by sqrt(2·sigma²·I(W; S)/n), with I(W; S) the mutual information between the output and the sample; Steinke and Zakynthinou's conditional mutual information (CMI) refines it and is always finite. Prove a bound on the CMI of SGD (or noisy SGD) trained to near-zero loss on an overparameterized two-layer network for a natural data distribution that is o(n), giving a non-vacuous generalization bound, or prove that CMI bounds are necessarily vacuous for some natural setting where SGD generalizes.
statement_caveat: CMI-based bounds can be tight for some algorithms and provably loose for others (to verify Haghifam et al. on convex optimization limitations).
source: A. Xu and M. Raginsky, Information-theoretic analysis of generalization capability of learning algorithms, arXiv:1705.07809 (2017); T. Steinke and L. Zakynthinou, Reasoning About Generalization via Conditional Mutual Information, arXiv:2001.09122 (2020)
locator: to verify: Steinke–Zakynthinou, open problems.
why_important: Information-theoretic bounds are algorithm-dependent and so escape the T374 impossibility; whether they work for networks is open.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2017 / COLT 2020.

title: A theory of weak-to-strong generalization
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Burns et al. fine-tune a strong pretrained model on labels produced by a weaker model and find that the strong student often exceeds its weak teacher's accuracy. Prove weak-to-strong generalization in a solvable model: e.g. a strong student with richer features (a random-features or two-layer model of larger width, or a model whose pretrained representation contains the target direction) trained on labels of a weaker model, and characterize when the student's error is strictly below the teacher's and how much of the gap to the strong ceiling it recovers.
statement_caveat: Several 2024-25 theoretical models (misfit-based bounds, high-dimensional ridge analyses) exist (to verify); no account covers the empirical phenomenon in networks.
source: C. Burns et al., Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Eliciting Strong Capabilities With Weak Supervision, arXiv:2312.09390 (2023)
locator: to verify: Burns et al., Section 6 (open questions).
why_important: It is the statistical core of supervising models more capable than their supervisors.
where_it_stands: Open (partial models).
note: Fame: OpenAI superalignment paper (ICML 2024), widely discussed.

title: Non-vacuous generalization bounds for large networks trained by SGD
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Dziugaite and Roy obtain non-vacuous PAC-Bayes bounds for stochastic networks on MNIST by optimizing the posterior; Arora et al. obtain bounds via compression. Prove, for a natural data model and SGD-trained two-layer networks of width much larger than n, a non-vacuous high-probability bound on the test error of the deterministic trained network (not a stochastic or compressed surrogate) that follows from properties provably produced by SGD (e.g. noise stability or flatness), with the bound tending to the true error rate as n grows.
statement_caveat: Existing non-vacuous bounds certify a modified predictor or rely on optimizing the bound itself; bounds for the trained network itself are rarely non-vacuous.
source: G. K. Dziugaite and D. M. Roy, Computing Nonvacuous Generalization Bounds for Deep (Stochastic) Neural Networks with Many More Parameters than Training Data, arXiv:1703.11008 (2017); S. Arora, R. Ge, B. Neyshabur and Y. Zhang, Stronger generalization bounds for deep nets via a compression approach, arXiv:1802.05296 (2018)
locator: to verify: Dziugaite–Roy, discussion of the gap between stochastic and deterministic networks.
why_important: A bound that certifies the network actually deployed is what learning theory is supposed to deliver.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: UAI 2017; started the PAC-Bayes revival in deep learning.

title: How much must calibrated language models hallucinate?
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Kalai and Vempala (arXiv:2311.14648, Theorem 1) prove, in a random-world model of factoids, that a language model calibrated in a coarsened sense hallucinates at rate at least the monofact rate (the fraction of facts seen once, the Good-Turing missing mass) minus its calibration error and a small term; their Lemma 3 gives a construction meeting the bound for arbitrary facts. For a stated class of partially structured fact distributions, in which some facts follow a rule learnable from the training data (systematic facts) and the rest are arbitrary, and a stated calibration statistic, determine the frontier between calibration error and hallucination rate, give an efficient estimator that attains it, and determine how the frontier moves when post-training has access to a stated source of side information.
statement_caveat: The lower bound is proved; tightness and structured cases are open (to verify follow-ups).
source: A. T. Kalai and S. S. Vempala, Calibrated Language Models Must Hallucinate, arXiv:2311.14648 (2023)
locator: to verify: Kalai–Vempala, the discussion of tightness.
why_important: It ties a practical failure of language models to the Good–Turing estimate of unseen probability mass.
where_it_stands: Open (tight version).
note: Fame: STOC 2024.

audit.status_ref: Kalai-Vempala2311.14648 Theorem1 PDF p14, fully opened with its proof p15, already has an additive TV/coarsened-calibration term in the hallucination lower bound under its random-world uncertainty model. Section7 Lemma3 PDF p16, opened in full with construction, gives hallucination<=MonoFacts and Mis_infinity<=3*sqrt(log(4/delta)/n) with probability>=1-delta. Thus a matching baseline upper construction and calibration-dependent lower bound are already in the cited source; unrestricted efficient/structured extensions are not settled.
audit.statement_ok: NO: statement inaccurately frames all tightness/calibration tradeoff as absent. Specify the random-world regularity/sparsity class, factoid partition/calibration definition, high-probability parameters and allowed factual side information. A lower frontier does not imply every post-training hallucination reduction must monotonically increase calibration error, especially with slack or new information.
audit.replace_with: Fix a tractable class of partially structured fact distributions and an explicit semantic calibration statistic. Ask an efficient estimator attaining a specified calibration-hallucination frontier, separating arbitrary unseen facts from inferable systematic facts and post-training side information.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: exact fixed-partition two-block frontier completed in T379_fixed_partition_tradeoff.md; it is a diagnostic consistent with the existing source and not a new unrestricted LM result. A finite structured-fact toy model is the next concrete target.
audit.locator: 2311.14648 Results PDF p4,Theorem1 p14 and proof p15,Section7/Lemma3 p16,Conclusions/limitations p18. Exact structured-facts future-work passage is p18, not an unverified generic tightness question.

title: Provable self-supervised learning with networks trained by gradient descent
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: HaoChen, Wei, Gaidon and Ma prove that the minimizer of a spectral contrastive loss over a rich function class yields representations with which a linear classifier achieves small error, under a population augmentation-graph assumption. Prove a comparable guarantee for a neural network trained by gradient descent on the contrastive (or a non-contrastive, e.g. SimSiam/BYOL) loss from finite data, for a natural data and augmentation model, including absence of collapse for the non-contrastive objectives.
statement_caveat: Analyses of non-contrastive dynamics exist in linear models (Tian et al.); network results for gradient training are limited (to verify).
source: J. Z. HaoChen, C. Wei, A. Gaidon and T. Ma, Provable Guarantees for Self-Supervised Deep Learning with Spectral Contrastive Loss, arXiv:2106.04156 (2021)
locator: to verify: HaoChen et al., conclusion.
why_important: Pretraining without labels is how foundation models are built; the augmentation-graph analysis is a spectral graph theory of learning.
where_it_stands: Open for gradient-trained networks.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2021 oral (to verify).

title: Robust undetectable watermarks for language models
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Christ, Gunn and Zamir (arXiv:2306.09194) construct language-model watermarks that are computationally undetectable without the key, from one-way functions and enough empirical entropy in the output, robust only to limited edits, and prove (Theorem 11) that every undetectable watermark can be removed by an attacker who can query watermarked generation on chosen prefixes. Mazor, Morgan and Pass (arXiv:2604.12051) build, from a suitable binary pseudorandom code, a watermark that survives a constant fraction of adversarial substitutions, insertions and deletions. For a stated edit channel (a fraction rho of token insertions, deletions and substitutions), a stated empirical-entropy condition and no generation oracle for the attacker, construct an undetectable watermark detectable after any rho-fraction edit from a weaker assumption than theirs (for example one-way functions alone), or prove that this is impossible; for semantic robustness, fix an equivalence relation on texts and the attacker's access to fresh generation, and prove a positive or a negative result in that model.
statement_caveat: Impossibility results against strong adversaries with quality oracles (Zhang et al. 2023, to verify) and robust schemes against restricted edit models (Christ and Gunn, pseudorandom error-correcting codes) exist.
source: M. Christ, S. Gunn and O. Zamir, Undetectable Watermarks for Language Models, arXiv:2306.09194 (2023)
locator: to verify: Christ–Gunn–Zamir, open problems.
why_important: Detecting machine-generated text is a practical problem whose limits are set by the entropy of the model's distribution.
where_it_stands: Open (partial positive and negative results).
note: Fame: COLT 2024.

audit.status_ref: Christ-Gunn-Zamir2306.09194 Theorem11 PDF p28, opened completely with Section6.2 p27 and Section7 p29, already proves efficient removal for any undetectable watermark when the model is prefix-specifiable and the attacker may query watermarked generation once per output token. Mazor-Morgan-Pass2604.12051 Theorem4 (informal) PDF p6, opened completely, supplies a conditional constant-fraction adversarial-edit construction from a suitable binary PRC and a constant fraction of sufficiently entropic tokens. Its corollary uses a nonstandard permuted-codes assumption; this does not prove unconditional robustness to all semantic paraphrasers.
audit.statement_ok: NO: formalize semantic preservation, fractional edit distance, output length, entropy, attacker access and cryptographic assumptions. The broad removability alternative is already answered under a prefix-specifiable generation oracle, which differs from bounded postprocessing of one text. Constant-fraction adversarial edits also have later conditional positive results, so restricted edits versus all efficient paraphrasers cannot be conflated.
audit.replace_with: Specify one edit channel and empirical-entropy condition, then compare a concrete construction/lower bound against current PRC assumptions. For semantic robustness, explicitly define the equivalence relation and whether fresh conditional-generation access is available.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: soundness-plus-resampling TV obstruction completed in T381_resampling_obstruction.md; check whether a proposed semantic channel satisfies it. Novel robustness beyond current coding predicates needs a narrower target and a fresh security review.
audit.locator: 2306.09194 Section6.2 pp27-28,Theorem11 p28,Section7 Open Problems p29.2604.12051 Theorem4 and conditional corollary p6;2602.15323 Theorem1.5 framework concerns an explicit block-closeness predicate and robust signatures, not arbitrary semantic robustness.

title: Sample-efficient reinforcement learning with linearly realizable optimal value functions
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Weisz, Amortila and Szepesvári prove that planning in MDPs whose optimal action-value function Q* is linear in known d-dimensional features requires exponentially many queries to a generative model when the number of actions is large. Determine whether online RL (or planning) with linearly realizable Q* and a constant (or polynomially bounded) number of actions can be done with poly(d, H) samples, and characterize the role of the action count and of a suboptimality gap.
statement_caveat: With a large action set the lower bound is exponential; with a constant number of actions and a gap, positive results exist under extra conditions (to verify Weisz et al. 2022 'TensorPlan', Yin et al.).
source: G. Weisz, P. Amortila and C. Szepesvári, Exponential Lower Bounds for Planning in MDPs With Linearly-Realizable Optimal Action-Value Functions, arXiv:2010.01374 (2020)
locator: to verify: Weisz et al., the stated open question on small action sets.
why_important: Linear Q* realizability is the simplest form of value-function approximation; whether it suffices for efficient RL is the basic question behind deep RL's function approximation.
where_it_stands: Open for small action sets as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: ALT 2021 best paper (to verify); a central problem of RL theory.

title: How many linear regions does a typical deep ReLU network have?
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: A ReLU network computes a piecewise linear function; its maximal number of linear regions grows exponentially in depth (Montúfar et al.; Raghu et al.), but Hanin and Rolnick prove that for random initialization (and empirically along training) the expected number of regions meeting a line or a bounded set grows only like (number of neurons)^{input dim}, independent of depth. Prove that this polynomial count persists along gradient-descent training for a natural data model (e.g. the expected density of regions near the data stays bounded by a constant times the number of neurons), or show that training can create exponentially many regions in some natural task.
statement_caveat: Hanin–Rolnick bound the count at initialization and for any weights drawn from distributions with bounded densities; the training-time statement is empirical.
source: B. Hanin and D. Rolnick, Deep ReLU Networks Have Surprisingly Few Activation Patterns, arXiv:1906.00904 (2019); M. Raghu, B. Poole, J. Kleinberg, S. Ganguli and J. Sohl-Dickstein, On the Expressive Power of Deep Neural Networks, arXiv:1606.05336 (2016)
locator: to verify: Hanin–Rolnick, discussion of training.
why_important: The gap between worst-case expressivity and what trained networks use is the expressivity side of the depth question.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2019 / ICML 2019 (Hanin–Rolnick).

title: Heavy-tailed weights at infinite width: the stable process limit
domain_name: Deep learning: random networks and infinite-width or infinite-depth limits
statement: If the weights of a deep fully connected network are iid with an α-stable law (α < 2) and scaled by n^{-1/α}, the infinite-width limit of the network is a stable process rather than a Gaussian process (Favaro, Fortini and Peluchetti). Characterize the training dynamics of such networks in the infinite-width limit: is there an analogue of the neural tangent kernel (a deterministic or random kernel limit), and does gradient descent in this limit perform feature learning?
statement_caveat: The kernel in the stable limit is random (it does not concentrate); training-dynamics results exist for special cases (to verify 2023-25 work).
source: S. Favaro, S. Fortini and S. Peluchetti, Stable behaviour of infinitely wide deep neural networks, arXiv:2003.00394 (2020)
locator: to verify: Favaro et al., conclusion.
why_important: Trained network weights are often heavy-tailed (Martin and Mahoney); the stable limit is the matching probabilistic model.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: AISTATS 2020.

title: The spectrum of the Fisher information of wide random networks
domain_name: Deep learning: random networks and infinite-width or infinite-depth limits
statement: Empirical NTK Gram matrix of a random network of fixed depth L >= 2: inputs x_1..x_n iid N(0, I_d / d), hidden widths m, Gaussian weights in the NTK parametrization, a fixed smooth activation, scalar output, all layers' Jacobians included; n, d and m tend to infinity proportionally (n/m -> gamma, d/m -> beta). Karakida, Akaho and Amari (arXiv:1806.01316, Theorems 1, 3 and 4) compute the mean, second moment and largest eigenvalue of the Fisher information under a forward-backward independence assumption. Determine the limiting spectral distribution of the n x n Gram matrix after removing a stated finite number of spikes (from the mean of the activation and its low-order Hermite components), and its outliers, without the independence assumption; the nonzero eigenvalues of the empirical Fisher are the same up to normalization.
statement_caveat: The two-layer and linear cases are known (Pennington and Worah; to verify); for deep networks the bulk spectrum is known only in special limits.
source: R. Karakida, S. Akaho and S. Amari, Universal Statistics of Fisher Information in Deep Neural Networks: Mean Field Approach, arXiv:1806.01316 (2018)
locator: to verify: Karakida et al., open questions on the bulk.
why_important: The Fisher spectrum sets the conditioning of natural-gradient and second-order training, and is built from the same per-sample Jacobians whose singular values T247 asks about.
where_it_stands: Open for the deep bulk as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: AISTATS 2019.

audit.status_ref: Karakida-Akaho-Amari1806.01316 Theorems1,3,4 PDF pp4-5, fully read with Assumption1, give mean, second moment and maximum eigenvalue under a forward/backprop independence assumption. Theorem4 gives order width M, not parameter count P. Corollary2 p5 already records rank <=CT. For fixed output dimension and P~m^2,n~gamma*m, the full parameter-normalized empirical Fisher ESD tends trivially to delta_0; the nonzero Gram bulk remains a distinct target.
audit.statement_ok: NO: order-P outliers misquote order-M Theorem4. Fisher and NTK Gram have the same nonzero eigenvalues only with matching normalization; their full normalized ESDs differ. Specify empirical versus population Fisher, input/output dimension scaling, parameterization, activation class, centering/outlier removal and nonzero/Gram spectral normalization.
audit.replace_with: Ask the nonzero empirical NTK Gram bulk for a specified fixed-depth network and proportional input/sample/width dimensions, separating finite-rank spikes. Retain source independence assumptions only as hypotheses rather than a theorem about unrestricted actual backprop.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: completed rank/normalization obstruction in T385_rank_diagnostic.md. A finite-depth linear or two-layer special case with a precisely normalized Gram matrix is concrete; generic deep nonlinear bulk is a PROGRAMME.
audit.locator: 1806.01316 Eq(2) PDF p2;architecture p3;Assumption1/Theorem1 p4;Corollary2,Theorems3/4 p5;dual FIM p6. Introduction pp1-2 motivates universal geometry, but does not pose this exact proportional-limit bulk conjecture.

title: Agnostic learning of a single neuron by gradient descent: the optimal approximation factor
domain_name: Deep learning: training dynamics and optimization
statement: Frei, Cao and Gu prove that gradient descent on the square loss of a single ReLU neuron, with arbitrary (agnostic) labels and suitably nice marginals, reaches error O(sqrt(OPT)) where OPT is the best neuron's error; Diakonikolas et al. give algorithms achieving O(OPT) and show computational lower bounds for OPT + ε. Determine whether gradient descent (or SGD) from a random start achieves C·OPT + ε for a constant C under Gaussian marginals, or prove that its error is necessarily ω(OPT) for some distributions.
statement_caveat: Constant-factor guarantees are known for some non-GD algorithms and for GD on surrogate losses under conditions (to verify 2022-25 work).
source: S. Frei, Y. Cao and Q. Gu, Agnostic Learning of a Single Neuron with Gradient Descent, arXiv:2005.14426 (2020)
locator: to verify: Frei–Cao–Gu, conclusion.
why_important: It is the simplest test of whether gradient descent is robust to label noise in a nonconvex model.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2020.

title: Does a curriculum provably speed up SGD on sparse parities?
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Sparse parities with a curriculum: k-sparse parity on inputs in {-1, 1}^d, k = k(d) with k fixed or growing slowly; a fraction rho of the samples have iid coordinates with mean mu (biased), the rest are uniform. Learner: a two-layer ReLU network of width poly(d), all layers trained jointly by online SGD with batch size 1, square or hinge loss, a stated initialization, step size bounded by eta and gradients computed to precision tau. Cornacchia and Mossel (arXiv:2301.13833) and Abbe, Cornacchia and Lotfi (arXiv:2306.16921, Theorems 3-5) prove positive results for layer-wise curricula and a lower bound for noisy-gradient learners depending on the number of steps, the parameter count, the gradient range and tau. Find a sufficient rho(d, k, mu) for this jointly trained architecture to reach error 1/4 in poly(d) steps, and prove a lower bound, in the same resource model (same steps, precision and gradient range), below which every such learner fails.
statement_caveat: The upper bounds hold for particular architectures and training schedules (to verify which); the lower bounds are statistical-query and noisy-gradient bounds and may not match the achievable fractions.
source: E. Cornacchia and E. Mossel, A Mathematical Model for Curriculum Learning for Parities, arXiv:2301.13833 (2023); E. Abbe, E. Cornacchia and A. Lotfi, Provable Advantage of Curriculum Learning on Parity Targets with Mixed Inputs, arXiv:2306.16921 (2023)
locator: to verify: the open questions in the conclusions of both papers.
why_important: It is the cleanest setting where the order and mixture of training data change the complexity of SGD by more than a polynomial factor.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: ICML 2023 (Cornacchia-Mossel), NeurIPS 2023 (Abbe-Cornacchia-Lotfi). Replaces a duplicate of T289 (16 Oct).

audit.status_ref: Cornacchia-Mossel2301.13833 Theorems3/4 PDF pp7-8, fully opened, prove two-stage layerwise curriculum results: Ramp/hinge or ReLU/covariance loss, special initialization and large batches. Abbe-Cornacchia-Lotfi2306.16921 Theorem3/Corollary1 p6 and Theorem4 p7 give layerwise mixed-input curriculum bounds; Theorem5 p7 fully read gives success <=1/2+(TPA/tau)*sqrt(1/binom(d,k)+C_k*rho^2*mu^(4k)+1/B). This is not a parameter-free matching online joint-SGD threshold.
audit.statement_ok: NO: define growing-k regime and the fixed polynomial budgets, initialization, loss, step schedule, noise and gradient range. An upper threshold for one joint-SGD algorithm and a lower threshold for every noisy-gradient algorithm need not coincide. The source negative bound depends on T,P,A,tau,B; B=1 makes its displayed estimate vacuous. Uniform parity is easy for unrestricted noiseless sample algorithms.
audit.replace_with: Fix k=k(d),mu(d),width,loss,initialization,online batch1,step bound and noise precision. First ask a sufficient rho for that particular jointly trained architecture; formulate any competing lower bound in exactly the same resource model.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: mixed-input correlation support-recovery bound completed in T387_moment_diagnostic.md. It isolates rho/mu/k dependence for a moment learner; it does not solve joint ReLU SGD or establish novelty.
audit.locator: 2301.13833 Theorems3/4 PDF pp7-8;Definition4 and continuous-curriculum conjecture p7.2306.16921 Theorem3/Cor1 p6;Remark4,Theorems4/5 p7. Exact offline-SGD lower-bound gap is Remark4 p7; current joint-training threshold is an extrapolation.

title: Learning from higher-order cumulants: the spiked cumulant model
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Székely, Bardone, Gerace and Goldt study data whose only signal lies in a fourth-order cumulant (a non-Gaussian direction hidden in otherwise Gaussian inputs) and show a sample-complexity gap: the hypothesis test is possible with n ~ d samples information-theoretically, but low-degree methods need n ~ d² and neural networks trained by SGD learn the direction only with roughly that many. Prove that two-layer networks trained by online SGD learn the spike with n = Θ(d²) (up to logs) and fail with n = o(d²), matching the low-degree lower bound.
statement_caveat: The low-degree lower bound is proved; the network upper bound is empirical or for modified algorithms (to verify).
source: E. Székely, L. Bardone, F. Gerace and S. Goldt, Learning from higher-order statistics, efficiently: hypothesis tests, random features, and neural networks, arXiv:2312.14922 (2023)
locator: to verify: Székely et al., conclusion.
why_important: Real data carry signal beyond second moments; this is the cleanest model of how networks extract it.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2024 (to verify).

title: Classifying high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures with a two-layer network: the Bayes-optimal gap
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: For data from a mixture of two Gaussians in R^d with n = αd samples, the Bayes-optimal test error is computed by replica methods and proved for convex losses on linear classifiers (Mignacco et al.; Loureiro et al.). Prove the asymptotic test error of a two-layer network trained by gradient descent (in a regime where features are learned) on the XOR-type Gaussian mixture (four clusters, labels by the sign of the product of two coordinates), and determine whether it reaches the Bayes-optimal error at the information-theoretic threshold.
statement_caveat: Exact asymptotics are known for linear and random-features classifiers; for trained networks only partial results exist (to verify Ben Arous, Gheissari and Jagannath on SGD summary statistics).
source: B. Loureiro, G. Sicuro, C. Gerbelot, A. Pacco, F. Krzakala and L. Zdeborová, Learning Gaussian Mixtures with Generalised Linear Models: Precise Asymptotics in High-dimensions, arXiv:2106.03791 (2021); F. Mignacco, F. Krzakala, Y. M. Lu and L. Zdeborová, The role of regularization in classification of high-dimensional noisy Gaussian mixture, arXiv:2002.11544 (2020)
locator: to verify: Loureiro et al., conclusion on nonlinear classifiers.
why_important: Gaussian mixtures are the solvable classification model; the XOR mixture is the simplest one that needs feature learning.
where_it_stands: Open for trained networks as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2021 (Loureiro et al.).

title: The statistical efficiency of score matching
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Koehler, Heckett and Risteski prove that the statistical efficiency of score matching for an exponential family is controlled by the log-Sobolev (or Poincaré) constant of the distribution: score matching is nearly as efficient as maximum likelihood for well-mixing distributions and can be exponentially worse for multimodal ones. Determine the sample complexity of learning a mixture of k well-separated Gaussians in R^d by (denoising) score matching at a small noise level versus by maximum likelihood, and whether annealing over noise levels (as in diffusion models) closes the gap polynomially.
statement_caveat: Annealed / diffusion-based score estimation for mixtures has positive results under assumptions (to verify Gatmiry, Kelner and Lee; Chen et al.).
source: F. Koehler, A. Heckett and A. Risteski, Statistical Efficiency of Score Matching: The View from Isoperimetry, arXiv:2210.00726 (2022)
locator: to verify: Koehler et al., conclusion.
why_important: Score matching is the training objective of diffusion models; its efficiency is governed by functional inequalities.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: ICLR 2023 (oral, to verify).

title: Diffusion models adapt to the intrinsic dimension of the data manifold
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: When the data lie on (or near) a k-dimensional smooth manifold in R^d, score-based diffusion models empirically generate well with sample complexity depending on k, not d. Prove that a diffusion model with a score estimated by empirical risk minimization over a natural network class, run with a standard discretization, achieves distribution error (e.g. in Wasserstein distance) n^{-c/k} up to logs, with the number of steps polylogarithmic or polynomial in k rather than d, and with matching minimax lower bounds.
statement_caveat: Results with intrinsic-dimension rates exist under assumptions (to verify 2024-25 work, e.g. Tang and Yang; Azangulov, Deligiannidis and Rousseau); the discretization's dependence on d is the open part.
source: I. Azangulov, G. Deligiannidis and J. Rousseau, Convergence of Diffusion Models Under the Manifold Hypothesis in High-Dimensions, arXiv:2409.18804 (2024)
locator: to verify: Azangulov et al., open questions.
why_important: It is the statistical explanation of why diffusion models work on images, whose dimension is far above their intrinsic dimension.
where_it_stands: Partly solved; the full statement is open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: the manifold question is the standard theory question for diffusion models.

title: What classifier-free guidance does to the sampled distribution
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Classifier-free guidance on a Gaussian mixture with common nondegenerate covariance Sigma, K components with positive weights and centers mu_1..mu_K, exact conditional and unconditional scores of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck forward process, and the guided score s_uncond + w (s_cond - s_uncond), w > 1. Wu et al. (arXiv:2403.01639, Theorems 3.3 and 4.2) prove that guidance raises the posterior class probability and lowers the differential entropy of the DDIM (probability-flow) output; Bradley and Nakkiran (arXiv:2408.09000) solve a Gaussian example in which the DDIM endpoint, the DDPM endpoint and the tilted law p(x)^(1-w) p(x | c)^w all differ. In continuous time and for the DDPM (stochastic) sampler, give the law of the output, or bounds on its entropy and on its distance from the tilted law, as explicit functions of w and of the center separation, and compare them with the DDIM endpoint.
statement_caveat: Results exist for Gaussian mixtures and for linear diffusions (to verify Chidambaram et al. 2024).
source: Y. Wu, M. Chen, Z. Li, M. Wang and Y. Wei, Theoretical Insights for Diffusion Guidance: A Case Study for Gaussian Mixture Models, arXiv:2403.01639 (2024)
locator: to verify: Wu et al., conclusion.
why_important: Guidance is used in essentially every text-to-image system; what distribution it samples from is not known.
where_it_stands: Open beyond special models.
note: Fame: ICML 2024 (to verify).

audit.status_ref: Wu-Chen-Li-Wang-Wei2403.01639 Theorem3.3 PDF p7, fully read, gives classification-confidence comparison under Assumption3.1 (isotropic common covariance and center conditions). Theorem4.2 p11, fully read, gives DDIM differential-entropy comparison for nondegenerate common covariance, positive mixture weights and finite initial entropies; it does not require the center assumptions. Bradley-Nakkiran2408.09000 equations(10)-(12) PDF p5 explicitly solve a Gaussian example with distinct DDIM,DDPM and tilted endpoint laws; Theorem3 p8, fully read with proof, identifies CFG with a particular predictor-corrector in the SDE limit.
audit.statement_ok: NO: repaired pointwise-tilt caveat is correct, but define DDIM versus DDPM, forward diffusion, initialization, mixture family, score error and concentration/diversity metrics. Source classification confidence is posterior class probability, not conditional density likelihood. Vanishing step size alone gives the specified reverse dynamics; a general high-likelihood concentration theorem needs additional assumptions and a quantitative claim.
audit.replace_with: Choose common-covariance mixtures, exact scores and one sampler, then ask a quantitative output-law/entropy bound as a function of guidance and center separation. Separate finite-step approximation from the continuous-time endpoint and DDPM entropy from the already-proved DDIM comparison.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: exact Gaussian endpoint check completed in T392_Gaussian_diagnostic.md, reproducing known Bradley-Nakkiran equations. A rigorously specified two-component perturbation or DDPM entropy special case is concrete; no new broad mixture characterization is established.
audit.locator: 2403.01639 Assumption3.1/Theorem3.3 PDF p7;Theorem4.2 p11;Sec6 pp13-14;future directions pp14-15. Exact outstanding direction: DDPM diversity characterization p15.2408.09000 Sec3.1/Eqs10-12 p5 and Theorem3 p8.

title: Minimax rates of generative adversarial networks with trained networks
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Liang proves rates for GAN-type density estimation in adversarial (integral probability metric) losses, showing GANs can achieve minimax rates when generator and discriminator classes are rich enough and the min-max problem is solved exactly. Prove a rate for a GAN with neural generator and discriminator whose parameters are computed by an actual gradient-based algorithm (e.g. simultaneous gradient descent-ascent from random initialization) for a natural target class, matching the minimax rate for that class up to logs.
statement_caveat: All statistical rates assume an exact or approximate global solution of the min-max problem (compare T312).
source: T. Liang, How Well Generative Adversarial Networks Learn Distributions, arXiv:1811.03179 (2018)
locator: to verify: Liang, conclusion (optimization as open).
why_important: It joins the statistics and the optimization of adversarial generative modelling into one guarantee.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: JMLR 2021.

title: Posterior collapse in variational autoencoders
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: A VAE with a flexible decoder can ignore its latent code ('posterior collapse'): the approximate posterior equals the prior and the decoder models the data alone. Lucas, Tucker, Grosse and Norouzi show that in linear VAEs collapse is caused by local maxima of the marginal likelihood related to probabilistic PCA and the observation-noise parameter. Characterize, for a nonlinear VAE with a two-layer decoder, the set of data distributions and noise levels at which the ELBO's global optimum (or every local optimum reachable by gradient ascent) collapses some latent dimensions, and prove the threshold.
statement_caveat: The linear case is solved; nonlinear analyses are limited (to verify).
source: J. Lucas, G. Tucker, R. Grosse and M. Norouzi, Don't Blame the ELBO! A Linear VAE Perspective on Posterior Collapse, arXiv:1911.02469 (2019)
locator: to verify: Lucas et al., discussion.
why_important: Posterior collapse is the main failure mode of latent-variable deep generative models.
where_it_stands: Open for nonlinear models as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2019.

title: Deep-learning PDE solvers: does training beat the curse of dimensionality?
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: E, Han and Jentzen's deep BSDE method solves semilinear parabolic PDEs in hundreds of dimensions; Grohs, Hornung, Jentzen and von Wurstemberger prove that deep networks can approximate solutions of Kolmogorov PDEs (e.g. Black-Scholes) with size polynomial in d and 1/ε. Prove that the full method — sampling, a network class and a training algorithm actually used (SGD) — computes the solution at a point to accuracy ε with cost polynomial in d and 1/ε for a natural class of Kolmogorov or semilinear PDEs.
statement_caveat: Approximation and generalization parts are proved; the optimization part (finding the network by SGD) is the gap.
source: W. E, J. Han and A. Jentzen, Deep learning-based numerical methods for high-dimensional parabolic partial differential equations and backward stochastic differential equations, arXiv:1706.04702 (2017); P. Grohs, F. Hornung, A. Jentzen and P. von Wurstemberger, A proof that artificial neural networks overcome the curse of dimensionality in the numerical approximation of Black-Scholes partial differential equations, arXiv:1809.02362 (2018)
locator: to verify: Grohs et al., introduction (training not covered).
why_important: It is the main applied-probability use of deep learning (high-dimensional option pricing, stochastic control); its full guarantee is missing.
where_it_stands: Open (training part).
note: Fame: E–Han–Jentzen (PNAS 2018 version) is very widely cited; Grohs et al. in Memoirs AMS.

title: Oversmoothing in deep graph neural networks: a sharp theory
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: As a graph neural network gets deeper, node representations converge to a common value (oversmoothing): Oono and Suzuki prove exponential convergence to a low-dimensional subspace for GCNs with ReLU and weights of small enough singular value. Determine, for random or trained weights at standard initialization and for message passing with attention (graph attention networks), whether oversmoothing occurs at an exponential rate, and characterize the depth at which node classification accuracy on a stochastic block model degrades.
statement_caveat: Wu et al. prove that attention does not prevent oversmoothing (to verify 2305.16102); finite-depth analyses on contextual SBMs exist.
source: K. Oono and T. Suzuki, Graph Neural Networks Exponentially Lose Expressive Power for Node Classification, arXiv:1905.10947 (2019); X. Wu, A. Ajorlou, Z. Wu and A. Jadbabaie, Demystifying Oversmoothing in Attention-Based Graph Neural Networks, arXiv:2305.16102 (2023)
locator: to verify: Oono–Suzuki, discussion of the singular-value condition.
why_important: Oversmoothing limits the depth of graph networks; it is a question about products of random Markov-type operators.
where_it_stands: Open (sharp form).
note: Fame: ICLR 2020; NeurIPS 2023.

title: Graph neural networks for community detection at the Kesten–Stigum threshold
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: Chen, Li and Bruna propose line-graph neural networks for community detection in the stochastic block model and observe performance near the information-theoretic thresholds. Prove that a graph neural network of depth O(log n) with trained (or explicitly chosen) weights achieves nontrivial correlation with the communities in the two-community sparse SBM for every signal-to-noise ratio above the Kesten–Stigum threshold, and determine whether a GNN trained by gradient descent from random initialization does so.
statement_caveat: Message passing algorithms (non-backtracking spectral methods, belief propagation) reach the threshold; GNNs can simulate them with chosen weights in principle; the trained-GNN statement is open (to verify).
source: Z. Chen, L. Li and J. Bruna, Supervised Community Detection with Line Graph Neural Networks, arXiv:1705.08415 (2017)
locator: to verify: Chen–Li–Bruna, discussion.
why_important: It tests whether learned message passing reaches the sharp statistical thresholds that belief propagation reaches.
where_it_stands: Open (trained case).
note: Fame: ICLR 2019.

title: Can graph neural networks beat greedy algorithms on random combinatorial problems?
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: Angelini and Ricci-Tersenghi show that a GNN-based solver for maximum independent set on random d-regular graphs performs worse than a simple greedy algorithm, and Boettcher similarly for max-cut. By the overlap gap property, local algorithms cannot find independent sets of density above (1+1/√2)·(log d)/d on random d-regular graphs for large d (Gamarnik and Sudan; improved to (1+ε)·(log d)/d by Rahman and Virág), and Gamarnik notes that this covers constant-depth GNNs, which were reported to solve such problems (Schuetz, Brubaker and Katzgraber). Determine whether GNNs of depth growing with n, trained by gradient methods, can exceed the greedy density (log d)/d on random d-regular graphs, or prove a lower bound for this class.
statement_caveat: The local-algorithm barrier is proved; depth-growing message passing and learned algorithms are not covered (to verify).
source: M. C. Angelini and F. Ricci-Tersenghi, Modern graph neural networks do worse than classical greedy algorithms in solving combinatorial optimization problems like maximum independent set, arXiv:2206.13211 (2022); D. Gamarnik, Barriers for the performance of graph neural networks (GNN) in discrete random structures, arXiv:2306.02555 (2023)
locator: to verify: Gamarnik, the GNN barrier paper's open questions.
why_important: It is the clean test of learned algorithms against the overlap gap barrier from spin-glass theory.
where_it_stands: Open for deep GNNs.
note: Fame: Nature Machine Intelligence 2023 (Angelini–Ricci-Tersenghi).

title: When does next-token prediction fail to learn planning tasks?
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: Bachmann and Nagarajan show that teacher-forced next-token prediction fails on a simple path-finding task on star graphs ('the Clever Hans cheat'), while other objectives succeed. Prove a separation: for a natural class of planning or lookahead tasks, any autoregressive model trained by teacher forcing on next-token loss (with a natural architecture and gradient training) has error bounded below by a constant, while a model trained with a multi-token or reverse-order objective learns the task with polynomial samples.
statement_caveat: The star-graph task is analyzed empirically and partly theoretically; a general separation theorem is open (to verify 2024-25 follow-ups).
source: G. Bachmann and V. Nagarajan, The Pitfalls of Next-Token Prediction, arXiv:2403.06963 (2024)
locator: to verify: Bachmann–Nagarajan, conclusion.
why_important: It asks whether the training objective of language models limits what they can learn, independent of scale.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: ICML 2024.

title: Regret of neural contextual bandits beyond the lazy regime
domain_name: Deep learning: high-dimensional learning, statistical physics and computational limits
statement: Zhou, Li and Gu prove that NeuralUCB, a UCB algorithm on the neural tangent features of an overparameterized network, achieves regret Õ(d̃ √T), where d̃ is the effective dimension of the NTK Gram matrix. Prove a regret bound for a neural bandit algorithm that learns features (e.g. a two-layer network in a regime where features move) that improves on all kernel-based bounds for a natural reward class, such as a single-index reward with unknown direction.
statement_caveat: Kernel-regime analyses give bounds governed by the NTK effective dimension, which can be polynomial in T; feature-learning bounds are lacking (to verify).
source: D. Zhou, L. Li and Q. Gu, Neural Contextual Bandits with UCB-based Exploration, arXiv:1911.04462 (2019)
locator: to verify: Zhou et al., conclusion.
why_important: Exploration with learned representations is the decision-making counterpart of the feature-learning question.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: ICML 2020.

title: Do deep ensembles approximate Bayesian model averaging?
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Wilson and Izmailov argue that deep ensembles (independently trained networks averaged) are a practical approximation to the Bayesian posterior predictive. Prove, in a solvable model (e.g. wide two-layer networks or random-features regression with random initializations), a quantitative relation between the predictive distribution of an ensemble of M gradient-trained networks and the Bayesian posterior predictive under a natural prior, including when ensembles are better or worse calibrated than the posterior.
statement_caveat: In the NTK limit, ensembles of trained networks correspond to a Gaussian process whose posterior differs from the NNGP posterior (He, Lakshminarayanan and Teh, to verify); outside special limits there is no comparison theorem.
source: A. G. Wilson and P. Izmailov, Bayesian Deep Learning and a Probabilistic Perspective of Generalization, arXiv:2002.08791 (2020)
locator: to verify: Wilson–Izmailov, discussion of ensembles.
why_important: Ensembles are the most reliable uncertainty method in practice; whether and why they are Bayesian is open.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2020.

title: When does the kernel Stein discrepancy control convergence?
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Gorham and Mackey prove that the kernel Stein discrepancy (KSD) with the inverse multiquadric kernel controls weak convergence to a target that is distantly dissipative, while Gaussian and Matérn kernels fail to detect non-convergence in dimension d ≥ 3. Characterize the kernels and targets (e.g. heavy-tailed or multimodal) for which KSD convergence to zero implies weak convergence, and give quantitative rates relating KSD to Wasserstein distance with explicit dependence on dimension.
statement_caveat: Sufficient conditions are known; tight dimension-dependent comparisons are open (to verify Kanagawa et al. 2022).
source: J. Gorham and L. Mackey, Measuring Sample Quality with Kernels, arXiv:1703.01717 (2017)
locator: to verify: Gorham–Mackey, open questions.
why_important: KSD is the standard tool for measuring the quality of samples from learned or approximate samplers and underlies SVGD (T310).
where_it_stands: Open (quantitative form).
note: Fame: ICML 2017.

title: Is there an information bottleneck in deep learning?
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Tishby and Zaslavsky propose that training compresses each layer's representation T, reducing I(X; T) while keeping I(T; Y). For a deterministic network with continuous inputs, I(X; T) is infinite or constant, so the claim needs a noisy or quantized formulation; Goldfeld et al. study noisy networks and tie 'compression' to clustering of representations. State a well-defined version (e.g. a network with additive Gaussian noise in each layer, or the quantized network) and prove or refute that gradient training on a natural classification task makes I(X; T_l) decrease in a late phase of training while test error improves.
statement_caveat: Saxe et al. (2018) show compression depends on the activation and need not occur; Goldfeld et al. relate it to geometric clustering.
source: N. Tishby and N. Zaslavsky, Deep Learning and the Information Bottleneck Principle, arXiv:1503.02406 (2015); Z. Goldfeld, E. van den Berg, K. Greenewald, I. Melnyk, N. Nguyen, B. Kingsbury and Y. Polyanskiy, Estimating Information Flow in Deep Neural Networks, arXiv:1810.05728 (2018)
locator: to verify: Goldfeld et al., discussion of what compression measures.
why_important: The information bottleneck was the most widely discussed information-theoretic account of deep learning; whether it is true in any precise form is unsettled.
where_it_stands: Open (precise form) as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: Tishby's talks (2017) and the Saxe et al. ICLR 2018 rebuttal made this a widely known controversy.

title: Simplicity bias of the parameter-function map
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Valle-Pérez, Camargo and Louis observe that for random networks the probability that randomly sampled parameters give a Boolean function f is exponentially concentrated on functions of low descriptional complexity, roughly P(f) ≤ 2^{−a·K(f) + b}, and propose this as the reason networks generalize. Prove a rigorous form: for a fully connected ReLU network with iid Gaussian weights on {0,1}^n inputs, show that the induced distribution over Boolean functions satisfies an upper bound P(f) ≤ exp(−c·C(f)) for an explicit complexity measure C (e.g. a sensitivity, decision-tree or Fourier-based measure), with C small for the functions networks are known to learn.
statement_caveat: De Palma, Kiani and Lloyd prove that random networks are biased towards low sensitivity (to verify 1812.10156); the full Kolmogorov-type statement is heuristic.
source: G. Valle-Pérez, C. Q. Camargo and A. A. Louis, Deep learning generalizes because the parameter-function map is biased towards simple functions, arXiv:1805.08522 (2018); G. De Palma, B. T. Kiani and S. Lloyd, Random deep neural networks are biased towards simple functions, arXiv:1812.10156 (2018)
locator: to verify: Valle-Pérez et al., Section 3 (the bound's assumptions).
why_important: If the prior over functions induced by random parameters favours simple functions, PAC-Bayes bounds follow; making that prior bound rigorous is the missing step.
where_it_stands: Open (rigorous form) as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: ICLR 2019.

title: Distributional simplicity bias: networks learn low-order statistics first
domain_name: Deep learning: training dynamics and optimization
statement: Refinetti, Ingrosso and Goldt show that networks trained by SGD first learn the parts of the target that depend on the input's mean and covariance, and only later higher-order cumulants; Nakkiran et al. show networks first fit a function close to the best linear classifier. Prove, for two-layer networks trained by SGD on data with a Gaussian-equivalent part and a non-Gaussian part (e.g. the spiked cumulant model of T388), that the network's predictions during an initial phase of length T_1 ∝ d agree with those of the best Gaussian-equivalent model, and that the higher-order structure is learned only after time T_2 ∝ d^{k−1} for a cumulant of order k.
statement_caveat: Empirical evidence and partial proofs for specific architectures exist (to verify).
source: M. Refinetti, A. Ingrosso and S. Goldt, Neural networks trained with SGD learn distributions of increasing complexity, arXiv:2211.11567 (2022); P. Nakkiran, G. Kaplun, D. Kalimeris, T. Yang, B. L. Edelman, F. Zhang and B. Barak, SGD on Neural Networks Learns Functions of Increasing Complexity, arXiv:1905.11604 (2019)
locator: to verify: Refinetti et al., conclusion.
why_important: It is the time-resolved form of simplicity bias, and links to the information-exponent theory of single-index learning (T230).
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: ICML 2023 (Refinetti et al.); NeurIPS 2019 (Nakkiran et al.).

title: A proof of hyperparameter transfer under the maximal-update parameterization
domain_name: Deep learning: training dynamics and optimization
statement: Yang et al. propose the maximal-update parameterization (μP), in which the optimal learning rate and other hyperparameters for a network of width n converge as n → ∞, so they can be tuned on a small model and transferred to a large one; depth-wise analogues use scaled residual branches. Prove hyperparameter transfer for a natural model: e.g. for a deep network in μP trained on a natural task, show that the loss after a fixed number of steps, as a function of the learning rate, converges uniformly as width → ∞, with the minimizer converging at an explicit rate.
statement_caveat: Infinite-width limits under μP are proved (Tensor Programs); convergence of the optimal hyperparameter itself, with rates, is open (to verify; compare depth-μP by Yang et al. 2310.02244 and Bordelon et al. 2309.16620).
source: G. Yang et al., Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer, arXiv:2203.03466 (2022); G. Yang, D. Yu, C. Zhu and S. Hayou, Tensor Programs VI: Feature Learning in Infinite-Depth Neural Networks, arXiv:2310.02244 (2023); B. Bordelon, L. Noci, M. B. Li, B. Hanin and C. Pehlevan, Depthwise Hyperparameter Transfer in Residual Networks, arXiv:2309.16620 (2023)
locator: to verify: Tensor Programs V, Section 'limitations'.
why_important: μP is used to tune large models in practice; why the optimum transfers is only heuristically explained.
where_it_stands: Open as far as the writer knows.
note: Fame: used in training large language models; Tensor Programs V is widely cited.

title: Sample-complexity separation between convolutional and fully connected networks
domain_name: Deep learning: approximation, expressivity, attention and architectures
statement: Li, Zhang and Arora prove a separation for a fixed Gaussian quadratic target: a convolutional network trained by gradient descent on its second layer learns it from O(1) samples, while every orthogonally equivariant learner needs Omega(d^2) samples. For that target, prove or refute a lower bound Omega(d^2 / epsilon) at excess risk epsilon. Then, for Gaussian inputs, square loss and targets that are sums of degree-q functions of non-overlapping patches of size p (q >= 2; degree-one additive targets are learnable from O(d) samples by an equivariant learner), give matching sample bounds for a concrete convolutional network with all layers trained jointly and for equivariant learners, at a stated risk and confidence, as functions of p, the number of patches and q.
statement_caveat: Separations are known in special models; the locality-based sample complexity is characterized for kernels (to verify Misiakiewicz and Mei on convolutional kernels).
source: Z. Li, Y. Zhang and S. Arora, Why Are Convolutional Nets More Sample-Efficient than Fully-Connected Nets?, arXiv:2010.08515 (2020)
locator: to verify: Li–Zhang–Arora, conclusion.
why_important: It is the theoretical basis of architectural inductive bias, the reason CNNs beat MLPs on images.
where_it_stands: Open (sharp form).
note: Fame: ICLR 2021.

audit.status_ref: Li-Zhang-Arora2010.08515 Theorem5.2 PDF p7, fully read, gives a fixed Gaussian/quadratic classification task with orthogonal-equivariant Omega(d^2) lower bound and constant-in-d CNN ERM sample upper bound, realizable by gradient descent on the second layer only. Theorems5.3/5.4 p8, fully read, already give parameterized diagonal-quadratic families and matching-order different architecture/equivariance sample separations for classification and regression. Table1 p5 distinguishes SGD rotational equivariance from Adam/AdaGrad permutation equivariance. Additional recent theorem fully opened: Waber-Piccolo-Dandi-Krzakala2610.08420 Ass1 p5/Ass2-3 p7 and Theorem3.2 p8 compare tied/augmented online spherical-SGD weak direction recovery at ~d^(p-1) samples against untied ~r d^(p-1), with a fixed Hermite information exponent p>=3, cyclic orbit r=d^delta,0<delta<1/2, special step sizes and correlation loss. This is not a general lower bound for every equivariant learner or a prediction-risk theorem.
audit.statement_ok: NO: identify the input law, patch overlap, function class/norm/degree, noise, risk/confidence, trainable layers and algorithm. The cited CNN theorem permits second-layer-only GD; it is not arbitrary joint CNN SGD. Degree-one additive targets need only O(d) noiseless Gaussian regression samples for an equivariant learner, so no universal quadratic separation follows from locality alone.
audit.replace_with: Use the explicit fixed Gaussian quadratic target and ask whether the lower bound sharpens to Omega(d^2/epsilon), or fix an additive patch class and a concrete jointly trained CNN with a prescribed risk. Do not combine kernel ERM and trained-feature claims.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: degree-one locality diagnostic completed in T407_equivariance_diagnostic.md. Reproduce the source quadratic packing calculation or one disjoint-patch regression model; general image-like data and joint CNN training is a PROGRAMME.
audit.locator: 2010.08515 Definitions3.2/3.3 p4;Table1 p5;Theorem5.2 p7;Theorems5.3/5.4/5.5 p8;Remark5.2/conclusion p9. Exact open question is a fixed single task with Omega(d^2/epsilon) lower bound, PDF p8, not an unspecified natural-image minimax class.

title: The sample-complexity gain from invariance
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Bietti, Venturi and Bruna show that for kernels invariant to a finite group G acting on the sphere, the sample complexity of learning a smooth invariant target is reduced by roughly a factor |G| in high-dimensional regimes (Mei, Misiakiewicz and Montanari give a similar result). Determine the sample-complexity gain from invariance for neural networks trained by gradient descent (rather than kernels) on invariant targets, and for continuous groups, where the gain is in the effective dimension.
statement_caveat: Kernel results are established; network results are partial (to verify).
source: A. Bietti, L. Venturi and J. Bruna, On the Sample Complexity of Learning under Invariance and Geometric Stability, arXiv:2106.07148 (2021)
locator: to verify: Bietti et al., conclusion.
why_important: Geometric deep learning rests on the claim that building symmetry into a model reduces the data it needs.
where_it_stands: Open for trained networks.
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2021.

title: Testing the manifold hypothesis
domain_name: Deep learning: generalization, implicit bias and overparametrization
statement: Fefferman, Mitter and Narayanan give an algorithm that, from n iid samples of a distribution in a separable Hilbert space, tests whether the data lie near a d-dimensional manifold of volume at most V and reach at least τ, with sample complexity independent of the ambient dimension but exponential in d. Determine the optimal sample complexity and running time of this test as a function of d, V, τ and the accuracy, and give a test whose running time is polynomial in the ambient dimension and the number of samples.
statement_caveat: Sample complexity bounds are close to optimal up to exponents; computational efficiency is the main open part (to verify).
source: C. Fefferman, S. Mitter and H. Narayanan, Testing the Manifold Hypothesis, arXiv:1310.0425 (2013)
locator: to verify: Fefferman–Mitter–Narayanan, Section on open questions.
why_important: The manifold hypothesis underlies the explanations of why deep learning escapes the curse of dimensionality (compare T391).
where_it_stands: Open (computational part).
note: Fame: J. Amer. Math. Soc. 2016.

title: Limits of autoregressive models: distributions with easy densities but hard next-token conditionals
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Lin, Jaech, Li, Gormley and Eisner (Limitations of autoregressive models and their alternatives) give distributions over strings whose unnormalized weights are efficiently computable but whose next-symbol conditional probabilities are hard to compute at some prefixes. For a length-indexed family of targets with efficiently computable weights, decide whether NP not contained in P/poly suffices for an inverse-polynomial gap in the forward divergence KL(target | model) between the target and every polynomial-size autoregressive model with polynomial-precision parameters, or whether an average-case (cryptographic) assumption is necessary, since hardness at the worst prefix need not give an average gap. Energy-based models represent such targets trivially; for them the question is efficient sampling or normalization, stated separately.
statement_caveat: Exact representability is ruled out; quantitative approximation bounds are open (to verify).
source: C.-C. Lin, A. Jaech, X. Li, M. R. Gormley and J. Eisner, Limitations of Autoregressive Models and Their Alternatives, arXiv:2010.11939 (2020)
locator: to verify: Lin et al., conclusion.
why_important: Language models are autoregressive; this asks what they cannot model in principle.
where_it_stands: Open (quantitative form).
note: Fame: NAACL 2021.

audit.status_ref: Lin-Jaech-Li-Gormley-Eisner2010.11939 Theorem1 PDF p6, fully read, separates EC normalizable weighted languages from ELNCP under NP not subset P/poly. Theorem4 PDF p7, fully read, already rules out constant-factor approximation to positive local probabilities, including randomized computation, compact parameters and full-support variants. Sections4.1/4.2 pp7-8 explain EBM and latent alternatives; Theorem7 p8 gives a light marginalization of an ELN distribution with NP-complete support. These do not establish a specified average-case KL lower bound.
audit.statement_ok: NO: authors now repaired, but fix KL direction, distribution family indexed by length, conditioning, parameter bits, precision and the desired positive gap. Worst-prefix conditional hardness does not imply average KL hardness. Polynomial-size EBM representation is immediate for efficiently computable unnormalized weights; efficient normalization/sampling/learning is a separate question.
audit.replace_with: Define a length-indexed efficiently weighted target and ask whether NP not subset P/poly suffices for an inverse-polynomial forward-KL gap or whether an explicit average-case cryptographic assumption is necessary. State what efficient operation the alternative model must retain.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: exact rare-prefix KL-chain-rule diagnostic completed in T410_KL_diagnostic.md. A specified finite family/average-case reduction is concrete; a universal complexity classification is a PROGRAMME.
audit.locator: 2010.11939 Theorems1/2 PDF p6;Sec3.4/Theorem4 p7;Sec4.1 pp7-8;Sec4.2/Theorem7 p8;Sec6 p10. Original remaining question p10 concerns most languages in P/average complexity, not a stated KL theorem.

title: The computational complexity of posterior sampling with diffusion priors
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Gupta, Jalal, Parulekar, Price and Xun show that sampling from the posterior p(x | y) for y = A x + noise, with a diffusion prior given by an accurate score oracle, can be computationally hard under cryptographic assumptions although unconditional sampling is easy. Fix a structured prior class (for example mixtures of a stated number of Gaussians, or priors whose scores are L2-accurate along the forward process and which satisfy a stated smoothness or log-Sobolev condition), a posterior error metric (total variation or W2) and runtime counted in score-oracle calls. Prove a polynomial-time posterior sampler in an explicit regime of operators and noise levels (for example noise variance above a threshold relative to the prior's scale) outside the existing rejection-sampling bounds, and hardness just outside that regime within the same prior class.
statement_caveat: Hardness is established in the worst case; positive results under special conditions exist (to verify).
source: S. Gupta, A. Jalal, A. Parulekar, E. Price and Z. Xun, Diffusion Posterior Sampling is Computationally Intractable, arXiv:2402.12727 (2024)
locator: to verify: Gupta et al., open problems.
why_important: Diffusion priors are used for inverse problems (imaging, inpainting); this decides when that can be done exactly.
where_it_stands: Open (positive side).
note: Fame: ICML 2024 (to verify).

audit.status_ref: Gupta-Jalal-Parulekar-Price-Xun2402.12727 Theorem1.7 PDF p5, fully read with Definitions1.1-1.6 pp4-5, gives rejection runtime poly(d)*(O(1)/(beta*sqrt(delta)))^m for inverse-polynomial noise/failure and well-modeled scores. Theorems1.8/1.9 p5, fully read, give superpolynomial hardness from OWFs for m>d^0.01 and exponential-in-m hardness from exponentially hard OWFs, respectively, with beta~1/log^2 d. The posterior accuracy is (tau,delta) coupling-distance on most observations, not exact equality.
audit.statement_ok: NO: repaired authors match. Define prior class, score oracle, observation distribution, measurement norm, approximation metric and runtime dependence. A small missing inpainting mask has m=d-k observed coordinates and does not mean few measurements. Operator and noise alone need not characterize efficiency uniformly over otherwise unrestricted priors.
audit.replace_with: Specify a structured prior class and posterior error metric beyond generic well-modeledness, then prove a polynomial-time posterior sampler in a noise/operator regime outside existing rejection bounds. Gaussian priors supply a baseline and few measurements already give some polynomial regimes.
audit.solver_shape: DAYS: Gaussian conditional law and polynomial-regime calculation completed in T411_Gaussian_diagnostic.md. These are classical/source corollaries; use a specified non-Gaussian prior to seek new progress.
audit.locator: 2402.12727 Definitions1.1-1.5 PDF p4;Definition1.6/Theorems1.7-1.9 p5;Section5 Conclusion and Future Work PDF p14 (printed p12).

title: Convergence of discrete diffusion models
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Campbell et al. formulate diffusion on discrete state spaces as a continuous-time Markov chain whose reverse rates are learned, and give error bounds with tau-leaping. Prove sharp bounds on the total-variation (or KL) error of discrete diffusion sampling for sequences of length L over an alphabet of size S, in terms of the score-estimation error and the number of steps, with the number of steps nearly linear in L (or sublinear, for parallel sampling), and matching lower bounds.
statement_caveat: Bounds with polynomial dependence exist (to verify 2024-25 work on masked diffusion and uniformization); optimal dependence is open.
source: A. Campbell, J. Benton, V. De Bortoli, T. Rainforth, G. Deligiannidis and A. Doucet, A Continuous Time Framework for Discrete Denoising Models, arXiv:2205.14987 (2022)
locator: to verify: Campbell et al., conclusion.
why_important: Discrete diffusion is an alternative to autoregressive language models; how many parallel steps it needs is the question of whether it can be faster.
where_it_stands: Open (sharp form).
note: Fame: NeurIPS 2022.

title: Theory of consistency models and one-step generation
domain_name: Deep learning: sampling, diffusion and generative models
statement: Song, Dhariwal, Chen and Sutskever train consistency models that map any point on a probability-flow ODE trajectory to its origin, enabling one- or few-step sampling.
